docs.text: Streets of Rage 2 New Era Modding Docs ¶ Welcome to the modding documentation for Streets of Rage 2 New Era . These docs cover the full modding workflow: playing mods made by other people, creating and exporting your own mods, editing characters, building levels and cutscenes, replacing classic game content, adding audio, creating palettes, and using Lua scripts when editor-driven behavior is not enough. Choose Your Path ¶ I want to play a mod : start with Installing Community Mods . I want to make a full custom mod : follow Create a Custom Mod . I want to reskin the classic game : start with the Reskin Workflow . I want to edit a character : open the Character Editor docs. I want to build levels or cutscenes : open the Level Editor docs. I want to replace music or sounds : open the Audio Editor docs. I want to script behavior : start with Lua Scripting . How the Docs Are Organized ¶ The site has two main learning paths. The Editors section documents each tool as a reference: the in-game editor, Character Editor, Level Editor, Audio Editor, and Lua scripting. Use this when you want to understand a screen, setting, panel, or file. The Build a Mod and Reskin the Classic Game sections are practical guides. Use them when you have a concrete goal, such as creating a playable character, adding cutscenes, replacing classic music, or exporting a mod for friends. Important Folders ¶ Mods : exported mods ready to play. Editor : source mods that can be opened from the in-game editor menu. Entities : custom characters, enemies, items, and containers inside a source mod. Levels : custom level art, level definitions, cutscenes, and special screen data. Sounds and Musics : custom audio used by mods. Palettes : color palettes created in the built-in palette editor. Scripts : Lua scripts used by character logic, events, and custom behavior. Multiplayer Compatibility ¶ When playing a mod online, every player must use the same exported mod version. New Era checks whether the mod checksum matches, so a tiny file difference is enough to make two copies incompatible.

docs.text: Editors Reference ¶ Start in the game's mod editor: create or select a mod, then open the tool for the content you want to change. Each tool writes into that mod's folder. The standalone editors save changes automatically. Make a copy of your mod before a large experiment. The in-game Gameplay Rules screen has explicit Save Rules and Cancel buttons. Editor Areas ¶ In-Game Mod Editor - create mods, configure settings, edit palettes, open the bundled tools, test, and export. Character Editor - create new characters or replace classic character visuals. Level Editor - create new levels or reskin the classic ones. Title screen and character select screen is also configured here. Audio Editor - add custom sounds and music or replace classic music, voices, and SFX. TAS Editor - build a frame-by-frame tool-assisted run and inspect the game state as it plays. Common Workflow ¶ Open the in-game editor and either create a new mod or choose an existing mod. Configure mod settings and optional difficulty settings . Use Open Tools to launch the Character Editor, Level Editor, or Audio Editor for the selected mod. Edit color palettes when needed. Use Test Mod regularly to play the mod with the same data the game will load, except for color palettes. When the mod is ready, export it . Mode Terms ¶ Several tools ask whether you want to edit Mod content or Classic Reskin content. Mod mode adds new content to your mod, such as new characters, new levels, custom sounds, and custom music. Classic Reskin mode replaces content from the original SOR2 while keeping the original gameplay intact. For tool-specific differences, see Mod Characters vs Classic Reskin , Mod Levels vs Classic Reskin , and Mod Audio vs Classic Reskin . See Editor feature coverage for remaining gaps and settings that still need a configuration file.

docs.text: Editor feature coverage ¶ The game can load some settings that do not yet have a dedicated editor control. This page separates those gaps from options that belong to a play session or are not implemented by the game. Area Available in the editors Remaining gaps or limits Mod rules Gameplay Rules covers combat toggles, player limits, health, global multipliers, randomization, score lives and classic behaviour. Difficulty Settings handles per-difficulty/per-player balance. additionalCharacters , additionalMechanics , allowedCharacters and global pre/post-update Lua hooks still need config.json . Characters Sprites, animations, boxes, behaviour, logic events, script references and audio references. The Add Event picker includes all 24 current concrete event types, including Spawn Enemy. Audio pickers recognize WAV, MP3 and OGG in both Sounds and Musics. Lua source is edited in a text editor. Palettes are edited in-game. Levels Scenes, spawns, walls, scrolling, layers, animation, music and special screens. Widescreen centering and special-screen character-image flags are exposed in the Inspector. copyAltPalette is preserved in files but currently has no runtime consumer; it is not offered as a working toggle. Audio Sound/music imports, Classic replacements, playback and loop points. Audition loops in the game too; editor playback alone does not test gameplay triggering or mixing. Palettes Editable variants, reference images, colour groups and frame previews. Default palettes are read-only. Deleting a variant renumbers later variants; spawn references need checking. Rules with engine limits ¶ Enemy count: the current game queues one extra spawn when enemiesMultiplier is at least 2. Its session serializer also clamps this field to 1–2. Values such as 4 or 8 do not currently produce four or eight times the enemies. The mod-rules editor therefore offers 1–2. Randomizer seed: the session format stores one byte, so the editor accepts 0–255. Shared lives, duplicate characters and stiffness: these are session configuration values, not fields in GameSessionData . Making them permanent mod rules needs engine/configuration support first. Best next usability improvements ¶ Add undo/redo and a visible saved/error indicator across all three standalone tools. Autosave is convenient, but users need a clear recovery path. Add guided character and stage templates that start with a playable example. Add asset pickers for pack imports and allowed characters, with missing-dependency checks, instead of requiring names or hashes in JSON. Add a pre-export check that links missing sprites, audio, scripts and invalid references back to their editor fields. For manual configuration, use the pack config reference . This is a source review of editor coverage, not a guarantee that every supported combination has been tested in gameplay.

docs.text: Audio Editor ¶ The Audio Editor manages custom sounds, custom music with their loop points, and Classic Reskin audio replacements. It is launched from the in-game editor menu and saves into the currently selected mod folder. Audio is added by drag and drop. WAV, MP3 and OGG are supported. The editor stores sounds under Sounds , music under Musics , loop metadata beside each music file, and classic replacement maps under Audio Replacements/Classic . Throughout the editors, audio is referenced by file base name without the extension — so laser_fire.wav is laser_fire . Renaming a file after assigning it breaks every reference to it. Start Here ¶ The Audio Editor Workspace — the tabs, how drag-and-drop behaves, and the waveform timeline's controls. Then read Mod Audio vs Classic Reskin before adding anything: Mod mode adds sounds and music to your own mod. Classic Reskin mode replaces the original SOR2 music, voice and SFX — and applies to every mod that uses classic content, such as 30th Anniversary. Reference Pages ¶ The Audio Editor Workspace Mod Audio vs Classic Reskin Custom Sounds Custom Music Loop Points Replace Classic Music Replace Classic Sounds Related editor areas: Character Audio Events , Scene Settings , Test Mod .

docs.text: Custom Music ¶ Custom music is used by levels, cutscenes, character events, scripts, and Classic Reskin music replacements. Adding Music ¶ Open the Audio Editor from the in-game editor menu. Choose Mod . Open the Music tab. Drag WAV, MP3, or OGG files into the list. The editor copies files into the mod's Musics folder. The file base name becomes the music name used by the Level Editor and character logic events. Music Metadata ¶ When you enable a loop point, the editor saves a small JSON file beside the music file. The metadata stores loopStartTimeInSeconds and loopEndTimeInSeconds , which the game uses when looping the track. Use Loop Points for detailed loop editing. Assigning Music ¶ Use the Level Editor's Scene Settings to assign scene music. Use Audio Events if a character animation should trigger music directly. Practical Advice ¶ Keep music names stable once assigned. If you rename a music file, you have to manually update all scene settings, logic events, and replacement mappings that point to it. Test music in-game after adding it. Related pages: Replace Classic Music , Test Mod .

docs.text: Custom Sounds ¶ Custom sounds are short audio files used by characters, items, weapons, projectiles, scripts, and logic events. Add them in the Audio Editor's Mod mode. Adding Sounds ¶ Open the Audio Editor from the selected mod's in-game editor menu. Choose Mod . Open the Sounds tab. Drag WAV, MP3, or OGG files into the list. The editor copies files into the mod's Sounds folder. If a dropped file already exists with the same checksum, the editor reuses the existing file. If the name conflicts but the audio differs, it creates a unique name. Naming ¶ Other editors reference sounds by file base name, without the extension. Keep sound names short, readable, and stable. Renaming a file after assigning it to hitboxes or events can break references. Good examples: axel_special_hit laser_fire boss_laugh knife_wall_hit Preview and Delete ¶ Activate a sound entry to preview it. Select entries and press Delete to remove them. Deleting a sound can leave broken references in characters or scripts, so search affected content before exporting. Using Sounds ¶ Assign sounds in Audio Events , hitboxes, projectile settings, and level or script logic where applicable. Related pages: Replace Classic Sounds , Test Mod .

docs.text: Loop Points ¶ Loop points tell the game where a music track should restart. The track plays from the beginning, and when it reaches Loop End it jumps back to Loop Start and continues from there — indefinitely. Editing a Loop ¶ Open the Audio Editor. Choose Mod mode, or Classic Reskin mode. Select a music file. In Mod mode, from the Music tab; in Classic Reskin mode, from the Loop Points tab. Enable Loop . Set Loop Start (red flag) — the point the music jumps to . Set Loop End (blue flag) — the point the music jumps from . Use playback and Test Loop to check the seam. Enabling looping saves a small JSON file beside the music file containing loopStartTimeInSeconds and loopEndTimeInSeconds , written to millisecond precision. Loop End Trims the Track ¶ Loop End defaults to the full length of the music , and anything after it is never played in game. It is also trimmed when the mod is exported . That makes Loop End do double duty: it is both the loop boundary and an implicit end-of-track marker. If your source file has a fade-out or a tail you do not want, setting Loop End before it removes that audio from the exported mod, which keeps the download smaller. Conversely, if you set Loop End early by accident, you silently lose the rest of the track on export. Placing the Markers ¶ Both flags are dragged on the waveform timeline. See The Audio Editor Workspace for the full timeline controls; the essentials: Wheel zooms 15% per notch, anchored at the pointer, up to about 1000×. Right-drag or middle-drag scrolls along the track. Click on empty timeline seeks playback there. Markers grab within about 15 pixels, and when they overlap the priority is Loop End, then Loop Start, then the playhead . If you cannot grab the marker you want, zoom in until the markers separate. This is the usual frustration when setting a short loop. Seconds vs Samples ¶ The unit selector switches how loop times are displayed and entered. Seconds are easier to read and to adjust roughly. Samples are exact — use them when a loop must land precisely on a beat or a zero crossing, especially for WAV files, where playback can use sample-accurate loop values. A practical approach: find the loop roughly in seconds, then switch to samples to nudge it onto the exact point. Test Loop ¶ Test Loop plays from just before Loop End and jumps back to Loop Start , so you hear only the seam rather than waiting through the whole track. Listen for three things, which fail independently: Rhythm — does the beat stay in time across the jump? Ambience — do sustained pads or room tone change level abruptly? Tails — does a decaying note get cut off mid-decay? A loop that passes the rhythm check can still be obvious because of a tail. If a seam is stubborn, moving Loop End slightly later so it lands after a note has decayed is usually easier than moving Loop Start. Related pages: The Audio Editor Workspace , Custom Music , Replace Classic Music , Scene Settings .

docs.text: Mod Audio vs Classic Reskin ¶ The Audio Editor starts by asking what you want to edit: Mod audio or Classic Reskin audio. Mod Audio ¶ Use Mod to add and manage all sounds and music included with your mod. Mod audio is useful for: Character voices and attack effects. Custom enemy, item, weapon, or projectile sounds. Music used by custom levels. Music triggered by character logic events. Shared audio that scripts or editor events reference by name. In Mod mode, the editor shows sound and music lists. Drag WAV, MP3, or OGG files into the appropriate tab. The file base name becomes the audio name used by other editors. Classic Reskin Audio ¶ Use Classic Reskin mode to replace original SOR2 voice, SFX, and music entries. This mode shows replacement tabs for Voice, SFX, and Music. Drop audio onto a replacement entry or choose an existing sound/music from the mod. Classic Reskin audio is useful for: Replacing original stage music. Replacing original character voices. Replacing common SFX. Creating a complete audio reskin for classic based mods. Shared Music Loop Editing ¶ For Mod mode, loop points are edited directly from the music list. In Classic Reskin mode, the music list shows the original music replacements. There is an additional loop points tab for editing the loop start and loop end of the music used as replacements. Next pages: Custom Sounds , Custom Music , Replace Classic Music , Replace Classic Sounds .

docs.text: Replace Classic Music ¶ Classic music replacements map original SOR2 music entries to music files in your mod. Replacement Workflow ¶ Open the Audio Editor from the in-game editor. Choose Classic Reskin . Open the Music replacement tab. Find the original track you want to replace. Drag and drop a music file onto that entry, or choose an existing music from your mod. Set a loop point from the music list if the track should loop. The editor saves mappings in Audio Replacements/Classic/music-replacements.json . Each mapping points from a classic music key to a replacement mod and music name. Classic Music Names ¶ The replacement list labels original tracks using their original track name. Loop Points for Replacements ¶ After assigning a replacement track, open the Loop Points tab to configure how each track loops. See Loop Points . Testing ¶ Export your mod. See Export Mod . Exit the in-game editor. From the SOR2 New Era main menu, access the Skin selection: Options -> Game Skin . Select your mod. Start a game in a mod using the classic content (e.g. 30th Anniversary, Ninpo Kage Bunshin or Classic). Confirm that your replacement musics play. Related pages: Loop Points , Custom Music .
docs.title: Replace Classic Music

docs.text: Replace Classic Sounds ¶ Classic sound replacements map original SOR2 voice and SFX entries to sounds in your mod. Use the Audio Editor's Classic Reskin mode. Replacement Workflow ¶ Open the Audio Editor from the in-game editor menu. Choose Classic Reskin . Open the Voice or SFX replacement tab. Find the original sound you want to replace. Drop a sound file onto that entry, or choose an existing sound from your mod. The editor copies dropped files into the mod's Sounds folder and saves replacement mappings in Audio Replacements/Classic/sound-replacements.json . Voice vs SFX ¶ Voice channel is used for original voice and vocal entries such as grunts, defeated voices, laughs, and character callouts, as well as main hit impacts. SFX channel is used for general gameplay effects. Testing ¶ Export your mod. See Export Mod . Exit the in-game editor. From the SOR2 New Era main menu, access the Skin selection: Options -> Game Skin . Select your mod. Start a game in a mod using the classic content (e.g. 30th Anniversary, Ninpo Kage Bunshin or Classic). Confirm that your replacement sounds play. Related pages: Custom Sounds , Audio Events , Test Mod .

docs.text: The Audio Editor Workspace ¶ The Audio Editor opens on a Choose what to edit screen with two cards: Mod and Classic Reskin . The choice changes which tabs exist, so it is not a cosmetic mode switch. The 🏠 button returns you to this screen at any time. Imports, replacement assignments and loop settings save automatically. Tabs by Mode ¶ Tab Mod mode Classic Reskin mode Sounds Your mod's sound library Your mod's sound library Voice — Replacements for original voice entries Sfx — Replacements for original SFX entries Music Your mod's music library Replacements for original music entries Loop Points — (loops are edited from the Music tab) Loop editing for tracks used as replacements In Mod mode the last tab is called Music and holds your tracks. In Classic Reskin mode that same tab becomes Loop Points , and it lists only the music currently used by replacements — the editor says as much on the tab itself. Replacement tabs show how many entries are assigned in their title, so you can see progress without opening each one. Adding Audio ¶ Drag WAV, MP3 or OGG files onto the relevant list. The editor copies them into the mod — Sounds or Musics — and the file base name, without the extension , becomes the name other editors use to reference it. Dropping onto a replacement field does two things at once: it adds the file to your mod and assigns it as that replacement. Duplicate handling is automatic. If a dropped file matches an existing one by checksum, the editor reuses the existing file rather than storing it twice. If the name collides but the audio differs, it generates a unique name. Replacement Entries ¶ Each entry in a replacement tab has: A picker button — click to choose from the mod's audio, or drop a file directly onto it. A preview button — plays the assigned replacement; click again to stop. Disabled when nothing is assigned. A None option in the picker — clears the replacement so the original Classic audio is used again. Every list has a search box that filters to entries whose name contains the text. The Waveform Timeline ¶ The timeline is where loop points are set. It is a zoomable, scrollable waveform with three draggable markers. Input Action Wheel up / down Zoom in / out by 15% per notch, anchored at the pointer. Right-drag or Middle-drag Scroll along the track. Left-drag on empty space Scroll along the track. Left-click on empty space Seek playback to that point. Left-drag on a marker Move that marker. The click-to-seek is distinguished from a scroll by both distance and time: a press that moves less than a few pixels and releases within about a third of a second counts as a click. If seeking is not working, you are probably dragging slightly. Zoom ranges from fully zoomed out to roughly 1000×, which is enough to place a loop point on an individual transient. At high zoom the time ruler switches to a finer format automatically. The Three Markers ¶ Loop Start (red flag) — the point the music jumps to . Loop End (blue flag) — the point the music jumps from . Playhead — the current playback position. Markers are grabbed within about 15 pixels, and they have a fixed priority when they overlap: Loop End wins, then Loop Start, then the playhead . This matters when a loop is very short or you are zoomed out — if you cannot grab the marker you want, zoom in until they separate. Markers highlight on hover, so you can confirm which one you are about to grab before pressing. Related pages: Loop Points , Custom Sounds , Custom Music , Mod Audio vs Classic Reskin .

docs.text: Character Editor ¶ The Character Editor edits playable characters, enemies, and items. Use it to build new mod characters, or to create Classic Reskin replacements for original SOR2 entities. It is launched from the selected mod's in-game editor menu and saves directly into that mod folder. It covers importing sprites from files or from a SOR2 ROM hack, editing animation artwork and timing, configuring hit boxes, body boxes and throw data, adding logic and audio events, and setting entity-wide properties such as movement speeds, icon and portrait. Two things the editor does not do: colour palettes are edited in the game's built-in palette editor, and ROM import only supports hacks based on the US/western Streets of Rage 2 ROM — not Bare Knuckle 2, and not heavily rearranged hacks such as Streets of Rage 2 Syndicate Wars. New Here? ¶ Read these two first — they explain the interface itself, which the rest of this section assumes: The Workspace — the panels, the preview's mouse controls, and every keyboard shortcut. The Inspector — every setting, organised so you can find one when you do not know its name. Then read Mod Characters vs Classic Reskin before creating anything, because it decides where your work is saved and what it can do: Mod mode creates content under the mod's Entities folder. Use it for new playable characters, enemies, and items spawned in custom levels. Classic Reskin mode creates replacements under Entity Replacements/Classic . Use it when an original character, enemy, or item should look different while keeping its classic gameplay. docs.text: Animations and Frames ¶ Animations are listed in the left panel; the frames of the selected animation appear in the timeline along the bottom. Click an animation to edit it, click a frame to select it, and the Inspector follows your selection. The Animation List ¶ Use the search box at the top of the panel to filter the list by name — useful once a character has dozens of animations. Click an animation to edit it. Double-click its name to rename it. Drag entries to reorder them. Drop sprites or image files onto an animation to fill its frames. + adds a new empty animation; - deletes the selected one. ↑ / ↓ move between animations without touching the mouse. When you delete an animation you get a choice that matters: empty the slot , keeping the animation's position in the list, or remove it entirely and shift every later animation up. Why Order Is Load-Bearing ¶ Scripts, logic events, animation behaviour and level spawns refer to animations by index, not by name . Renaming an animation is free. Reordering or removing one silently re-points everything that referred to the animations after it. So: Keep the reference animations in their expected order. Add new moves at the end of the list. When you must remove an animation that others might reference, prefer emptying the slot over removing it. If you are hand-editing JSON or writing Lua, note that animation IDs are doubled internally — editor animation 7 is engine ID 14. The Timeline ¶ Each frame in the timeline stores: Image ID — which sprite is drawn. Changing it swaps the artwork without touching the frame's timing or logic. Duration — how long the frame stays on screen, in game frames. The game runs at 60 frames per second, so a duration of 6 is a tenth of a second. Pivot / sprite offset — through sprite settings, shared with every other frame using the same sprite. Weapon point — optional, per frame. You can drag sprites in from the All Sprites panel, reorder frames by dragging, and insert, replace or delete frames. ← / → step through frames. Space plays the animation using each frame's own duration, and stops back on the frame you were editing. Reusing Work Between Frames ¶ Similar attacks usually want similar boxes and events. Right-click a frame in the timeline for: Copy Logic — the frame's hit boxes, body boxes, events and throw data together. Paste Logic (Replace) — overwrite all of it. Paste Hitboxes Only / Bodyboxes Only / Events Only / Throw Data Only — paste one category and leave the rest of the target frame alone. Selective paste is the one to reach for when two attacks share a hit box shape but need different timings or sounds. Options that would paste nothing are greyed out, so the menu also shows you what is on the clipboard. The Sprite List ¶ Frames point at an Image ID in the character's effective sprite list. When sprite settings reference another entity's sprites, those referenced sprites occupy the first entries of that list and the character's own custom sprites are appended after them. There is no separate "reference frame" mode — every frame simply points at one image ID in that combined list. This is why enabling or disabling Use Sprites from can shift which artwork a frame shows: it changes what occupies the low image IDs. Changing Animation Length Safely ¶ Hit boxes, body boxes, events and throw offsets are all positioned by frame number. The editor shifts frame-based data when it can, but inserting or removing frames in the middle of an animation is the most common way to quietly break a working move. After any length change, test the attack, the throw, the landing, and the transition into whatever animation comes next. Related pages: The Workspace , Import Sprites , Pivots and Offsets , Logic Events , Behaviour Modes .

docs.text: Sounds and Music Events ¶ Character audio comes from four places, in rough order of how often you will use them: Source Where Use it for Default sound sets Sounds section, character selected Everything routine: running, jumping, attacking, dying. Hit box sounds Each hit box One attack that needs a specific impact sound. Logic events Play Sound / Play Music on a frame Audio tied to an exact moment of a move. Projectile hit sounds Projectile fields, or a Spawn Item event The sound a projectile makes on contact. Default Sound Sets ¶ The Sounds section lists: Run , Jump , Landing , Attack , Jump Attack , Weapon Throw , Blitz , Defensive Special , Offensive Special , Grab Move 1/2/3 , Quake , Low Health , Death , Last Life Death . Each entry is a list , and the game picks one at random when the action happens. This is the single most effective thing you can do for a character's audio: give attacks, jumps and hurt sounds two or three variations each. One sound repeated on every punch is noticeable within seconds. Use the pick button to browse the sounds actually present in the mod rather than typing names — a typo produces silence with no error. Sound Channels ¶ Every sound plays on a channel, and the channel decides how it interacts with everything else: Channel Behaviour Use for sfx Normal mixing. Most effects. voice Reserved for character voices. Voices and vocal hit reactions. sfxBgm Ducks the music while it plays. Sounds that need to cut through. prioritary Interrupts other sounds. Almost nothing. Be careful with the priority channel. Priority sounds cut each other off, and they cut game sounds you did not intend — a custom priority sound can silence the extra-life jingle. Use it only when a sound genuinely must be heard over everything, which is rarer than it seems. Referencing Sounds From Other Mods ¶ When a sound belongs to the current mod, the editor fills the mod name for you. To use a sound from elsewhere, set the mod name explicitly. You can only reference mods that your mod depends on . Every mod depends on the Classic mod by default, so Classic sounds are always available. One caveat with Classic sounds: they may play differently depending on the Game Skin the player has selected. If exact audio matters to a move, ship the sound in your own mod rather than borrowing it. Add custom audio with the Audio Editor before assigning it here — see Custom Sounds for effects and voices, and Custom Music for tracks. Testing ¶ Audio problems are mixing problems, and mixing problems only appear when things overlap. Test in crowded fights where several enemies, the player, and the music are all competing. A sound that is perfect in isolation can be inaudible, or grating, in a real fight. See Test Mod . Related pages: Logic Events , Body and Hit Boxes , The Inspector , Custom Sounds , Custom Music .

docs.text: Behaviour Modes ¶ "Behaviour" is the editor's name for the original game's move controllers, selected by objectMode in saved data. Use it when you want an animation to be driven by a classic controller instead of by your own events, or when a spawn event needs to say which variant of an entity to create. A Mode Value Is Not a Universal Action ¶ This is the thing to understand before anything else: mode values mean different things for different entities. The same number points at completely different controllers depending on which entity it is applied to. There is no global table of "mode 6 = walk". Under the surface, players and enemies map mode values to controller array indexes multiplied by two, and items map them to item controller indexes with 0x02 selecting the first one. You should not need this while using the editor — it matters only when hand-editing JSON or writing scripts. Use the editor's behaviour picker. It reads the classic behaviour catalogue for the selected reference entity and shows descriptive names instead of numbers. The raw objectMode values are documented in Entity Types and Behaviour Modes for the cases where you genuinely need them. Animation Behaviour Overrides ¶ With an animation selected, Add Behaviour Override creates a Behaviour section holding two things: A Behaviour Reference — the original SOR2 entity whose behaviour is borrowed. A Behaviour value — which variant of that entity's behaviour to use. The editor starts from the Classic entity your character is based on. The reference picker stays within the same entity family: playable characters can pick Max, Axel, Blaze or Skate; enemies pick classic enemies; items pick classic items. The Behaviour value can be left as Unchanged , which keeps the current default value while still using the selected reference entity. Set a specific value when you want a different classic controller — for example, giving Axel the behaviour of Max's offensive special. Remove Behaviour Override stops the animation borrowing behaviour. Behaviour and Events Are Mutually Exclusive ¶ If an animation defines custom logic events, the referenced classic controller is skipped for that animation . The events become the behaviour, with only the default physics step still applied around them. So an animation is driven either by a classic controller or by your events — never partly by both. If you add an event to an animation that was working through a behaviour override and it suddenly stops moving, this is why. Modes in Spawn Events ¶ Spawn Enemy and Spawn Item events both carry a mode. Pick the mode for the entity being spawned , not for the character doing the spawning. If a player spawns a classic knife, choose a mode from the knife's item mode list. When It Goes Wrong ¶ Start from the closest classic reference and change the mode only when you know which controller you want. A wrong mode has a recognisable signature. If a spawned enemy or item locks up, immediately switches animation, ignores collision, or disappears on spawn , suspect the mode before you suspect anything else. Related pages: Logic Events , Enemy Logic , Item Logic , Entity Types and Behaviour Modes .

docs.text: Body and Hit Boxes ¶ Body boxes say where a character can be hit . Hit boxes say where an attack does hit . Both are edited in two places at once: drag them in the preview for shape, type exact numbers in the Inspector. If you cannot see any boxes, turn on Logic in the preview toolbar — it hides all overlays. The Global Body Box Comes First ¶ Character logic has one global body box , in Logic Settings . It is used by every frame that does not define its own body box. Start here, and usually stop here. The original Streets of Rage 2 uses only this box for its characters. A single stable, predictable body box is normally better than one that changes shape frame by frame — players learn one hurtbox instead of guessing at each pose, and you have one thing to tune rather than dozens. Add frame-specific body boxes only where the character's body is genuinely, visibly different: a low crouch, a long ducking slide, a boss that curls up. If you find yourself adding one to most frames, the global box is probably wrong and you are compensating for it. Box Coordinates ¶ Both box types use the same convention in the Inspector, and it is not the one you might expect: X is the left edge , in pixels relative to the character's origin. Y is the bottom edge . Width grows to the right — the left edge stays put. Height grows upward. So changing Width does not re-centre the box. If you want to widen a box symmetrically, reduce X by half the amount you add to Width . Body boxes additionally have Depth : how far the box extends along the towards/away axis. Depth controls how far apart two characters can be on the depth axis and still collide, which in a belt-scroller decides whether attacks that "look" aligned actually connect. Keep depth consistent across a character, and consistent with other characters they will fight. The saved JSON stores body boxes as a centre with a half-width, but the editor shows and edits them as plain rectangles. You only need to care about this if you hand-edit logic.json . Timing Within a Frame ¶ A hit box or body box is not simply "on" for the whole sprite frame. Each has: Relative Frame — the game frame, counted from the start of the selected sprite frame, on which the box becomes active. 0 is the first frame. Duration — how many game frames it stays active. This is what lets a single long sprite frame have a brief active hit window rather than being dangerous for its entire duration. It is also the usual fix when an attack feels like it hits too early, too late, or for too long: adjust the timing, not the sprite. Hit Box Properties ¶ Beyond the rectangle and its timing, each hit box carries the properties of the hit itself: Property Effect Damage Damage dealt to an opponent caught by the box. Hit Pause Game frames both characters freeze on a successful hit. This is the main dial for how heavy a hit feels. Knockdown Knocks the opponent down instead of just staggering them. Hit Backwards Knocks the opponent away from the direction this character faces, rather than towards it. Sound ID / Mod / Channel An impact sound specific to this hit box, overriding the character's default attack sound. Classic Hitbox Uses the original SOR2 hit detection instead of the editor's own box. A frame can hold several hit boxes with different timings — that is how you build a multi-hit attack inside one animation. Editing in the Preview ¶ The cursor tells you what you are about to grab: Move cursor over the box body — dragging moves the whole box. Horizontal or vertical resize cursor over an edge — dragging resizes that one side. Diagonal resize cursor over a corner — dragging resizes both directions. Drag for the rough shape, then type exact values in the Inspector. Boxes snap to whole pixels. Order of Work ¶ Pivots first, boxes second. Boxes are positioned relative to the character's origin, so if you move a pivot after tuning boxes, the visible relationship between sprite and box shifts and you will be re-tuning. If a pivot does change late, revisit that frame's boxes. See Pivots and Offsets . Testing ¶ Boxes are the part of a character most likely to feel wrong in ways that are invisible in the editor. Test in gameplay, and specifically test: Grabs, at the edge of grab range. Jump attacks landing on a standing opponent. Being thrown, and landing among other enemies. Projectiles and weapon attacks. Crowding — several enemies pressed against the character at once. Use hot-reload while testing so you can adjust and re-check without restarting. See Test Mod . Related pages: The Inspector , Pivots and Offsets , Player Logic , Enemy Logic , Item Logic .
docs.title: Body Boxes and Hit Boxes

docs.text: Body boxes say where a character can be hit . Hit boxes say where an attack does hit . Both are edited in two places at once: drag them in the preview for shape, type exact numbers in the Inspector. If you cannot see any boxes, turn on Logic in the preview toolbar — it hides all overlays.
docs.title: Body and Hit Boxes

docs.text: Character logic has one global body box , in Logic Settings . It is used by every frame that does not define its own body box. Start here, and usually stop here. The original Streets of Rage 2 uses only this box for its characters. A single stable, predictable body box is normally better than one that changes shape frame by frame — players learn one hurtbox instead of guessing at each pose, and you have one thing to tune rather than dozens. Add frame-specific body boxes only where the character's body is genuinely, visibly different: a low crouch, a long ducking slide, a boss that curls up. If you find yourself adding one to most frames, the global box is probably wrong and you are compensating for it.
docs.title: The Global Body Box Comes First

docs.text: Both box types use the same convention in the Inspector, and it is not the one you might expect: X is the left edge , in pixels relative to the character's origin. Y is the bottom edge . Width grows to the right — the left edge stays put. Height grows upward. So changing Width does not re-centre the box. If you want to widen a box symmetrically, reduce X by half the amount you add to Width . Body boxes additionally have Depth : how far the box extends along the towards/away axis. Depth controls how far apart two characters can be on the depth axis and still collide, which in a belt-scroller decides whether attacks that "look" aligned actually connect. Keep depth consistent across a character, and consistent with other characters they will fight. The saved JSON stores body boxes as a centre with a half-width, but the editor shows and edits them as plain rectangles. You only need to care about this if you hand-edit logic.json .
docs.title: Box Coordinates

docs.text: A hit box or body box is not simply "on" for the whole sprite frame. Each has: Relative Frame — the game frame, counted from the start of the selected sprite frame, on which the box becomes active. 0 is the first frame. Duration — how many game frames it stays active. This is what lets a single long sprite frame have a brief active hit window rather than being dangerous for its entire duration. It is also the usual fix when an attack feels like it hits too early, too late, or for too long: adjust the timing, not the sprite.
docs.title: Timing Within a Frame

docs.text: Beyond the rectangle and its timing, each hit box carries the properties of the hit itself: Property Effect Damage Damage dealt to an opponent caught by the box. Hit Pause Game frames both characters freeze on a successful hit. This is the main dial for how heavy a hit feels. Knockdown Knocks the opponent down instead of just staggering them. Hit Backwards Knocks the opponent away from the direction this character faces, rather than towards it. Sound ID / Mod / Channel An impact sound specific to this hit box, overriding the character's default attack sound. Classic Hitbox Uses the original SOR2 hit detection instead of the editor's own box. A frame can hold several hit boxes with different timings — that is how you build a multi-hit attack inside one animation.

docs.text: Create or Open a Character ¶ The Character Editor opens on a character selection screen for the current mod. The mod's name is the title, and everything on this screen is scoped to it. The Selection Screen ¶ Two rows of controls sit above the list: Mode — Mod or Classic Reskin . This decides where your work is saved and what it can do; read Mod Characters vs Classic Reskin if you are unsure. Filter — Players , Enemies , or Items . This filters the list below. Below them is the grid of characters. Click one to open it. You can also drag sprites, image files, or a SOR2 ROM onto this screen to start a new character from them. Opening an Existing Character ¶ In Mod mode the list shows characters in the current mod's Entities folder. Entries are grouped by entity type according to what their logic.json says they are — player, enemy, or item. If a character you expect is missing, check the filter first, then check its entity type. In Classic Reskin mode the list shows the original SOR2 characters. Ones that already have reskin data in this mod are highlighted, so you can see at a glance what the mod already replaces. Select one to create or edit its replacement. Creating a New Mod Character ¶ In Mod mode there are three ways to start: Create New ¶ Creates an empty character folder. You are asked for a name, which is also used as the folder name inside the mod, so it must be unique. You then choose a reference character . This is the most consequential choice on the screen, because the reference decides whether your character is a Player , Enemy , or Item — and that in turn decides how the game spawns and controls it. It also pre-populates: Animation names and their order. Reference timing, and the ghost/base artwork shown in the preview. A default body box and common logic defaults. Behaviour references in animations. Pick the closest classic character to what you are building. Starting from a reference you will fight against is more work than starting from a near-match. Drop Sprites ¶ Drop PNG or GIF files onto the editor. The editor asks for a classic character to act as the logic and animation reference — same effect as above — and creates the character with your sprites already imported. Drop a ROM ¶ Drop a modded SOR2 ROM and choose which classic character to import from it. See Import from ROM for the compatibility limits. A Reference Is Not Shared Artwork ¶ Choosing a reference character does not make your character reuse that character's sprites. New entities default to custom art only. Use Sprites from is a separate, optional setting. Turn it on only when you deliberately want to reuse another entity's sprite library — for example making a playable version of an enemy. Reused art has to follow the referenced entity's palette layout, so this is a commitment, not a convenience. Creating a Classic Reskin From a ROM ¶ Switch to Classic Reskin mode and drop a supported modded SOR2 ROM. The editor asks which player to import: Max , Axel , Blaze , Skate , or All Players . Each imported player is saved as a skin for the matching classic character under Entity Replacements/Classic . ROM compatibility is the same in both modes: hacks built on the US/western Streets of Rage 2 ROM are supported. Hacks built on the Japanese version (Bare Knuckle 2), or on heavily rearranged hacks such as Streets of Rage 2 Syndicate Wars, are not. Saving ¶ Every change is saved immediately and automatically. There is no save step. Tweak a value, switch to SOR2 New Era, hit hot-reload, and the change is already there. The 🏠 button closes the current character and returns you to this screen. What Is in a Character Folder ¶ File Contents 0.png , 1.png , … Sprite frames, numbered in the order they were added. spriteSettings.json Scale, pivots, icon selection, optional sprite reference data. animations.json Animation names, frames, timing, frame art references. logic.json Entity type, movement settings, sounds, body and hit boxes, events, scripts, animation behaviour. Classic Reskin replacements use the same file layout, under the classic replacement path. Next: Import Sprites , Import from ROM , Animations and Frames .

docs.text: Enemy Logic ¶ Enemy logic covers movement, attacks, sounds, hit reactions and AI. Most of the fields are the same ones described in Player Logic — this page covers what is different when the character is hostile. Enemy or Basic Enemy? ¶ Entity Type offers both. The distinction is about role: Basic Enemy — common, repeatable street enemies. Enemy — tougher enemies and bosses. This is not purely cosmetic. Some randomizers read the entity type to decide what to spawn where, so a boss marked as a basic enemy can end up appearing in crowds. As with players, entity type normally comes from the reference character you chose at creation. Choosing the closest reference matters more for enemies than for players, because it also determines whether the animation names and behaviour modes line up with the role you intend. Settings That Matter Most for Enemies ¶ Enemies share the full set of movement, combat and sound settings with players. The ones that repay attention, especially for bosses and large enemies: Setting Why it matters for enemies Global body box , especially Depth A large enemy with a small box feels like it phases through attacks; with too much depth it becomes hittable from implausible distances. Depth decides lane alignment in a belt-scroller. Grab Range , Front/Back Grab Offset Wrong offsets make a large enemy's grabs miss or clip into the player. Knockdown Quake / Thrown Quake The main lever for making a heavy enemy feel heavy when it hits the floor. Projectile Damage / Hit Pause Only if the enemy spawns projectiles. Default sounds Hurt, attack, jump, landing and special sounds are what make an enemy readable in a crowd. Building AI ¶ There are two routes, and they are mutually exclusive per animation: Logic events — move the enemy, change animation, spawn items, play audio, stop an action. Remember that adding any event to an animation switches off that animation's classic behaviour entirely; the events must then supply everything. Behaviour overrides — point an animation at a classic entity and behaviour value, and the original controller drives it. This is how you get authentically classic-feeling enemy AI without rebuilding it. Not every combination works. Behaviour values are tied to how the original game's code is structured, so a controller taken from one enemy may not make sense on another. See Behaviour Modes . Testing ¶ Enemies fail in ways that only appear in real fights. Test across difficulty levels and spawn modes, and specifically in crowds — an enemy that behaves well alone can lock up, refuse to approach, or stack badly with others. Work incrementally: one change, then test. Enemy logic has a lot of interacting values and a big batch of changes is hard to unpick when the result is wrong. Keep backups by copying character folders. Changes save immediately and automatically, so there is no unsaved state to fall back on if you take a wrong turn. Related pages: Player Logic , The Inspector , Body and Hit Boxes , Logic Events , Behaviour Modes , Spawns .

docs.text: Logic Event Examples ¶ Logic events add behaviour to animations, effectively replacing the classic reference behaviour: play this sound at frame 2, set this velocity at frame 4, spawn this projectile at frame 9, branch when landing, branch when the player enters a command. Use events when the behaviour follows a fixed timeline. Use Lua when the move needs target searches, damage scaling, cooldowns, or conditional state machines. The examples below show the saved JSON so you can see exactly what each event stores. You build all of it through the Events section of the Inspector — see Logic Events for the interface. Runtime Rules That Matter ¶ Exact-frame events run only when current_animation_frame equals their frame . Windowed events use afterFrame and beforeFrame ; if both are 0 , the event is active during the entirety of the animation. Events run before an animation's Lua script. Animation IDs in the engine are doubled internally, e.g. animation 7 has the ID 14 (or 0xD in hexadecimal). VelocityEvent and AccelerationEvent take character facing direction into account: positive means moving forward, negative means moving backward. In velocity and acceleration events, positive Y means upward in editor terms; Internally, the engine stores them with the inverse value, i.e. upward impulse as negative, downwards as positive. VelocityEvent and AccelerationEvent can enable or disable each affected axis. Disabled axis input boxes are ignored, which lets you set one component to zero while preserving the other components. InputVelocityEvent , InputAccelerationEvent , JumpToAnimationOnInputButton , and JumpToAnimationOnInputCombo only act on players. JumpToAnimationOnHit only acts on players and triggers when hitPauseTimer == 1 . GrabEvent needs attackedCharacterId to already point to a valid victim, usually because a hitbox connected earlier in the animation. Jump Startup With Events ¶ This event stack starts an airborne move by setting upward velocity, then applies gravity. It is useful for a jump attack or special that should not need Lua. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.VelocityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "velocity": { "x": 90, "y": 360, "z": 0 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.AccelerationEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 1, "acceleration": { "x": 0, "y": -18, "z": 0 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnLanding, Sor2NewEra", "initialFrame": 4, "animationId": 0, "animationFrame": 0 } ] Field notes: velocity.x moves forward because the event multiplies it by facing direction. velocity.y is written as positive upward in the event, then converted to negative internal vertical impulse. acceleration.y is negative here because after conversion it becomes downward gravity. JumpToAnimationOnLanding waits until impulse.y > 0 , the frame is at least initialFrame , and height has reached the ground. Aerial Spinning Kick ¶ This is an event-only version of a forward aerial spinning special. It starts with a lift, moves forward, becomes briefly invincible, spawns sound, then returns to standing on landing. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SoundEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "packName": "My Pack", "soundName": "spin-start", "channel": 2 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.InvincibilityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "invincible": true }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.VelocityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "velocity": { "x": 180, "y": 250, "z": 0 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.AccelerationEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 1, "acceleration": { "x": -4, "y": -12, "z": 0 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.InputVelocityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "afterFrame": 2, "beforeFrame": 18, "strength": { "x": 12, "y": 6 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SoundEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 8, "packName": "My Pack", "soundName": "spin-loop", "channel": 2 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.InvincibilityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 20, "invincible": false }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnLanding, Sor2NewEra", "initialFrame": 10, "animationId": 0, "animationFrame": 0 } ] Why this works: The first velocity starts the arc. Acceleration gradually removes forward speed and pulls the character down. InputVelocityEvent adds held input to velocity , not impulse. That makes it a direct per-frame nudge during the active window. The landing event clamps height to ground and queues the standing animation. If this move also needs complex hit-pause rebound, a Lua script should handle the rebound and return false during the custom physics frames. Projectile Attack ¶ A projectile attack usually needs two animations: the character's firing animation and the projectile item's active animation. Character firing animation: [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SoundEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 6, "packName": "My Pack", "soundName": "projectile-release", "channel": 2 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SpawnItemEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 7, "packName": "My Pack", "entityName": "Energy Projectile", "animationId": 0, "mode": -1, "lifetime": 80, "positionOffset": { "x": 1100, "y": 0 }, "velocity": { "x": 520, "y": 0 }, "isProjectile": true, "damage": 8, "hitPause": 4, "hitSoundName": "projectile-hit", "hitSoundPack": "My Pack", "hitSoundChannel": 0 } ] Projectile impact animation: [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SoundEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "packName": "My Pack", "soundName": "projectile-impact", "channel": 0 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.DestroyEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 5 } ] Field notes: SpawnItemEvent.positionOffset is converted by the engine and applied relative to the source convention. Test positive and negative values in-game because spawn helpers intentionally negate the stored offsets before calling the original item spawner. animationId is the projectile's editor animation ID. isProjectile enables projectile hit metadata: damage, hit pause, and hit sound. If the projectile needs custom movement, attach a Lua script to the projectile's active animation and let the spawn event handle only creation. Input Combo Special ¶ Use JumpToAnimationOnInputCombo for command moves. This example watches for a quarter-turn-style chain during a normal animation and jumps to a special animation. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnInputCombo, Sor2NewEra", "afterFrame": 0, "beforeFrame": 12, "input": "v>b", "animationId": 42 } ] Field notes: input is parsed by the player input chain parser. The event checks the player's input history, not just the current frame. When the chain matches, the event sets the target animation and returns false internally, stopping later event evaluation for that controller path. Button Cancel Window ¶ This event lets an attack cancel into another animation only during frames 9 through 16. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnInputButton, Sor2NewEra", "afterFrame": 9, "beforeFrame": 16, "input": 16, "animationId": 18 } ] input is the numeric InputButtons value. Common values are 16 for B (attack), 32 for C (jump), 64 for A (special), 65536 for X (back attack), 131072 for Y (pick-up), and 1048576 for Z (super move). Use this for simple cancels. Use Lua when the cancel depends on hit_pause_timer , attacked_character_id , or custom_value_* . Hit-Confirm Branch ¶ This branch changes animation when the player's hitbox connects during a window. Internally it checks hitPauseTimer == 1 , so it reacts to the first hit-pause frame. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnHit, Sor2NewEra", "afterFrame": 5, "beforeFrame": 18, "animationId": 27 } ] Use this when the follow-up should happen only after contact. If the move must distinguish blocked hits, projectiles, wall hits, or different victims, use Lua. Hitbox Into Grab ¶ Use GrabEvent when a hitbox should convert into a grab. The hitbox must have already set attackedCharacterId . [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.GrabEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 6 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 7, "animationId": 4, "animationFrame": 0 } ] Authoring notes: Place the hitbox on the same frame or an earlier frame than the GrabEvent . Let the animation recover naturally may the hit grab miss. For scripted throws, events can start the grab, then a Lua grab controller can own victim positioning. Teleport Or Step Offset ¶ PositionOffsetEvent changes real position immediately and marks the object as teleported for the animation system. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.PositionOffsetEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 3, "offset": { "x": 24, "y": 0, "z": -8 } } ] Field notes: offset.x follows facing direction. offset.z moves along the belt-scroller depth axis. offset.y is added to vertical velocity, not height position directly. Use this for short steps, snaps, and throw alignment. Use Lua if the offset depends on target position. Health Cost Or Healing ¶ HealthEvent adds or removes to health. Use a negative value for a health cost. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.HealthEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "health": -8 } ] Common scenario is for health cost during a custom special move. For moves that are not classic specials and should fail if health is too low, use Lua. This event itself always applies the value, ideal for use in classic special moves. Custom Value Marker ¶ Use SetCustomValueEvent when events need to communicate with Lua scripts or global hooks. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SetCustomValueEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "valueId": 1, "value": 3 } ] Example use: set custom_value_1 to 3 at the start of a move, then have a shared Lua air-control script choose a movement profile from that value. Choosing Events Or Lua ¶ Use events when the answer is fixed by frame number: play sound start movement spawn item toggle invincibility jump on landing branch on simple input Use Lua when the answer depends on runtime state: target distance current health or meter victim existence hitbox result with custom recoil weapon type multiple hits with cooldowns grab victim alignment enemy AI phase Event-driven moves and Lua scripts can be combined. A good pattern is events for the predictable timeline and Lua for the exceptional branches.

docs.text: This event stack starts an airborne move by setting upward velocity, then applies gravity. It is useful for a jump attack or special that should not need Lua. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.VelocityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "velocity": { "x": 90, "y": 360, "z": 0 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.AccelerationEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 1, "acceleration": { "x": 0, "y": -18, "z": 0 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnLanding, Sor2NewEra", "initialFrame": 4, "animationId": 0, "animationFrame": 0 } ] Field notes: velocity.x moves forward because the event multiplies it by facing direction. velocity.y is written as positive upward in the event, then converted to negative internal vertical impulse. acceleration.y is negative here because after conversion it becomes downward gravity. JumpToAnimationOnLanding waits until impulse.y > 0 , the frame is at least initialFrame , and height has reached the ground.
docs.title: Jump Startup With Events

docs.text: This is an event-only version of a forward aerial spinning special. It starts with a lift, moves forward, becomes briefly invincible, spawns sound, then returns to standing on landing. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SoundEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "packName": "My Pack", "soundName": "spin-start", "channel": 2 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.InvincibilityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "invincible": true }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.VelocityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "velocity": { "x": 180, "y": 250, "z": 0 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.AccelerationEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 1, "acceleration": { "x": -4, "y": -12, "z": 0 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.InputVelocityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "afterFrame": 2, "beforeFrame": 18, "strength": { "x": 12, "y": 6 } }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SoundEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 8, "packName": "My Pack", "soundName": "spin-loop", "channel": 2 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.InvincibilityEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 20, "invincible": false }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnLanding, Sor2NewEra", "initialFrame": 10, "animationId": 0, "animationFrame": 0 } ] Why this works: The first velocity starts the arc. Acceleration gradually removes forward speed and pulls the character down. InputVelocityEvent adds held input to velocity , not impulse. That makes it a direct per-frame nudge during the active window. The landing event clamps height to ground and queues the standing animation. If this move also needs complex hit-pause rebound, a Lua script should handle the rebound and return false during the custom physics frames.
docs.title: Aerial Spinning Kick

docs.text: A projectile attack usually needs two animations: the character's firing animation and the projectile item's active animation. Character firing animation: [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SoundEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 6, "packName": "My Pack", "soundName": "projectile-release", "channel": 2 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SpawnItemEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 7, "packName": "My Pack", "entityName": "Energy Projectile", "animationId": 0, "mode": -1, "lifetime": 80, "positionOffset": { "x": 1100, "y": 0 }, "velocity": { "x": 520, "y": 0 }, "isProjectile": true, "damage": 8, "hitPause": 4, "hitSoundName": "projectile-hit", "hitSoundPack": "My Pack", "hitSoundChannel": 0 } ] Projectile impact animation: [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SoundEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "packName": "My Pack", "soundName": "projectile-impact", "channel": 0 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.DestroyEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 5 } ] Field notes: SpawnItemEvent.positionOffset is converted by the engine and applied relative to the source convention. Test positive and negative values in-game because spawn helpers intentionally negate the stored offsets before calling the original item spawner. animationId is the projectile's editor animation ID. isProjectile enables projectile hit metadata: damage, hit pause, and hit sound. If the projectile needs custom movement, attach a Lua script to the projectile's active animation and let the spawn event handle only creation.
docs.title: Projectile Attack

docs.text: Use JumpToAnimationOnInputCombo for command moves. This example watches for a quarter-turn-style chain during a normal animation and jumps to a special animation. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnInputCombo, Sor2NewEra", "afterFrame": 0, "beforeFrame": 12, "input": "v>b", "animationId": 42 } ] Field notes: input is parsed by the player input chain parser. The event checks the player's input history, not just the current frame. When the chain matches, the event sets the target animation and returns false internally, stopping later event evaluation for that controller path.
docs.title: Input Combo Special

docs.text: This event lets an attack cancel into another animation only during frames 9 through 16. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnInputButton, Sor2NewEra", "afterFrame": 9, "beforeFrame": 16, "input": 16, "animationId": 18 } ] input is the numeric InputButtons value. Common values are 16 for B (attack), 32 for C (jump), 64 for A (special), 65536 for X (back attack), 131072 for Y (pick-up), and 1048576 for Z (super move). Use this for simple cancels. Use Lua when the cancel depends on hit_pause_timer , attacked_character_id , or custom_value_* .
docs.title: Button Cancel Window

docs.text: This branch changes animation when the player's hitbox connects during a window. Internally it checks hitPauseTimer == 1 , so it reacts to the first hit-pause frame. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationOnHit, Sor2NewEra", "afterFrame": 5, "beforeFrame": 18, "animationId": 27 } ] Use this when the follow-up should happen only after contact. If the move must distinguish blocked hits, projectiles, wall hits, or different victims, use Lua.
docs.title: Hit-Confirm Branch

docs.text: Use GrabEvent when a hitbox should convert into a grab. The hitbox must have already set attackedCharacterId . [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.GrabEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 6 }, { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 7, "animationId": 4, "animationFrame": 0 } ] Authoring notes: Place the hitbox on the same frame or an earlier frame than the GrabEvent . Let the animation recover naturally may the hit grab miss. For scripted throws, events can start the grab, then a Lua grab controller can own victim positioning.
docs.title: Hitbox Into Grab

docs.text: PositionOffsetEvent changes real position immediately and marks the object as teleported for the animation system. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.PositionOffsetEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 3, "offset": { "x": 24, "y": 0, "z": -8 } } ] Field notes: offset.x follows facing direction. offset.z moves along the belt-scroller depth axis. offset.y is added to vertical velocity, not height position directly. Use this for short steps, snaps, and throw alignment. Use Lua if the offset depends on target position.
docs.title: Teleport Or Step Offset

docs.text: HealthEvent adds or removes to health. Use a negative value for a health cost. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.HealthEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "health": -8 } ] Common scenario is for health cost during a custom special move. For moves that are not classic specials and should fail if health is too low, use Lua. This event itself always applies the value, ideal for use in classic special moves.
docs.title: Health Cost Or Healing

docs.text: Use SetCustomValueEvent when events need to communicate with Lua scripts or global hooks. [ { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.SetCustomValueEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 0, "valueId": 1, "value": 3 } ] Example use: set custom_value_1 to 3 at the start of a move, then have a shared Lua air-control script choose a movement profile from that value.
docs.title: Custom Value Marker

docs.text: Use events when the answer is fixed by frame number: play sound start movement spawn item toggle invincibility jump on landing branch on simple input Use Lua when the answer depends on runtime state: target distance current health or meter victim existence hitbox result with custom recoil weapon type multiple hits with cooldowns grab victim alignment enemy AI phase Event-driven moves and Lua scripts can be combined. A good pattern is events for the predictable timeline and Lua for the exceptional branches.
docs.title: Choosing Events Or Lua

docs.text: Icon and Portrait ¶ Two different images represent a character outside of gameplay, and they behave differently. Icon ¶ The icon is picked from the character's own sprites, in Visual Settings : Field Meaning Icon The sprite used as the character's portrait in menus such as character select. You can drop an image here to add it to the character and use it as the icon. Icon Offset X / Y Shift of the icon sprite relative to its pivot, in pixels, to centre it in menus. The saved iconIndex points at the chosen sprite. Choose something that reads at small size — a neutral face or bust works; a mid-action pose usually does not. Use the offset fields to centre it rather than editing the source sprite, since that sprite may also be used by animations. Portrait ¶ The portrait is the larger image shown on the Character Select screen. Keep it consistent with the character's art, and do not just reuse the small icon sprite scaled up. Palettes ¶ The icon uses the character's colour palette. The portrait does not. That single difference drives how you should test each. If your character supports palettes, check the icon under every one of them — a palette that looks fine in gameplay can make the icon unreadable against the menu background. The portrait is palette-independent, so it needs no such check, and it does not have to match the palette layout the sprites use. Palettes are edited in the game's built-in palette editor, not in the Character Editor. See Color Palettes . Testing Checklist ¶ The Character Select screen, for the portrait. The in-game player, enemy or item icon, under each colour palette. Related pages: The Inspector , Create/Open Characters , Mod Characters vs Classic Reskin , Test Mod .
docs.title: Icon and Portrait

docs.text: Import From SOR2 ROM ¶ The Character Editor can extract character data straight out of a Streets of Rage 2 ROM, giving you original sprites, animations and timing as a starting point. Compatibility ¶ Only ROM hacks built on the US/western Streets of Rage 2 ROM are supported. Not supported: The Japanese version, Bare Knuckle 2 . Heavily rearranged hacks such as Streets of Rage 2 Syndicate Wars . If import produces garbled sprites or fails outright, the ROM's base version is the first thing to check. Accepted file extensions: .bin , .gen , .md , .smd , in any letter case ( SOR2.BIN works). Interleaved .smd copier dumps are converted on load. A file without a Genesis ROM header is refused with a message rather than imported as garbage. How to Import ¶ Drop the ROM anywhere on the Character Editor window, including the preview or the animation list. What happens next depends on the mode: Mod mode — the editor reads the ROM and shows a character selection dialog. Filter by Players, Enemies, or Items, then choose the entity to import. The entity you pick determines the new character's Entity Type — Player, Enemy, or Item — and therefore how the game spawns and controls it. Classic Reskin mode — the editor asks which player skin to import: Max , Axel , Blaze , Skate , or All Players . Each is saved to the matching classic replacement slot under Entity Replacements/Classic . What You Get ¶ In Mod mode, import creates a character folder containing: Numbered sprite PNGs. Sprite settings with pivots and scale. Animation definitions. Logic defaults and reference information. An entity type based on the imported classic entity. In Classic Reskin mode, import creates or updates a classic replacement folder with the extracted sprites and animation frame lists, while the replacement stays tied to Classic reference logic. Everything imported remains editable. You can replace sprites, rename animations, adjust pivots, edit boxes where local logic applies, add logic events, assign audio, and set the icon and portrait. Choosing the Right Mode ¶ Mod mode — when you want a faithful original as a starting point for a new entity that you will then modify. Classic Reskin mode — when you want sprites from a ROM hack to replace Max, Axel, Blaze or Skate while the original Classic gameplay stays exactly as it is. Note that ROM import is a custom-art workflow, not a sprite-reuse one. The imported sprites are copied into your character as its own art; you do not need Use Sprites from , and setting it would mean something different. See Mod Characters vs Classic Reskin . After Importing ¶ Work through, in order: Animations and Frames , Pivots and Offsets , Body and Hit Boxes , and Behaviour Modes . Related pages: Create/Open Characters , Import Sprites .
docs.title: Import From SOR2 ROM

docs.text: Import From Sprites ¶ The Character Editor imports PNG and GIF files as sprite frames. You can import when creating a character, or at any time afterwards by dropping files onto the editor. What Gets Imported ¶ PNG files become individual sprite frames. Animated GIF files are split into their frames, and the GIF's own timing is converted into frame durations automatically. Prefer GIFs. Importing an animated GIF gives you a working animation with sensible timing in one step, where importing loose PNGs leaves you setting every duration by hand. Imported sprites are copied into the character folder and registered in spriteSettings.json , named by index in the order they were added. Imported sprites are custom art . They do not require Use Sprites from , even when the character uses a Classic character as its logic reference. Those are separate concepts — see below. Where to Drop Them ¶ The drop target decides what happens, which makes this the fastest part of the editor once you know it: Drop onto Result All Sprites panel Adds sprites to the character's library without touching any animation. Preview The currently selected frame uses the dropped art. Good for replacing one reference frame with custom art. Timeline Adds or replaces animation frames. Dropping over existing placeholder or reference frames fills them while keeping the animation's structure. An animation in the left panel Creates or fills that animation's frames. Reusing Another Entity's Art ¶ Use Sprites from is not part of sprite import and most characters should leave it empty. Set it only when this entity should genuinely reuse another entity's whole sprite library — a playable version of an enemy, or an enemy version of a playable character. It is a real commitment: the reused art must follow the referenced entity's palette layout , and should stay compatible with palettes made for that entity. When Use Sprites from is set, an extra action appears in animation settings: Fill From Ref , which replaces the current animation from one of the referenced entity's animations. What it copies depends on the mode you are in, and the difference matters: Mod characters — copies the frame art and the animation logic, replacing existing hit boxes, body boxes, events, script references and throw data. This applies whether the referenced art comes from Classic or from another mod entity. Classic Reskins — copies frame and art data only . The Classic reference logic is left intact. So for a mod character, Fill From Ref is destructive to work you have already done on that animation. Use it early, not late. Import Tips ¶ Keep canvas size and sprite scale consistent across frames. Inconsistent canvases mean every frame needs its own pivot correction, and the boxes drift with them — this is the single biggest source of avoidable alignment work. After importing, work through Pivots and Offsets , then Animations and Frames , then Body and Hit Boxes , in that order. Related pages: Create/Open Characters , Import from ROM , Mod Characters vs Classic Reskin .
docs.title: Import From Sprites
