docs.text: The Inspector ¶ The Inspector is the right-hand panel. It always shows the settings for whatever you last selected , so its contents change as you click around: select the character and you get character-wide settings; select an animation and you get animation settings; select a frame and you get that frame's boxes, events and throw data. Every field in the editor has a tooltip. This page is the same information organised so you can find a setting when you do not yet know what it is called. Sections are collapsible — click a section header to expand or collapse it. Sections that were added optionally (Script, Behaviour, Throw Logic, Weapon) also have a remove button that deletes the section and everything in it. Character Settings ¶ Shown when the character itself is selected, rather than a specific animation or frame. Visual Settings ¶ How the character is drawn. Field Meaning Scale Size multiplier applied to every sprite when drawn in game. 1 keeps sprites at original size. Shadow Always On The character always casts a shadow, even in animations where it would normally be hidden. Icon Sprite used as the character's portrait in menus such as character select. Drop an image here to add it and use it as the icon. Icon Offset X / Y Shift of the icon sprite relative to its pivot, in pixels. Use it to centre the portrait in menus. Use Sprites from Mod providing fallback sprites. Any animation frame without its own sprite falls back to the character picked below. from Character Character inside that mod whose sprites and animations are used as the fallback. Logic Settings ¶ How the character behaves. Not every field applies to every entity type. Field Meaning Ref Mod Mod providing the behaviour this character inherits. Leave empty to use Classic content. Ref Name Character inside the reference mod whose behaviour is inherited when this one has no logic of its own. Entity Type Player, Enemy, Basic Enemy, or Item. Decides how the game spawns and controls it. Walk Speed Movement speed while walking. Run Speed Movement speed while running. Jump Force Upward impulse on jump. Higher jumps higher. Jump Delay Game frames between pressing jump and leaving the ground. Can Use Weapons Whether the character may pick up and use weapons. Combo Repetitions How many times the standard attack combo can repeat before resetting. Grab Combo Repetitions How many times the grab attack combo can repeat before resetting. Charge Delay Game frames the attack button must be held before the charged move becomes available. Grab Range How close an opponent must be to be grabbed. Front / Back Grab Offset Distance at which a grabbed opponent is held, when grabbed from the front or from behind. Knockdown Quake Screen shake strength when this character hits the ground after a knockdown. 0 disables it. Thrown Quake Screen shake strength when this character lands after being thrown. 0 disables it. Projectile fields ( Damage , Hit Pause ) appear here for characters that spawn projectiles. Hit Pause is how many game frames both characters freeze for when the projectile connects — it is what makes a hit feel heavy. Global Body Box ¶ The character's default body box, used by any frame that does not define its own. Field Meaning X Left edge, in pixels relative to the character's origin. Y Bottom edge, in pixels relative to the origin. Width Width in pixels. The left edge stays put as the box grows. Height Height in pixels. Depth Depth along the towards/away axis. Controls how far apart two characters can be and still collide. See Body and Hit Boxes for how this interacts with per-frame boxes. Sounds ¶ Default sounds for common actions: Run , Jump , Landing , Attack , Jump Attack , Weapon Throw , Blitz , Defensive Special , Offensive Special , Grab Move 1/2/3 , Quake , Low Health , Death , Last Life Death . Each is a list . When more than one sound is listed, the game picks one at random — this is how you stop a repeated action from sounding mechanical. Use the pick button to browse sounds in the mod rather than typing names. See Audio Events . Entity Scripts ¶ Lua hooks for the whole entity, shown whether or not the character uses reference logic. Each one picks a script from the mod's Scripts/ folder, with an optional Mod Name ; the x on its header removes it. The Add buttons offered depend on the Entity Type , but a hook that is already set is always shown. Section Meaning AI Script Enemies: runs every frame before the built-in AI, whatever the animation. Returning false skips the built-in AI for that frame. Pickup Script Items: runs when a player picks the item up. Returning true consumes the item. Player Update Script Players: runs once per frame before the player's controller, in every animation. Special Move Script Players: decides whether a defensive or offensive special may start, and its cost. HUD Script Players: view-only script drawing extra HUD sprites next to the health bar. Invincible Offensive Special Players: offensive specials start invulnerable, without the classic vulnerable window. No Charge Flash Players: no white flash when holding attack completes the charge ( noChargeFlash ). The charged attack still works. Animation Settings ¶ Shown when an animation is selected. Name — the name shown in the animation list. Afterimages — draws a trail of afterimages behind the character during this animation, like the Ninpo clones. Visual only. Script — an optional custom Lua script driving this animation's behaviour. Added with Add Script Data , removed with Remove Script (which detaches it; the script file itself is not deleted). Behaviour — an optional override making this animation borrow an original SOR2 entity's behaviour. Added with Add Behaviour Override . See Behaviour Modes . Frame Settings ¶ Shown when a frame is selected in the timeline. Field Meaning Image ID Sprite drawn on this frame. Changing it swaps the artwork without touching timing or logic. Duration How long this frame stays on screen, in game frames. Sprite Offset ¶ Offset X / Y position the sprite relative to the character's origin, in pixels. Negative X moves left, negative Y moves up. This offset is shared by every frame using the same sprite. That is the whole reason it exists as a separate concept from the pivot — see Pivots and Offsets . Weapon ¶ Where a held weapon is drawn on this frame. Enable it with the checkbox; turning it off remembers the settings, so you can turn it back on without losing them. Field Meaning X / Y Position of the weapon point, in pixels relative to the character's origin. Direction Direction the held weapon points in on this frame. Show Behind Draw the weapon behind the character on this frame instead of in front. Hitboxes ¶ Areas that damage opponents during this frame. A frame can have several, each with its own timing and damage. Field Meaning Relative Frame Game frame, counted from the start of the selected sprite frame, on which this hitbox becomes active. 0 is the first frame. Duration How many game frames the hitbox stays active. Damage Damage dealt to an opponent caught by this hitbox. Knockdown The hit knocks the opponent down instead of just staggering them. Hit Backwards The opponent is knocked away from the direction this character faces, rather than towards it. Hit Pause Game frames both characters freeze for on a successful hit. Sound ID , Sound Mod , Sound Channel The impact sound for this specific hitbox. Classic Hitbox Use the original SOR2 hit detection instead of the editor's own box. X / Y / Width / Height The box itself, in pixels. Bodyboxes ¶ Areas that can be hit during this frame. Same Relative Frame and Duration timing as hitboxes, plus X , Y , Width , Height — where X is the left edge and Y the bottom edge, and the left edge stays put as the width grows. Events ¶ Things that happen at specific moments of this frame — movement, sounds, spawning, jumping to another animation. Add one with the add button, which opens a searchable list of event types. Each event row can be expanded to show its settings or removed. See Logic Events and Logic Event Examples . Throw Logic ¶ How the character carries and releases an opponent during this animation. Added with Initialize Throw Logic ; Remove Throw Logic deletes it along with all its opponent offsets. Field Meaning Release Damage Damage dealt by the projectile at the moment it is released. Legacy Mechanics Use the original SOR2 movement and combat rules for this character instead of the newer ones. Relative To Attacker Hold the opponent relative to this character's current position and height, without the classic grab distance. Use it, with Legacy Mechanics off, for aerial or moving throws. X / Y Release velocity. Offsets hold where the carried opponent is positioned at each moment of the throw: Field Meaning Relative Frame Frame, counted from the start of the selected sprite frame, on which this offset applies. Opponent Anim Animation the held opponent is put into while this offset applies. Opponent Frame Frame of that animation to show. Same Direction The opponent faces the same way as this character instead of facing them. X / Y Distance the opponent is held at, in pixels. Positive X puts them in front; positive Y moves them up. You can drag the opponent directly in the preview instead of typing these values. Axis Conventions ¶ Wherever a field has X, Y and Z components, the editor uses one consistent convention: X — forward and backward. Positive is forward , in the direction the character faces. Y — up and down. Positive is up , as shown in the editor. Z — towards and away from the camera (the belt-scroller depth axis). Movement events ( Set Velocity , Set Acceleration , and their input-driven versions) have a checkbox per axis. When an axis checkbox is off, that axis value is ignored and the character's existing movement on that axis is left alone. This lets you zero one component without disturbing the others. Related pages: The Workspace , Body and Hit Boxes , Logic Events , Pivots and Offsets .

docs.text: The Inspector is the right-hand panel. It always shows the settings for whatever you last selected , so its contents change as you click around: select the character and you get character-wide settings; select an animation and you get animation settings; select a frame and you get that frame's boxes, events and throw data. Every field in the editor has a tooltip. This page is the same information organised so you can find a setting when you do not yet know what it is called. Sections are collapsible — click a section header to expand or collapse it. Sections that were added optionally (Script, Behaviour, Throw Logic, Weapon) also have a remove button that deletes the section and everything in it.
docs.title: The Inspector

docs.text: Shown when the character itself is selected, rather than a specific animation or frame.
docs.title: Character Settings

docs.text: How the character is drawn. Field Meaning Scale Size multiplier applied to every sprite when drawn in game. 1 keeps sprites at original size. Shadow Always On The character always casts a shadow, even in animations where it would normally be hidden. Icon Sprite used as the character's portrait in menus such as character select. Drop an image here to add it and use it as the icon. Icon Offset X / Y Shift of the icon sprite relative to its pivot, in pixels. Use it to centre the portrait in menus. Use Sprites from Mod providing fallback sprites. Any animation frame without its own sprite falls back to the character picked below. from Character Character inside that mod whose sprites and animations are used as the fallback.
docs.title: Visual Settings

docs.text: How the character behaves. Not every field applies to every entity type. Field Meaning Ref Mod Mod providing the behaviour this character inherits. Leave empty to use Classic content. Ref Name Character inside the reference mod whose behaviour is inherited when this one has no logic of its own. Entity Type Player, Enemy, Basic Enemy, or Item. Decides how the game spawns and controls it. Walk Speed Movement speed while walking. Run Speed Movement speed while running. Jump Force Upward impulse on jump. Higher jumps higher. Jump Delay Game frames between pressing jump and leaving the ground. Can Use Weapons Whether the character may pick up and use weapons. Combo Repetitions How many times the standard attack combo can repeat before resetting. Grab Combo Repetitions How many times the grab attack combo can repeat before resetting. Charge Delay Game frames the attack button must be held before the charged move becomes available. Grab Range How close an opponent must be to be grabbed. Front / Back Grab Offset Distance at which a grabbed opponent is held, when grabbed from the front or from behind. Knockdown Quake Screen shake strength when this character hits the ground after a knockdown. 0 disables it. Thrown Quake Screen shake strength when this character lands after being thrown. 0 disables it. Projectile fields ( Damage , Hit Pause ) appear here for characters that spawn projectiles. Hit Pause is how many game frames both characters freeze for when the projectile connects — it is what makes a hit feel heavy.
docs.title: Logic Settings

docs.text: The character's default body box, used by any frame that does not define its own. Field Meaning X Left edge, in pixels relative to the character's origin. Y Bottom edge, in pixels relative to the origin. Width Width in pixels. The left edge stays put as the box grows. Height Height in pixels. Depth Depth along the towards/away axis. Controls how far apart two characters can be and still collide. See Body and Hit Boxes for how this interacts with per-frame boxes.
docs.title: Global Body Box

docs.text: Default sounds for common actions: Run , Jump , Landing , Attack , Jump Attack , Weapon Throw , Blitz , Defensive Special , Offensive Special , Grab Move 1/2/3 , Quake , Low Health , Death , Last Life Death . Each is a list . When more than one sound is listed, the game picks one at random — this is how you stop a repeated action from sounding mechanical. Use the pick button to browse sounds in the mod rather than typing names. See Audio Events .
docs.title: Sounds

docs.text: Lua hooks for the whole entity, shown whether or not the character uses reference logic. Each one picks a script from the mod's Scripts/ folder, with an optional Mod Name ; the x on its header removes it. The Add buttons offered depend on the Entity Type , but a hook that is already set is always shown. Section Meaning AI Script Enemies: runs every frame before the built-in AI, whatever the animation. Returning false skips the built-in AI for that frame. Pickup Script Items: runs when a player picks the item up. Returning true consumes the item. Player Update Script Players: runs once per frame before the player's controller, in every animation. Special Move Script Players: decides whether a defensive or offensive special may start, and its cost. HUD Script Players: view-only script drawing extra HUD sprites next to the health bar. Invincible Offensive Special Players: offensive specials start invulnerable, without the classic vulnerable window. No Charge Flash Players: no white flash when holding attack completes the charge ( noChargeFlash ). The charged attack still works.
docs.title: Entity Scripts

docs.text: Shown when an animation is selected. Name — the name shown in the animation list. Afterimages — draws a trail of afterimages behind the character during this animation, like the Ninpo clones. Visual only. Script — an optional custom Lua script driving this animation's behaviour. Added with Add Script Data , removed with Remove Script (which detaches it; the script file itself is not deleted). docs.title: Animation Settings

docs.text: Shown when a frame is selected in the timeline. Field Meaning Image ID Sprite drawn on this frame. Changing it swaps the artwork without touching timing or logic. Duration How long this frame stays on screen, in game frames.
docs.title: Frame Settings

docs.text: Offset X / Y position the sprite relative to the character's origin, in pixels. Negative X moves left, negative Y moves up. This offset is shared by every frame using the same sprite. That is the whole reason it exists as a separate concept from the pivot — see Pivots and Offsets .
docs.title: Sprite Offset

docs.text: Where a held weapon is drawn on this frame. Enable it with the checkbox; turning it off remembers the settings, so you can turn it back on without losing them. Field Meaning X / Y Position of the weapon point, in pixels relative to the character's origin. Direction Direction the held weapon points in on this frame. Show Behind Draw the weapon behind the character on this frame instead of in front.
docs.title: Weapon

docs.text: Areas that damage opponents during this frame. A frame can have several, each with its own timing and damage. Field Meaning Relative Frame Game frame, counted from the start of the selected sprite frame, on which this hitbox becomes active. 0 is the first frame. Duration How many game frames the hitbox stays active. Damage Damage dealt to an opponent caught by this hitbox. Knockdown The hit knocks the opponent down instead of just staggering them. Hit Backwards The opponent is knocked away from the direction this character faces, rather than towards it. Hit Pause Game frames both characters freeze for on a successful hit. Sound ID , Sound Mod , Sound Channel The impact sound for this specific hitbox. Classic Hitbox Use the original SOR2 hit detection instead of the editor's own box. X / Y / Width / Height The box itself, in pixels.
docs.title: Hitboxes

docs.text: Areas that can be hit during this frame. Same Relative Frame and Duration timing as hitboxes, plus X , Y , Width , Height — where X is the left edge and Y the bottom edge, and the left edge stays put as the width grows.

docs.text: Things that happen at specific moments of this frame — movement, sounds, spawning, jumping to another animation. Add one with the add button, which opens a searchable list of event types. Each event row can be expanded to show its settings or removed. See Logic Events and Logic Event Examples .
docs.title: Events

docs.text: How the character carries and releases an opponent during this animation. Added with Initialize Throw Logic ; Remove Throw Logic deletes it along with all its opponent offsets. Field Meaning Release Damage Damage dealt by the projectile at the moment it is released. Legacy Mechanics Use the original SOR2 movement and combat rules for this character instead of the newer ones. Relative To Attacker Hold the opponent relative to this character's current position and height, without the classic grab distance. Use it, with Legacy Mechanics off, for aerial or moving throws. X / Y Release velocity. Offsets hold where the carried opponent is positioned at each moment of the throw: Field Meaning Relative Frame Frame, counted from the start of the selected sprite frame, on which this offset applies. Opponent Anim Animation the held opponent is put into while this offset applies. Opponent Frame Frame of that animation to show. Same Direction The opponent faces the same way as this character instead of facing them. X / Y Distance the opponent is held at, in pixels. Positive X puts them in front; positive Y moves them up. You can drag the opponent directly in the preview instead of typing these values.

docs.text: Item and Container Logic ¶ "Item" covers everything that is not a player or an enemy: weapons, pickups, breakable containers, projectiles, debris, and scenery objects. Set Entity Type to Item and the game treats the entity as an object rather than a character. Items can be spawned from levels, from animation events, from containers, from projectiles, and from scripts. What Items Are Used For ¶ Pickups — food, money, extra lives. Weapons — knives, pipes, swords, thrown weapons. Breakable containers. Projectiles and spawned effects. Scenery and helper objects. Most of the character-oriented settings in Logic Settings are irrelevant to an item. The ones that matter are the body box, the projectile fields, and the animation logic. Projectiles ¶ An item becomes a projectile in one of two places: On the item itself — the Damage and Hit Pause projectile fields in Logic Settings, plus Hit Sound , Hit Sound Mod and Hit Channel . On the spawning event — a Spawn Item event can mark the spawned item as a projectile with isProjectile , and then supply its own damage , hitPause , hitSoundName , hitSoundPack and hitSoundChannel , along with velocity , lifetime and positionOffset . The event route is the flexible one: the same item can be spawned as a weak fast projectile by one move and a heavy slow one by another. Lifetime is in game frames, and 0 means the projectile persists until something destroys it — a common cause of projectiles that never disappear. If a projectile needs movement more complex than a constant velocity, give its active animation a Lua script and let the spawn event handle only creation. Behaviour Modes for Items ¶ Items use behaviour modes on a different numbering scheme from players and enemies. In saved data, item mode values are even numbers starting at 0x02 for the first controller. Use the editor's mode picker rather than typing numbers. Guessing a mode value is the usual reason a spawned item vanishes, freezes, ignores collision, or immediately switches to the wrong animation. See Behaviour Modes . Testing ¶ An item has more states than a character, and each is a chance to get it wrong. For a weapon, walk through the whole life cycle: Lying on the ground. Picked up by a player, and by an enemy. Swung, and connecting. Thrown, in flight. Hitting a wall. Falling and landing. Being destroyed or expiring. Containers need the same treatment: intact, being hit, breaking, and whatever they spawn on breaking. Related pages: The Inspector , Body and Hit Boxes , Logic Events , Logic Event Examples , Behaviour Modes , Audio Events , Spawns .

docs.text: Logic Events ¶ Logic events add frame-based behaviour to an animation: move the character, play a sound, spawn a projectile, branch to another animation, toggle invincibility, change health. They are the way to build a custom move without writing Lua. Adding an Event ¶ Select a frame, open the Events section in the Inspector, and use the add button. A searchable list of event types appears — type to filter it, then pick one. The new event appears as a row you can expand to edit its settings, or delete. Events are stored inside animation logic in logic.json . The One Rule That Surprises People ¶ If an animation defines any logic events, its default classic behaviour is switched off. The events become the animation's behaviour. Movement, branching, spawning and everything else must now come from the events themselves or from Lua — the original controller will not contribute any of it. Only the default physics step still runs around your events, giving you gravity and world collisions. This is deliberate: it stops original controller side effects from leaking into a custom move. But it means you cannot add one small event to an otherwise-classic animation and expect the classic behaviour to continue underneath. If you want classic behaviour, use a behaviour override and no events. Event Timing ¶ Events are placed in time in one of two ways: Exact frame — the event fires only on the frame that matches. Most events work this way. Frame window — the event is active between an after-frame and a before-frame. If both are 0 , the event is active for the whole animation. Frames are counted from the start of the selected sprite frame, so 0 is its first frame. Events run before the animation's Lua script, so a script can react to what the events have already done on that frame. Event Types ¶ Names below are exactly as they appear in the editor's list. Movement Event Effect Set Velocity Sets speed directly along each axis. Set Acceleration Applies acceleration along each axis. Input -> Velocity Translates held player input into velocity. Players only. Input -> Acceleration Translates held player input into acceleration. Players only. Set Pos Offset Shifts real position immediately, and marks the object as teleported. Stop Stops the character. AccX(0) -> Stop Stops when horizontal acceleration reaches zero. Animation branching Event Effect Set Anim Switches to another animation. Input Button -> Set Anim Switches when a button is pressed during the window. Players only. Input Combo -> Set Anim Switches when an input chain matches. Players only. Hit -> Set Anim Switches when this character's hit box connects. Players only. Land -> Set Anim Switches on landing. Land -> Set Frame Jumps to a frame of the current animation on landing. AccX(0) -> Set Frame Jumps to a frame when horizontal acceleration reaches zero. Spawning and state Event Effect Spawn Enemy Creates an enemy. Spawn Item Creates an item, optionally as a projectile with its own damage and hit sound. Grab Converts a connected hit into a grab. Flip Flips the character's facing. Destroy Removes the entity. Set Invincibility Turns invincibility on or off. Add Health Adds health; use a negative value for a cost. Set Value Writes to a custom value slot, for Lua scripts to read. Audio Event Effect Play Sound Plays a sound from a chosen mod on a chosen channel. Play Music Plays a music track. Axis Conventions ¶ For every event with X, Y and Z components: X is forward/backward — positive is forward, relative to the direction the character faces . You do not need separate events for facing left and right. Y is up/down — positive is up in the editor. The engine stores it inverted internally, but you never have to think about that while editing. Z is towards/away from the camera. Movement events have a checkbox per axis. Unticking an axis means "leave the character's existing movement on this axis alone" — which is different from setting it to zero. This lets you kill horizontal speed while preserving a jump arc, for example. Events or Lua? ¶ Use events when the answer is fixed by frame number: play a sound at frame 6, launch at frame 0, spawn at frame 7, branch on landing, cancel on a button. Use Lua when the answer depends on runtime state: how far away the target is, current health, whether a victim exists, weapon type, multi-hit cooldowns, enemy AI phase, custom recoil on hit. They combine well, and the combination is usually the right answer for a complex move: events for the predictable timeline, Lua for the exceptional branches. For worked examples with real JSON, see Logic Event Examples . Related pages: The Inspector , Behaviour Modes , Audio Events , Player Logic , Enemy Logic , Item Logic .

docs.text: Mod Characters vs Classic Reskin ¶ The Character Editor opens in one of two modes, and the choice determines where your work is saved and what it is allowed to do. Decide before you start, because moving work between the two afterwards means rebuilding it. Mod Classic Reskin Purpose Add a new entity to your mod Change how an original SOR2 entity looks Saved under Entities Entity Replacements/Classic Logic Yours — custom, or referenced from a classic entity Stays Classic Referenced by Levels, logic events, scripts, other editor data The original entity's own slot Boxes, events, throw data Editable Not editable — Classic logic governs Mod Characters ¶ Use Mod mode when the character should be part of your mod's own entity list: new playable characters, new enemies, new items, weapons, projectiles, containers, or scenery objects. Mod characters can use custom sprites and custom logic, or reference classic behaviour as a starting point. The logic reference and the sprite-art reference are two different settings. Choosing a reference entity for logic does not mean the character reuses that entity's sprites, and reusing sprites does not import its logic. Keeping these separate in your head prevents most of the confusion new authors run into. Classic Reskin ¶ Use Classic Reskin when you want an original character, enemy, or item to look different while playing exactly as it always did. A reskin uses its own custom art by default. The preview's Base toggle shows the Classic sprite behind yours, faded, which is the main tool for getting a reskin to line up with the original frame by frame — see The Workspace . Because the logic stays Classic, a reskin is a smaller job than a mod character: you are matching artwork to existing timing, not designing behaviour. Sprite Art Reuse ¶ Use Sprites from is optional and should normally be left empty — including for new characters, ROM imports, new skins, and ROM-imported skins. Enable it only when you deliberately want to extend an existing entity's art: a playable version of an enemy, an enemy version of a playable character. Reused art has to respect the referenced entity's palette layout , and should keep working with palettes made for that entity. With it enabled, you can fill an animation from one of the referenced entity's animations. What that copies depends on your mode: Mod characters — frame art and animation logic, replacing existing hit boxes, body boxes, events, script references and throw data. Classic Reskins — frame and art data only; Classic logic is untouched. For a mod character this is destructive to per-animation work you have already done. Use it early. Choosing ¶ Pick Mod when you need a new named entity. Pick Classic Reskin when you need a replacement for an existing original one. A single mod can contain both, but it is usually better not to. Reskins and new characters serve different purposes and players tend to want them separately — keep them in separate mods unless you have a reason not to. Test through Test Mod . Next: Create/Open Characters .

docs.text: Pivots, Offsets, and Alignment ¶ Pivots and offsets decide where a sprite sits relative to the character's actual gameplay position. Get them right and animations sit still, hit boxes line up, and the character stops sliding between frames. Get them wrong and every box you tune afterwards is tuned against a moving target. Pivot vs Sprite Offset ¶ These are two different things and the difference is the whole point of this page. The pivot is stored per sprite , in spriteSettings.json . It is the anchor point used to place that sprite in the world. Because it belongs to the sprite, changing it affects every animation frame that uses that sprite — across every animation in the character. The sprite offset ( Offset X / Offset Y in the Inspector) is an additional shift applied on top of the pivot. So when one frame is misaligned but other frames share the same sprite and look correct, do not move the pivot — you will break the others. That is what the sprite offset is for. In the Inspector, negative Offset X moves the sprite left and negative Offset Y moves it up. Where the Pivot Should Be ¶ The pivot should track the character's feet , and it should keep tracking them consistently. This includes jump animations. It is tempting to raise the pivot on airborne frames to make the character look like they are in the air — do not. Height in the air is produced by physics, not by art offsets. If you fake it with the pivot, the character's real position no longer matches where they appear, so hit boxes, shadows, and landings all disagree with the visuals. The same applies to attacks that lunge forward: move the character with a velocity event, not by walking the pivot sideways. Editing the Pivot ¶ The pivot is the small magenta square in the preview. Hover it and the cursor becomes a pointing hand. Drag it to adjust. Dragging up moves the pivot up — the preview matches the editor's convention that positive Y is up, even though the underlying data stores it inverted. If you cannot see the pivot handle, turn on Logic in the preview toolbar. Use Ghost while aligning: it draws a faded copy of the previous frame behind the current one, which makes drift between consecutive frames immediately visible. Base does the same with the reference character's sprite for that frame, which is what you want when matching original artwork. Opponent Offsets ¶ During a throw, the character carries the opponent through a sequence of positions before releasing them. Those positions are the Offsets inside Throw Logic , set frame by frame: X — how far in front the opponent is held (positive is in front). Y — how high (positive is up). Opponent Anim and Opponent Frame — which pose the opponent is shown in. Same Direction — whether the opponent faces the same way as the thrower instead of facing them. You can drag the opponent's sprite directly in the preview instead of typing numbers, which is much faster for getting a slam or a swing to read well. Order of Work ¶ Alignment work has a dependency order, and skipping it means doing the later steps twice: Pivots for idle and movement frames — these set the character's resting position. Pivots for attack and hit-reaction frames. Sprite offsets for individual frames that still look wrong. Hit boxes, body boxes, weapon points, and throw offsets. Boxes come last because they are positioned relative to the origin. Move a pivot after tuning boxes and the boxes are now wrong. Related pages: Animations and Frames , Body and Hit Boxes , The Inspector , Logic Events .
docs.title: Pivots, Offsets, and Alignment

docs.text: Pivots and offsets decide where a sprite sits relative to the character's actual gameplay position. Get them right and animations sit still, hit boxes line up, and the character stops sliding between frames. Get them wrong and every box you tune afterwards is tuned against a moving target.
docs.title: Pivots, Offsets, and Alignment

docs.text: These are two different things and the difference is the whole point of this page. The pivot is stored per sprite , in spriteSettings.json . It is the anchor point used to place that sprite in the world. Because it belongs to the sprite, changing it affects every animation frame that uses that sprite — across every animation in the character. The sprite offset ( Offset X / Offset Y in the Inspector) is an additional shift applied on top of the pivot. So when one frame is misaligned but other frames share the same sprite and look correct, do not move the pivot — you will break the others. That is what the sprite offset is for. In the Inspector, negative Offset X moves the sprite left and negative Offset Y moves it up.
docs.title: Pivot vs Sprite Offset

docs.text: The pivot should track the character's feet , and it should keep tracking them consistently. This includes jump animations. It is tempting to raise the pivot on airborne frames to make the character look like they are in the air — do not. Height in the air is produced by physics, not by art offsets. If you fake it with the pivot, the character's real position no longer matches where they appear, so hit boxes, shadows, and landings all disagree with the visuals. The same applies to attacks that lunge forward: move the character with a velocity event, not by walking the pivot sideways.
docs.title: Where the Pivot Should Be

docs.text: The pivot is the small magenta square in the preview. Hover it and the cursor becomes a pointing hand. Drag it to adjust. Dragging up moves the pivot up — the preview matches the editor's convention that positive Y is up, even though the underlying data stores it inverted. If you cannot see the pivot handle, turn on Logic in the preview toolbar. Use Ghost while aligning: it draws a faded copy of the previous frame behind the current one, which makes drift between consecutive frames immediately visible. Base does the same with the reference character's sprite for that frame, which is what you want when matching original artwork.
docs.title: Editing the Pivot

docs.text: During a throw, the character carries the opponent through a sequence of positions before releasing them. Those positions are the Offsets inside Throw Logic , set frame by frame: X — how far in front the opponent is held (positive is in front). Y — how high (positive is up). Opponent Anim and Opponent Frame — which pose the opponent is shown in. Same Direction — whether the opponent faces the same way as the thrower instead of facing them. You can drag the opponent's sprite directly in the preview instead of typing numbers, which is much faster for getting a slam or a swing to read well.
docs.title: Opponent Offsets

docs.text: Player Logic ¶ Settings that apply to a playable character as a whole. They live in Logic Settings in the Inspector, with the character itself selected rather than an animation or frame. Set Entity Type to Player . This decides which runtime systems treat the entity as player-controlled and which behaviour modes are available to it. In practice the entity type is usually already correct, because it comes from the reference character you chose when creating the character. Movement and Combat Values ¶ Field What it changes Walk Speed Movement speed while walking. Run Speed Movement speed while running. Jump Force Upward impulse on jump. Higher jumps higher. Jump Delay Game frames between pressing jump and actually leaving the ground. Can Use Weapons Whether the character may pick up and use weapons. Combo Repetitions How many times the standard attack combo can repeat before resetting. Grab Combo Repetitions How many times the grab attack combo can repeat before resetting. Charge Delay Game frames the attack button must be held before the charged move becomes available. Grab Range How close an opponent must be to be grabbed. Front Grab Offset Distance a grabbed opponent is held at, when grabbed from the front. Back Grab Offset Distance a grabbed opponent is held at, when grabbed from behind. Knockdown Quake Screen shake when the character hits the ground after a knockdown. 0 disables it. Thrown Quake Screen shake when the character lands after being thrown. 0 disables it. Treat all of these as feel, not numbers. Jump Delay in particular changes how responsive the character reads, and Grab Range together with the grab offsets decides whether grabs connect reliably or feel like a coin flip. Change one at a time and test. Custom Moves From Input ¶ Player-only events let you build move transitions that respond to the pad: Input Button -> Set Anim — watches a single button during a frame window. Input Combo -> Set Anim — watches an input chain, checked against the player's input history rather than just the current frame. Input -> Velocity and Input -> Acceleration — turn held directions into movement, giving a move air control or drift. The frame window is the design here, not an implementation detail. A cancel window of frames 9–16 on an attack means the player can flow into the follow-up only after commitment but before recovery — widening it makes the character feel loose, narrowing it makes the move feel strict. Set the after/before frames deliberately. See Logic Events for the full event list and Logic Event Examples for worked command moves and cancel windows. Sounds ¶ The Sounds section holds the character's default audio: Run , Jump , Landing , Attack , Jump Attack , Weapon Throw , Blitz , Defensive Special , Offensive Special , Grab Move 1/2/3 , Quake , Low Health , Death , Last Life Death . Each is a list, and the game picks randomly among the entries. Give repeated actions — attacks, jumps, hurt sounds — two or three variations, or the character will sound mechanical within a minute of play. See Audio Events . Scripts and Behaviour Overrides ¶ Individual animations can go beyond events: Script attaches Lua, for moves whose behaviour depends on runtime state. Behaviour borrows a classic controller wholesale, for moves that should feel exactly like an original one. These are per-animation, set in the Inspector with the animation selected. See Behaviour Modes . Related pages: The Inspector , Body and Hit Boxes , Logic Events , Behaviour Modes , Audio Events , Test Mod .

docs.text: Play a Different Animation for a Held Weapon ¶ This tutorial makes an existing move branch to a different animation while the character holds a specific weapon. For example, pressing the usual blitz input can play Knife Blitz when a Classic knife is held and keep the normal blitz for every other weapon. This condition needs a small Lua script. Logic events can branch on frames, buttons, combos, hits, and landings, but they do not have a weapon-condition event. Before You Start ¶ You need: the normal animation that receives the input, such as Blitz ; a finished weapon-specific animation, such as Knife Blitz ; the exact weapon entity name and its mod name. Add the weapon-specific animation at the end of the animation list. Animation references use list positions, so inserting or reordering animations can silently change existing references. Note the number shown for the new animation; this tutorial calls it 41 . Enable Can Use Weapons under the character's Logic Settings if the character cannot already pick weapons up. Create the Redirect Script ¶ Create this file inside the editable mod: Editor/<Your Mod>/Scripts/Knife Blitz.lua Add: return function() local character = game.this_character if character == nil or not character.is_player then return true end local weapon = character.weapon if weapon == nil then return true end if weapon.pack_name == "Classic" and weapon.name == "Knife" then character.set_animation(41) return false end return true end Change 41 to the editor number of your weapon-specific animation. Change Classic and Knife if the weapon comes from another mod or has a different entity name. Name comparisons are case-sensitive. Using weapon.name is clearer and more portable than comparing a numeric entity_type . Custom entities use runtime hashes, while original entities may use legacy numeric IDs. Attach It in the Character Editor ¶ Open the character and select the normal animation that should redirect, such as Blitz . In the Inspector, find Script & Behaviour and choose Add Script Data . Set Mod Name to the mod containing the script. Set Script Name to Knife Blitz . Omit the .lua extension. Let the editor save, then launch Test Mod from the game's mod editor. Trigger the move once without a weapon, once with a different weapon, and once with the knife. The script's update function runs on every frame while the normal animation is active. When it finds the matching held weapon, set_animation(41) queues the alternate animation. Returning false stops the old animation's controller from continuing during that frame. Returning true in every non-matching case preserves the normal move. If You Want Several Weapon Variants ¶ Use one branch for each weapon, replacing the end of the update function: if weapon.pack_name == "Classic" and weapon.name == "Knife" then character.set_animation(41) return false elseif weapon.pack_name == "Classic" and weapon.name == "Pipe" then character.set_animation(42) return false elseif weapon.pack_name == "My Weapons" and weapon.name == "Hammer" then character.set_animation(43) return false end return true Keep this redirect script on the normal entry animation. Do not attach it to the target animations too, or they can continually queue themselves. Troubleshooting ¶ The normal animation always plays: check the spelling and capitalization of pack_name and name . Temporarily add print(weapon.pack_name, weapon.name) after the nil check, then read the Unity log while testing. The wrong animation plays: the number passed to set_animation is the animation's current editor list position. Check it again after adding, removing, or reordering animations. The target animation appears but immediately behaves like another move: select the target animation and configure its events, script, or behaviour override . The redirect only chooses the animation; it does not define that animation's controller. The character cannot pick up the weapon: enable Can Use Weapons in Player Logic . The weapon is drawn in the wrong place: select each target frame and configure its Weapon point, direction, and front/behind setting. See Pivots and Offsets . Related pages: Getting Started With Lua , Combat and Defense Examples , Animations and Frames .

docs.text: The Workspace ¶ Select an animation or frame to show its settings in the Inspector. Panel Layout ¶ Once a character is open, the window is divided into five areas: Area Position What it holds Animations Left, top The animation list, with a search box, + (add), - (delete) and the 🏠 home button. All Sprites Left, bottom Every sprite available to this character, with a search box. Drag from here into the timeline. Preview Centre The current frame, drawn with its boxes, pivot and weapon point. This is where you drag things. Timeline Bottom The frames of the selected animation, in order, plus the Play button. Inspector Right Every setting for whatever is currently selected. Its contents change with your selection. The 🏠 button closes the current character and returns to the startup screen. Normal edits save automatically. Preview Mouse Controls ¶ The preview is a zoomable canvas, not a fixed image. Input Action Wheel up / down Zoom in / out by 10% per notch, centred on the mouse pointer. Right-drag or Middle-drag Pan the view. Left-drag on empty space Pan the view. Left-click on empty space Deselect / select whatever is under the pointer. Left-drag on a gizmo Move or resize it (see below). Because a left-drag on empty space pans, the editor distinguishes a click from a drag by distance: if you press and release without moving far, it is treated as a click and selects; if you move, it pans. Reading the Cursor ¶ The pointer tells you what you are about to grab before you press the button. This is the fastest way to avoid dragging the wrong thing: Cursor Meaning Pointing hand Over the pivot handle, or over the character sprite. Move (four arrows) Over the body of a box, or the weapon point — dragging moves the whole thing. Horizontal / vertical resize Over a box edge — dragging resizes in that one direction. Diagonal resize Over a box corner — dragging resizes both directions. If you see no special cursor, the overlays are probably hidden. Turn Logic back on. Gizmos in the Preview ¶ Gizmo Appearance Drag behaviour Pivot Small magenta square Moves the sprite's pivot. Dragging up moves the pivot up. Body boxes Blue rectangles Move by the body, resize by edges and corners. Hit boxes Coloured rectangles Same as body boxes. Weapon point Cyan marker Drag the marker to move it; drag the rotation handle to change Direction . Opponent The held opponent's sprite Drag to set the opponent offset for this frame. Weapon direction snaps to the nearest of the available directions as you rotate, rather than being free-angle. Preview Toolbar ¶ Along the top of the preview: Ghost — shows a faded copy of the previous frame's sprite behind the current one, so you can line up movement between frames. Base — shows the sprite the reference character uses for this frame, faded behind the current one, as a guide for matching the original artwork. Alpha (the number next to Base, e.g. 0.45 ) — how visible the reference artwork is, from 0.1 for barely visible to 1 for fully opaque. Logic — shows or hides all the editing overlays: hit boxes, body boxes, the pivot handle, the weapon point and the opponent preview. Turn it off to judge the artwork on its own. Keyboard Shortcuts ¶ Key Action ↑ / ↓ Previous / next animation. ← / → Previous / next frame. Space Play or stop the animation. Ctrl+C Copy the current selection. Ctrl+V Paste. Ctrl+S Save. Delete Delete the current selection. Two things about these shortcuts are worth knowing, because they are not obvious: They are context-sensitive. Delete and copy/paste act on whatever you last selected — an animation, a frame, a hit box, or a body box. Selecting a hit box and pressing Delete removes that hit box, not the frame it sits on. They are suppressed while you are typing. Arrow keys, Space and Ctrl+C/V do nothing while a text field has focus, so you can type a name containing spaces without triggering playback. Click away from the field to get the shortcuts back. Copy and Paste Between Frames ¶ Beyond Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V, right-clicking a frame in the timeline gives you selective pasting, which is what you usually want when reusing work across similar attacks: Copy Logic — copies the frame's hit boxes, body boxes, events and throw data together. Paste Logic (Replace) — overwrites all of it on the target frame. Paste Hitboxes Only / Paste Bodyboxes Only / Paste Events Only / Paste Throw Data Only — pastes just that one category and leaves everything else on the target frame alone. Entries that would paste nothing are greyed out, so the menu also tells you what is currently on the clipboard. The same Copy Logic and Paste Logic buttons appear in the Inspector when a frame is selected. Saving ¶ Every change is saved immediately and automatically. There is no save step to remember and no unsaved-changes state during normal editing — Ctrl+S exists, but you rarely need it. This is what makes the hot-reload workflow practical: change a value here, switch to SOR2 New Era, hot-reload, and you are testing the new value. See Test Mod . Next: Create/Open Characters , Animations .

docs.text: In-Game Mod Editor ¶ The in-game mod editor is the main hub for mod authoring. It lets you create or edit an existing draft mod, configure the mod, launch the bundled editing tools, test gameplay, edit palettes, open scripts, delete drafts, and export a package. The Character Editor, Level Editor, and Audio Editor are included with the game and are launched from the selected mod's editor menu. They receive the selected mod folder automatically. Main Tasks ¶ Create New Mod - start a new editable mod folder. Mod Settings - edit the mod name, description, preview image, and gameplay settings. Difficulty Settings - configure difficulty names, initial lives, credits, game settings multipliers per player-count. Open Tools - launch Character Editor, Level Editor, Audio Editor, the palette editor, or the scripts folder. Test Mod - launch the selected mod in editor test mode. Color Palettes - edit palette variants through the built-in game editor. Export Mod - package the mod for use in the main game. Where Editor Data Lives ¶ Editor mods are stored as editable folders. The in-game editor creates and manages those folders for you. The bundled tools then add subfolders such as Entities , Levels , Sounds , Musics , Scripts , Palettes , and replacement data depending on what you edit. Avoid renaming or moving an editor mod folder while a tool is open. The tools save directly into the selected folder and expect the path passed by the game to stay valid. Save Expectations ¶ Changes are saved as you edit. Consider making frequent backups by copying the editable mod's folder to another location.Test frequently, see Test Mod . Related references: Character Editor , Level Editor , Audio Editor .

docs.text: Color Palettes ¶ Color palettes are edited through the game's built-in palette editor, opened from the selected mod's in-game editor menu. The Character Editor does not edit palettes; it focuses on character sprites, animation data, icon, portrait, boxes, logic, and audio events. What Palettes Affect ¶ Palettes define color variants for indexed character art and palette-enabled references. A palette can be local to your mod's character or can be an external palette entry that targets a character from another mod. Use palettes when you want alternate colors without duplicating every sprite. Use reskins in the Character Editor when the silhouette, pose, shading, or animation itself changes. Typical Workflow ¶ Open the selected mod in the in-game editor. Choose Palettes . Select the target character or entity. Choose Create New to make an editable copy of the default palette. Select a colour swatch, then adjust its sliders. Change the preview frame to check other parts of the character. Change precision to show fewer broad colour groups or more detailed groups. Precision changes the editing controls, not the sprite resolution. Back out to save. Changes also save when you switch palettes or precision. Use Test Mod to check the result and its current preview limitations. Default is read-only. Its disabled controls are intentional. Create a variant before editing or importing a reference image. When a variant already exists, the editor opens on an editable palette. You can select or drop a reference image onto an editable palette. The colour swatches rebuild after the image loads. Wait for the controls to become available before editing. Deleting a palette shifts later palette numbers down by one. Check any level spawns that refer to those numbers after deletion. Palette References ¶ Level spawns indicate which palette mod and palette index an enemy or item uses. See Spawns . Related pages: Icon and Portrait , Create/Open Characters , Test Mod .

docs.text: Difficulty Settings ¶ Difficulty Settings controls the mod's list of difficulties and how each difficulty scales for different player counts. It is available when Mod Settings has gameplay settings enabled. Difficulty List ¶ The editor lets you choose how many difficulty levels the mod exposes. Each difficulty has: A display name. Enemy difficulty value. Starting lives. Starting credits. Score thresholds for extra lives. The default table includes familiar difficulty names such as Very Easy, Easy, Normal, Hard, Hardest, Mania, Mania Plus, and MegaMania. You can rename, remove, or add difficulties to fit the mod. Per-Player Scaling ¶ Each difficulty stores separate settings for different player counts. This lets a four-player game spawn more enemies or activate waves faster than a solo game without changing the displayed difficulty name. Per-player settings include: Maximum enemies on screen. Enemy health multiplier. Boss health multiplier. Enemy damage multiplier. Enemy velocity multiplier. Enemy on-screen activation multiplier. Enemy timer activation multiplier. Player damage multiplier. Whether the next spawn difficulty tier is used. Testing Balance ¶ Always test the same level on multiple player counts after changing difficulty settings. Spawn density, activation speed, and boss health can feel correct for one player but become too easy or boring for four players. Related pages: Test Mod , Spawns , Enemy Logic .

docs.text: Export Mod ¶ Export packages an editable mod folder into a shippable mod file. Once exported, the mod becomes available in the main game. Export only after the mod has been tested from the in-game editor, making sure all content loads and behaves correctly. Before Exporting ¶ Run Test Mod first. Check that: The mod opens without missing dependency errors. Characters load with the correct icon, portrait, sprites, sounds, and behave correctly in all scenarios. Levels load with the intended art, spawns, walls, music, and cutscenes. Character color palettes can be tested in editor test mode, including through Hot Reload. Still test the exported package before distributing it. Don't make changes through the bundled editor tools during the export process. The exporter builds the playable package in the game's Mods folder. The export screen reports the current step, such as exporting entities, palettes, audio, levels, or scripts. The more content a mod has, the longer it takes to export. Try to keep mods small. Prefer having multiple mods with individual purposes (e.g. reskin, characters pack, new game mode), than a single monolitic mod with everything. After Exporting ¶ Test the exported content in the main game. This catches differences between editable folder loading and packaged loading. The file in Mods is the package to share. Upload it wherever you prefer, post a download link for other players, or send it directly to friends. New Era does not currently provide hosting for community mods. Lua scripts are precompiled during export. Keep the game executable updated together with the exporter: older executables cannot read newer bytecode formats. The current loader also repairs the function addresses in exports made with the older format, so those packages do not need to be exported again to use them with the updated game. Exported OGG music uses Unity's native audio decoder and retains the track's loop points. If an older executable plays WAV music but leaves OGG tracks silent, update the executable; the existing exported OGG files do not need to be converted or exported again. For netplay, every player must use the same exported version. The game compares the loaded mod checksum, so if you re-export the mod after a change, send the new package to every player. Related pages: Mod Settings , Difficulty Settings , Open Tools , Installing Community Mods .

docs.text: Mod Settings ¶ Mod Settings controls the public identity of the mod and optional gameplay rules. Open it from the selected mod's in-game editor menu. Basic Fields ¶ Name is the mod's display name and editable folder name. Avoid changing it, because character logic, sprite references, sounds, music, palettes, and replacement data may have direct references to the mod name - renaming the mod can break those references. Description is shown to players when browsing mods. Use it to describe the experience, required dependencies, or the scope of the mod. Preview Image changes the thumbnail shown for the mod in menus. Pick an image that identifies the mod clearly at small sizes. Gameplay Settings ¶ Enable gameplay settings when the mod should be playable and should not rely on existing settings from a dependency mod. Choose Gameplay Rules... for the mod's permanent rules. These are stored in the mod's config.json and travel with the exported mod. The Custom Game screen configures a play session instead. Group What you can change Combat and co-op Friendly fire, enemy infighting, direction on hit, shadow clones, killer or exploding enemies, instant spawns, infinite continues, starting health and player limits. Balance overrides Enemy health, damage and speed; player damage; scroll speed; doubled enemy spawns; enemy randomizer and seed; score thresholds for extra lives. Classic behaviour and controls Widescreen, New Era improvements, smooth controls, classic slowdown, camera advance checks and the sprite buffer fix. thrownCharactersSparePlayers has no button: set it in config.json to keep friendly fire while bodies thrown by a player never hit other players. See config.json . Click an On/Off button to switch a rule. Click a choice button to cycle its options. Scroll to see the remaining groups; keyboard/controller selection also brings rows into view. Save Rules validates and saves your changes. Cancel discards changes made on this screen. Opening the screen first saves the name, description and basic settings from the parent menu. For multipliers, 1 means 100% and 1.5 means 150%. Leave an override blank to use the difficulty's value; blank scroll speed uses the normal speed. Extra-life scores are comma-separated, for example 20000, 50000, 150000 . Use Difficulty Settings for lives, credits and balance that varies by difficulty or number of players. A global override takes precedence over its corresponding difficulty value. Disabling gameplay settings after changing them can discard those gameplay-specific values. The editor asks for confirmation when the current settings differ from the defaults. Practical Guidance ¶ Use gameplay settings for total conversions, curated level packs, balance mods, and mods that rely on a custom enemy count or damage curve. Leave them disabled for asset-only mods such as character packs, audio packs, or palette packs. A mod with just gameplay settings can be exported as a new way of playing the classic game. The Ninpo Kage Bunshin mod is an example of that: it uses the classic content, just with new gameplay settings. Pack imports, character restrictions and global Lua hooks still require config.json . Existing values are preserved when saving gameplay rules. Shared lives, duplicate character selection and stiffness belong to the current session configuration; they are not persistent mod fields. Related pages: Create New Mod , Difficulty Settings , Test Mod , Export Mod .

docs.text: Open Tools ¶ The selected mod's editor menu opens the bundled tools for that mod. The game passes the selected mod folder to each tool, so the tool opens directly into the right data. Tool Buttons ¶ Character Editor opens the character tool for mod characters and classic character reskins . Level Editor opens the level tool for mod levels and classic level reskins . It also includes cutscenes, character select and title screen reskins. Audio Editor opens the audio tool for custom audio and classic audio replacements . Palettes opens the game's built-in palette editor. Palettes are not edited in the Character Editor. See Color Palettes . Scripts opens the selected mod's Scripts folder. Lua scripts are edited using a basic text editor program or an IDE with support for Lua (not included). Launch Notes ¶ Keep the game and tool open while editing if that is convenient, but avoid opening the same mod in multiple copies of the same tool. Each tool saves into the same mod folder, so two copies can overwrite each other's recent changes. Test changes using Test Mod . Use hot-reloading for quick edit and test iterations.

docs.text: Test Mod ¶ Use Test from the selected mod's in-game editor menu to play the mod with editor data loaded. This is the fastest way to catch missing files, invalid references, bad loops, broken spawns, and gameplay balance problems before exporting. What Test Does ¶ Test mode sends you through difficulty selection and loads content from the editable mod folder. Gameplay mods use their own game pack, borrowing missing content from 30th Anniversary . Presentation-only reskins run 30th Anniversary with the editor mod applied as a skin, keeping gameplay and the roster supplied by the base pack. Test falls back to Classic if 30th Anniversary is unavailable. Use test mode after: Adding or changing character animations, boxes, logic, or audio events. Editing level scenes, spawns, walls, collision, or music. Adding custom sounds, music, loop metadata. Changing difficulty settings. Editing character color palettes. Choose a palette in character selection; players and enemy spawns use their configured palettes in-game. Classic character, level, audio and cutscene reskins can all be tested here without exporting. Test applies the editor skin temporarily and leaves your saved skin preferences unchanged. Hot Reload ¶ While testing, you do not have to quit and relaunch to pick up an edit. Pause the game and choose Hot Reload . This reloads the active content pack — and the editor pack too, when they differ — then resumes play. You stay in the same session, at the same point in the level, with your reloaded data in place. Test builds a stable color mapping from the character's base palette guide, then indexes only sprites requested by the normal loaders. Character selection loads its idle frames and icons; full animation art is loaded when that character is needed in gameplay. A cache in memory tracks source image hashes, indexed pixels and live textures. An unchanged Hot Reload reuses those textures. Editing an alternate palette updates colors without rebaking sprites; editing sprite art only rebakes that sprite. Changing the base guide invalidates dependent sprites, which are rebuilt when requested. Colors absent from the base guide use its nearest color, as in a palette preview, so keep the guide representative of your art. The cache survives Hot Reload and repeated tests of that draft, but is rebuilt after restarting the application or reopening the draft with a new provider. Source art is never overwritten. Verify the exported package too: export computes its mapping from the full sprite set. Hot Reload only appears in the pause menu while a mod is open in the editor. It is not present in a normal game, so if you cannot find it, you are probably running an exported mod rather than testing an editable one. This pairs with the editors saving every change immediately: there is no save step in the Character, Level or Audio Editor, so the loop is simply Change a value in the editor. Switch to the running game. Pause, and choose Hot Reload . Keep playing, now with the change applied. That makes it practical to tune things that can only be judged in motion — hit box timing, hit pause, jump arcs, grab range, enemy aggressiveness, music loop seams. Two caveats. Hot Reload re-reads content, so it does not undo anything that already happened in the session: enemies you have killed stay dead, and an enemy already on screen keeps the stats it spawned with. For changes to spawn data or level structure, restart the level. And because it discards palettes it no longer recognises, a palette you renamed mid-session may vanish rather than update. Good Test Passes ¶ For characters, test player control, enemy AI, hit reactions, throws, item pickup, weapon use, sounds, and portrait/icon presentation. See Character Editor . For levels, test scene transitions, scroll boundaries, wall collision, spawn triggers, enemy order, item placement, cutscenes, music, and special screens. See Level Editor . For audio, test replacement entries, music start points, loop transitions, and volume balance. See Audio Editor . Troubleshooting ¶ If something works in a tool preview but fails in test mode, check references first: mod names, entity names, sound names, music names, animation IDs, and classic replacement targets must match the saved data. Export only after the mod loads cleanly in Test. Related page: Export Mod .

It is launched from the selected mod's in-game editor menu and saves into that mod folder. Use it in Mod mode to create your own levels and cutscenes. docs.text: Art Animation ¶ Art animation lets background elements move independently of enemy and item gameplay. Use it for animated signs, water, fire, effects, doors, screen elements, or repeated environmental motion. Art Assets ¶ The Level Editor stores image assets in the level art folder. Drag PNG or GIF art into the editor to add images or create animations. GIF imports are split into frames, similar to the Character Editor workflow. Static images are placed directly on a layer. Animation references point to an animation definition and place that animation at a position on the current layer. Animation Definitions ¶ An art animation definition is a list of frames. Each frame can store: Image name. Delay frames. Pivot in pixels. Scale. The timeline lets you select, reorder, insert, replace, and delete frames. Animation References ¶ An animation reference is an instance of an animation placed in a layer. The same animation definition can be reused by multiple references. This is useful when several signs, lights, or moving elements share the same timing. Editing Tips ¶ Use static images for large stable art. Use animations for elements that need timing. Keep animation frames cropped consistently, or use pivots to remove jitter. For special screens, convert images to Title Screen Image entries when they need title-screen specific movement fields. See Special Screens . Related pages: Background Layers , Levels, Scenes, and Cutscenes .
docs.title: Art Assets and Animation Timeline

docs.text: Art animation lets background elements move independently of enemy and item gameplay. Use it for animated signs, water, fire, effects, doors, screen elements, or repeated environmental motion.
docs.title: Art Animation

docs.text: The Level Editor stores image assets in the level art folder. Drag PNG or GIF art into the editor to add images or create animations. GIF imports are split into frames, similar to the Character Editor workflow. Static images are placed directly on a layer. Animation references point to an animation definition and place that animation at a position on the current layer.
docs.title: Art Assets

docs.text: An art animation definition is a list of frames. Each frame can store: Image name. Delay frames. Pivot in pixels. Scale. The timeline lets you select, reorder, insert, replace, and delete frames.
docs.title: Animation Definitions

docs.text: An animation reference is an instance of an animation placed in a layer. The same animation definition can be reused by multiple references. This is useful when several signs, lights, or moving elements share the same timing.
docs.title: Animation References

docs.text: Use static images for large stable art. Use animations for elements that need timing. Keep animation frames cropped consistently, or use pivots to remove jitter. For special screens, convert images to Title Screen Image entries when they need title-screen specific movement fields. See Special Screens . Related pages: Background Layers , Levels, Scenes, and Cutscenes .
docs.title: Editing Tips

docs.text: Background Layers ¶ Background layers build the visual scene around the gameplay space. Each scene can have several layers, and each layer holds static images and animation references. A scene with no layers of its own reuses the art of the closest previous scene that has some, back to the last scene with an exit, as the game does. The preview draws that art for it too, though its layers stay listed under the scene that owns them. Layer Properties ¶ Property Meaning Layer Name Identifies the layer in the layer list. Editor-only. Z Order Drawing order. Layers with a higher value are drawn in front of those with a lower one. Position Offset Shift applied to everything on this layer, in pixels. Parallax How fast the layer scrolls compared to the camera. Auto Scroll Speed at which the layer keeps scrolling on its own, in pixels per second , independently of the camera. Scroll Loop Limits The range over which the layer repeats. Once it scrolls past these limits it wraps, tiling endlessly. Update Type Special runtime update behaviour. React to Quake Makes the layer shake along with the screen during a quake. Parallax Values ¶ Parallax is the depth cue, and its scale is easy to remember once stated plainly: 1 — moves exactly with the camera. This is the gameplay plane. Below 1 — moves slower. Reads as further away . Skylines, distant buildings, sky. Above 1 — moves faster. Reads as nearer than the action . Foreground railings, pillars, foliage. The further a value sits from 1, the stronger the depth effect. Very low values suit things that should feel effectively infinite, like a horizon. Position Offset is a placement correction, not a depth cue — use it to align art to the world instead of re-exporting the PNG. Auto Scroll and Looping ¶ Auto Scroll moves a layer continuously regardless of whether the player advances. It is what drives water, conveyor belts, drifting clouds, and passing scenery on a moving vehicle. Auto-scrolling art almost always needs Scroll Loop Limits as well, or it scrolls away and leaves a gap. Set the loop range to the art's repeat size so the seam falls where the art tiles. Looping is equally useful without auto scroll, for long stretches of repeating road or skyline that the camera pans across. Quake Reaction ¶ React to Quake is per layer, which lets you shake selectively. Shaking the gameplay-plane layers while a distant skyline stays still reads as a convincing earthquake; shaking everything equally tends to read as the camera wobbling. Visual Script ¶ Visual Script attaches a view-only Lua script to the layer. It can hide the layer, offset it, or drive its palette animation clock, and it never affects gameplay. Pick the script from the mod's Scripts/ folder, with an optional Mod ; X removes the reference. See Scripted stages . Indexed Tilemaps ¶ A layer can carry an indexed Genesis tilemap ( tilemap in the art file), usually written by ROM import tools. The preview draws it at the layer's top-left corner, with its palette as the stage starts (the first frame of each palette cycle, or the base colours where Keep Base is set); the cycles' animation and visual scripts only play in game. The Inspector shows its size and palette cycles, and edits: Field Meaning Scale Size multiplier of the tilemap around the layer's top-left corner. 0 is the same as 1 . Keep Base Per palette cycle: keep the base palette until the first cycle step is due, instead of starting on the first cycle frame. The tile art, cells and palettes are kept exactly as they are when the level is saved. Classic Reskin Layers ¶ In Classic Reskin mode, a new replacement level can copy its layer structure from the original SOR2 reference data. That preserves layer names, parallax, auto scroll, loop limits, update type, quake behaviour, offsets and z order — you supply only the replacement art. Start from the copied structure. The original values encode how the stage was designed to move, and matching them is most of what makes a reskin feel like the stage it replaces. Related pages: The Level Editor Workspace , Art Animation , Walls, Scroll, and Collision , Special Screens .

docs.text: Levels, Scenes, and Cutscenes ¶ The Level Editor organizes content into levels, scenes, layers, and cutscenes. Understanding that structure makes it easier to know where a setting belongs. Levels ¶ A level is a playable stage entry. In Mod mode, each level can have gameplay data and art data. Gameplay data controls entities scale, scenes, transitions, spawns, walls, scroll limits, and collision. Art data controls background scenes, layers, images, animations, music, and cutscene timing. Level files are saved with names such as level 1.json and level 1 - art.json . Scenes ¶ A scene is one playable section of a level. Scenes define how the player enters, how the scene exits, how far the camera scrolls, which enemies and items load, and which background scene is displayed. The sidebar lets you add, select, delete, and reorder scene-level content. The inspector shows scene fields when a scene is selected. Cutscenes ¶ Cutscenes use the same background/art data model as level backgrounds, but they are played as presentation sequences rather than normal beat-em-up scenes. A level can have its own cutscene file, and a mod can also define special presentation or ending data. Classic Reskin mode can also create cutscenes for classic levels and special screens. See Special Screens . Practical Order ¶ Build in this order: Create or select the level. Add scenes. Configure scene navigation and scroll settings. Add background layers and art. Place spawns. Tune walls and collision. Add music and cutscene timing. Related pages: Scene Settings , Background Layers , Spawns .

docs.text: Mod Levels vs Classic Reskin ¶ The Level Editor has two main modes: Mod and Classic Reskin . Choose the mode based on whether you need new playable level logic or replacement visuals for original SOR2 content. Mod Levels ¶ Use Mod mode to create a level set owned by your mod. Mod levels can define gameplay structure and art together. Mod levels can include: Level files such as level 1.json . Art files such as level 1 - art.json . Optional cutscene files such as level 1 - cutscenes.json . Level-specific entities scale. Scene navigation settings. Enemy and item spawns. Walls, scroll limits, diagonal limits, and custom collision shapes. Background layers, images, and animations. Scene music. Use Mod mode for new campaigns, custom stages, challenge rooms, or gameplay layouts that differ from classic SOR2. Classic Reskin ¶ Use Classic Reskin to replace the original SOR2 art and special screens while keeping the classic level structure. Classic reskin level art is saved under Level Replacements/Classic . Classic Reskin mode is best for: Replacing classic stage art. Adding replacement cutscenes for classic levels. Replacing title, presentation, or ending-style screens. Matching original scene counts and layer behavior. Classic Reskin mode does not focus on editing enemy waves or gameplay scene logic. Use Mod mode when you need to change spawns, walls, or level progression. Next: Levels, Scenes, and Cutscenes .
