docs.text: Scene Settings ¶ Scene settings control how a level section starts, ends, moves, and plays music. Select a scene to edit them in the Inspector. Entities Scale ¶ Entities Scale is the size multiplier applied to the characters and items in the scene, with 1 drawing them at original size. Change it with care. It alters how characters relate to the background art and to collision, so a scene that looked right can end up with characters standing too high on the floor line or unable to reach a walkable edge. If you change it, re-check walls and spawn positions afterwards. Scene Navigation ¶ Field Meaning Enter Type How players enter the scene. Exit Type How the scene exits or transitions to the next. Movement The scene's movement or shake style. Start Offset Special starting offset behaviour. These fields exist to support the original game's set pieces, so match them to what the scene is: a closed room, an elevator, a moving truck, a boat. A scene whose art implies motion but whose Movement is left at the default will feel static no matter what the background does. Presentation ¶ Field Meaning Alternative Palette Name of an alternative colour palette applied to this scene's artwork. Copy Alt Palette Copies the alternative palette from the previous scene instead of loading its own. Center Screen for Widescreen Centres the scene horizontally on widescreen displays instead of anchoring it to the left. Copy Alt Palette is how you keep a palette consistent across a run of scenes without repeating the name in each — set it on the scene where the palette is established, then copy through the rest. Center Screen for Widescreen matters for scenes whose art is not wide enough to fill a modern display. Anchored left, the empty space all lands on one side; centred, it splits evenly and usually reads better. Scripting ¶ Scenes can hand parts of their flow to Lua. Each script field takes a script name from the mod's Scripts/ folder (the v button lists them) and an optional Mod ; leave the mod empty for the current mod. Add Script creates the reference and X removes it; the script file itself is not touched. Field Meaning Enter Script Runs once when the scene starts, after the players are placed and before anything spawns. Update Script Runs once per gameplay update, before the entities update. Not during entrance and exit transitions. Post Update Runs once per gameplay update, after the entities animated and weapons were attached. Scripted Entrance Skip the automatic entrance walk; the Enter Script places the players. Scripted Progress Waves and scenes do not advance on their own; the script calls game.change_scene . Scripted Enemies Enemy cues do not spawn on their own; the script spawns them with game.spawn_scene_enemy(index) . Scripted Items Item cues do not spawn on their own; the script spawns them with game.spawn_scene_item(index) . Preload Items Spawn every item cue regardless of the camera position, for scenes the player walks back through. Scripted Clock The HUD clock no longer counts down or deals time-out damage; scripts set it. Scripted Enemies and Scripted Items address cues by their position in the list, so in those scenes the editor keeps the cues in the order they are stored instead of sorting them by X when it saves. Camera Route gives scripted cinematics a straight camera path for the scene: Route Start and Route End are absolute Lua camera_x / camera_y pixels at the configured viewport width. An end X larger than the start X means the camera travels right. It only informs presentation; the gameplay camera is unchanged. See Scripted stages for the Lua side. Music ¶ Each scene defines a Music Mod and Music Name . Leave the mod empty to use the current mod; you can also pick from Classic or another referenced mod. The picker offers a clear option, which makes the scene keep the original music rather than a replacement — useful in Classic Reskin mode when you want to replace some tracks but not others. Add music in the Audio Editor first, then assign it here, and set Loop Points so it loops cleanly rather than restarting abruptly. Cutscene Timing ¶ For cutscene scenes, End Time is how long the scene lasts before the game moves on, in seconds. A negative value means the scene does not auto-advance by time — it waits for something else to end it. Use that for cutscene beats that should be driven by their content rather than a timer. Related pages: The Level Editor Workspace , Levels, Scenes, and Cutscenes , Walls, Scroll, and Collision , Special Screens .

docs.text: Spawns ¶ Spawns place enemies and items into a scene. Select them in the preview, or step through them with the Inspector's previous/next buttons — usually easier once a scene is busy. Spawn Lists and Order ¶ Enemy spawns live in lists such as enemies1 , enemies2 , extraEnemies1 and extraEnemies2 . Item spawns live in items and extraItems . The Inspector lets you change two things about a spawn's placement in this structure: List — which spawn list it belongs to. Moving it to another list changes when and under what conditions the game spawns it. Index — its position within that list, which moves it earlier or later in the spawn order. Order matters because wave triggers depend on it. A spawn placed in the wrong list can appear at completely the wrong moment even though its position on screen is correct. Wave Triggers ¶ Trigger decides what makes a wave spawn. There are four patterns: Trigger Fires when Immediate As soon as the previous wave is cleared. Distance The player crosses a set distance. Enemy count Few enough enemies are left on screen. Delay A set time has passed. Supporting fields: Trigger X Pos — how far the player must travel before the wave spawns, in pixels. Delay — how long to wait after the trigger condition is met. Max Enemies — the wave spawns once there are fewer than this many enemies on screen. Time Limit — the wave also spawns once the timer drops below this many seconds, even if enemies are still on screen . Time Limit is the safety valve. Without it, a wave gated on enemy count can stall if a player refuses to engage the last enemy. Set it on waves that could otherwise deadlock. Enemy Spawn Fields ¶ Field Meaning Mod / Entity Name Which entity to spawn, and which mod it comes from. Leave the mod empty to use this mod. Display Name Editor-only label. Does not affect the game. Position Where the enemy appears within the layer, in pixels. Health Starting health. Death Score Points scored for defeating it. Aggressiveness How hard the enemy fights, from cautious at low values to relentless at high ones. Minimum Difficulty The lowest difficulty this enemy appears on. Below it, the enemy is left out of the level entirely. Palette Mod / Palette ID Which colour palette it is drawn with. The preview recolours an entity of this mod with its own Palettes/palette <ID>.png , falling back to its drawn colours when the palette doesn't exist. Spawn How and when the enemy enters the level. Introduction Type Which of the entity's introduction sequences plays when it appears. Use Boss Slot Treats the enemy as the level's boss — reserves the boss slot and shows the boss health bar. Biker Weapon Gives a biker their pipe. Biker Grenade Spawns a foot biker holding a grenade instead of a pipe. Ninja Hook Height The height a ninja hooks down from, in pixels. Two Players Only Only place this enemy when two players are in the game. Item Spawn Fields ¶ Field Meaning Mod / Entity Name Which item to spawn. Position and Height Where it sits, and how far above the ground, in pixels. Item Type Which item this is, deciding what the player gets on pickup. Animation ID The animation the spawned item starts in. Object Mode Which variant of the item to use — see Behaviour Modes . Palette Mod / Palette ID Colour palette. Minimum Difficulty Same meaning as for enemies. Containers ¶ An object that can be broken open carries two extra fields: Contained Item Mod and Contained Item Entity , naming the item that appears when it breaks. Difficulty Changes the Level Layout ¶ Minimum Difficulty removes an object from the level entirely on easier settings. It is not a scaling factor — it is presence or absence. Use the preview's difficulty selector to check each setting; it hides objects above the chosen difficulty, so you see exactly what an easy run will encounter. It is common to discover that an easy playthrough has been stripped nearly bare, or that every health pickup was marked for hard only. Test across difficulties and player counts, since Two Players Only objects change the layout too. See Difficulty Settings . Related pages: The Level Editor Workspace , Scene Settings , Behaviour Modes , Difficulty Settings .

docs.text: Special Screens ¶ Special screens are non-standard level visuals such as presentation scenes, title screen art, character-select-style presentation, ending screens, and level cutscenes. The Level Editor edits these using the same layer and art systems as level backgrounds, with extra fields for screen-specific movement where needed. Available Special Content ¶ Depending on mode, the sidebar can expose: Presentation. Title Screen. Ending. Level cutscenes. Classic Reskin replacement levels. Classic Reskin cutscenes. In Mod mode, special screens live alongside the mod's level data. In Classic Reskin mode, special screens are saved under Level Replacements/Classic so they replace classic presentation content. Title Screen Images ¶ Some images can be converted between normal static images and Title Screen Image entries. docs.text: Walls, Scroll, and Collision ¶ Walls, scroll limits and collision shapes decide where characters can move and how far the camera advances. Together they define the playable space, which is separate from — and easy to get out of step with — the background art. Walls ¶ Setting Effect Left Wall Blocks the left side of the scene so the player cannot walk past it. Right Wall Blocks the right side. Vertical Left Makes the left wall run straight up and down instead of slanting with the floor. Only available while Left Wall is on. Limit X The horizontal position, in pixels, at which a wall limit takes effect. Diagonal Limits Slanted boundaries of the walkable area, for scenes whose walls are not square to the screen. Walls are what create closed-room encounters, stop players at scene edges, and keep enemies inside the intended combat area. Vertical Left is the setting people miss. By default a wall slants to follow the floor's perspective; turning it vertical is what you want for a genuine flat surface such as a lift wall or a door frame, where a slanted boundary looks wrong as the player walks up and down. Diagonal Limits exist for scenes built at an angle — alleys, ramps, bridges — where a rectangular walkable area would either cut off usable floor or let characters walk into the scenery. Scroll Limits ¶ Scroll limits control how far the camera advances before the scene stops or transitions. A scene has an X limit and diagonal scroll limits. When a scene feels too short, too long, or transitions early, check the scroll limits before you touch the art. This is almost always the cause, and it is a much smaller fix than re-cutting a background. Custom Collision Shapes ¶ Where simple wall limits are not enough, custom shapes define collision from a list of points. Setting Meaning Points The corner points, in pixels. The shape is drawn by joining them in order. Closed Joins the last point back to the first, making a closed outline rather than an open line. Collision Side Which side of the shape blocks movement. Use custom shapes for slopes, irregular boundaries, stage-specific blockers, and anything a rectangle cannot describe. Collision Side is the field to check first when a shape appears to do nothing, or blocks from the wrong direction — the geometry is usually right and the side is backwards. Pits ¶ Pits use the same point-list model, plus Pit Damage : the damage taken by anyone who falls in. Setting it to 0 makes the pit harmless, which is useful for purely visual gaps or for a pit that only inconveniences. Walls have Max Height and Stops Knockdowns . With Max Height at 0 the wall blocks at any height. Above 0 it only blocks entities lower than that many pixels above the ground, like a rail or a low fence: walking characters stop, while jumps high enough pass over it and thrown characters always do. Tick Stops Knockdowns to also catch knocked-down characters (including script-driven knockdowns) at any height, so a knockdown never flies over the rail (for example, a rail in front of a pit). The interaction rule is worth stating explicitly: grounded players, enemies and items always collide with pit boundaries, but airborne objects can still fall through when there is no ground beneath them. So a character knocked into the air over a pit will drop into it, while one walking is stopped at the edge. Treadmills ¶ A shape can carry a Treadmill Velocity — the speed it pushes anyone standing on it, along the horizontal and depth axes. This drives conveyor belts and moving floors. Editing in the Preview ¶ The preview shows wall handles, scroll ranges, collision lines and scene objects. Handles stay a constant size on screen regardless of zoom, so you can zoom right out to set a scroll range and right in to place a collision point. Drag for the broad shape, then correct exact values in the Inspector. Testing ¶ Still previews hide collision problems. Test in gameplay and specifically with movement that leaves the ground: jump arcs, throws, and knockbacks are what find gaps in walls, pits that catch when they should not, and diagonal limits that stop short. Related pages: The Level Editor Workspace , Scene Settings , Spawns , Background Layers . round-layers.md).

docs.text: The Level Editor Workspace ¶ The Level Editor opens on a Choose what to edit screen, where you pick Mod or Classic Reskin . See Mod Levels vs Classic Reskin — the choice decides whether you are editing gameplay data or only replacement art. Changes save automatically into your mod folder; copy the folder before a large experiment. Layout ¶ Area Holds Left sidebar The content tree: levels, scenes, layers, objects, spawns, and special screens. Select here; edit in the Inspector. Preview The scene as it will appear, with editable handles for objects, walls, scroll limits and collision shapes. Inspector Properties of the current selection. Asset browser Images and animations available to the level. Drag from here into the scene. Timeline Frames of the selected art animation. Preview Controls ¶ Input Action Wheel up / down Zoom in / out by 10% per notch. Right-drag or Middle-drag Pan the view. Left-click Select the object under the pointer. Left-drag Move the selected object, or drag a handle. Delete Delete the current selection. Zoom is limited to a range of roughly 0.1× to 10×, so you can pull back to see a whole scene's scroll range or push in to place a spawn precisely. Handles scale inversely with zoom, so wall and scroll-limit grips stay the same size on screen whatever the zoom level. Keyboard ¶ Key Action Ctrl+C Copy the selection. Ctrl+V Paste. Delete Delete the selection — in the preview, in lists, and in the timeline. ← / → Step through values in the Inspector. Delete is context-sensitive: it removes whatever list, preview object, or timeline frame currently has your attention. Lists prompt for confirmation before deleting. Preview Toolbar ¶ Difficulty preview — shows the level as it appears on a chosen difficulty. Objects with a higher minimum difficulty are hidden. This is the fastest way to check that an easy playthrough is not accidentally empty, or that a hard one is not overloaded. In Classic Reskin mode there are three more controls: Show original artwork — draws the original SOR2 art behind your replacement, as an alignment guide. Original opacity — how visible that guide is, from 0 (hidden) to 1 (fully opaque). Replacement opacity — how visible your own art is, on the same scale. Cross-fading between the two is how you check a reskin lines up: set both to around half and any drift becomes obvious. Adding Art ¶ Drag PNG or GIF files into the editor. GIFs are split into frames, and their timing is carried across, the same as in the Character Editor. Dropping art adds it to the level's art folder; dragging from the asset browser into the preview places it on the current layer. Selecting Spawns ¶ Spawns are easier to work with from the Inspector's navigation row than by clicking in a crowded preview: Previous / Next step through the spawns in the current list. Index shows and changes the spawn's position in its list, which moves it earlier or later in the spawn order. List shows which spawn list it belongs to. Moving it to another list changes when and under what conditions the game spawns it. Related pages: Levels, Scenes, and Cutscenes , Spawns , Walls, Scroll, and Collision , Background Layers .

docs.text: TAS Editor ¶ The TAS (tool-assisted speedrun) editor lets you build a run one frame at a time. Instead of playing in real time, you stop on a single frame, decide exactly which buttons are held, and step forward. The game replays your recorded input deterministically, so the result is reproducible every time. You do not need to understand anything else in this page to get started. Open the editor, press F1 , and everything below is on screen. The screen ¶ Area What it is Top left The gameplay view. It is deliberately wider than the game camera so you can see enemies and items before they scroll on. Right The input timeline — the frame-by-frame grid, with the controls that move through it directly underneath. Bottom The overview bar, then one titled box per job. The timeline column is only as wide as the players in your run need, so a one-player TAS leaves most of the screen to the gameplay view. Every control lives in the box for the job it does, so you never have to hunt along a row of unrelated buttons: Box What it is for Input Timeline (right column) Choosing where in the run you are. Back / Play / Fwd and Prev Key / Next Key sit right under the grid they move. Session Read-only. Which frame you are on, which player and button you are editing, and whether anything still needs replaying. Write Input The buttons that change the movie: the eleven pad buttons, the tap-versus-hold hint, and Undo / Redo. Record The alternative to typing input by hand. Shows whether you are editing or recording, and holds Record and the playback speed. Macros Saving and re-applying short input sequences. Inspector Reading the game's live values. Trim Future and Help (F1) sit in the title bar, away from anything you use routinely. Reading the input timeline ¶ The timeline is a table. One row is one frame. One column is one button. frame UDLRABCXYZS 001230 ...R....... 001231 ...RA...... >001232* ...RA...... 001233 ...RA...... 001234 ....A...... A letter means that button is held on that frame. A dot means it is free. Because the columns are fixed, a button held over several frames draws a solid vertical bar. That is the fastest way to see the shape of a movement at a glance. > marks the frame you are on. The row is highlighted. The blue box marks the selected cell — the frame and button your next edit will apply to. * after the frame number means the frame still has to be replayed before its result can be trusted. This appears after you edit something in the past. ~ means a scene transition is playing on that frame. # means the game's luck seed changed on that frame. Useful when hunting for a specific enemy behaviour or item drop. The What the grid means key under the grid repeats all of this on screen. When more than one player is active, each gets its own group of columns, labelled P1 , P2 and so on above the grid. The lane you are editing is drawn brighter than the others. To switch lanes, click the P1 / P2 / P3 / P4 buttons next to Editing: at the top of the timeline column, press Tab , or click any cell in the lane you want. That row is hidden entirely in a one-player run. Moving through the run ¶ Do this To Up / Down Go back or forward one frame. Hold to run at 60 frames per second. Page Up / Page Down Jump 30 frames. Home / End Go to the first or last frame. Space Play or stop. Mouse wheel over the grid Scrub through frames. Click a frame number Jump straight to that frame. Drag up or down in the grid Scrub through frames. Drag the overview bar Scrub across the whole run. The mouse cursor turns into a vertical double arrow whenever it is over the grid or the overview bar, as a reminder that both are draggable. The overview bar under the gameplay view shows the entire run at once: orange ticks are level starts, smaller ticks are waves and saved states, and the red wash marks the region that still needs replaying. Editing input ¶ The vertical axis is time and the horizontal axis is buttons, so the arrow keys do what the grid looks like they should. Do this To Left / Right Pick which button column you are editing. Enter Tap the picked button on the current frame. Shift + Enter Hold the picked button from this frame onwards. Click a cell Move there. Click the same cell again to toggle it. 1 2 3 4 Up, Down, Left, Right. 5 6 7 8 9 0 A, B, C, X, Y, Z. - Start. Shift + Up / Down Shift this frame and every later frame back or forward in time. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y Undo / redo. Tap versus hold is the one thing worth learning. A plain toggle affects a single frame; the same toggle with Shift held changes the button from this frame to the end of the run. The hint line under the control panel tells you which one you are about to do, and changes as soon as you press Shift. Clicking a cell never edits it on the first click. The first click moves the cursor there; a second click on the same cell toggles it. A misplaced click cannot change your run. Recording instead of typing ¶ Typing every frame is slow for long stretches of ordinary movement. Press Ctrl+R to switch to recording, press Space to play, and whatever you hold on your controller is written into the movie as it advances. Drop the speed to 1/4 or 1/8 with Ctrl+F to get precise input at a manageable pace, then switch back to editing to clean it up frame by frame. The mode line in the control panel always says which of the two you are in. Macros ¶ Capture Macro saves the next ten frames of the current player's input under a name. Apply Macro writes it in at the current frame. Use Alt+Up / Alt+Down to pick which saved macro is applied. This is worth doing for any input sequence you repeat — a dash, a grab-and-throw, a specific combo. Replaying and trust ¶ When you change input in the past, everything after it is no longer valid — the game has not been simulated with the new input yet. Those frames get a * and the status panel says Needs replay from frame N . Stepping or playing forward through the region replays it and clears the mark. Next Key jumps forward to the next saved state that is already up to date, which is a fast way to check whether your change broke something later on. Trim Future deletes everything after the current frame. It asks first. Inspector ¶ Click any player, enemy, or item in the gameplay view, or use the target buttons, to see its live values. Values that changed on this frame are highlighted, which makes it practical to find the exact frame an attack connects or a state flips. The filter box takes a regular expression if the list is long. Gamepad ¶ Control Action D-pad Up / Down, or LB / RB Step frames D-pad Left / Right Pick a button column A, B, C, X, Y, Z Toggle that button on the current frame Back Open the menu Full shortcut list ¶ Press F1 at any time. Everything on this page is listed there, in the app.

docs.text: Add Custom Audio ¶ Audio can be owned by your mod or used as a replacement for audio from another pack. Goal ¶ Add custom sounds, voices, music, and optional Classic audio replacements. Prerequisites ¶ A source mod under Editor . Audio files in WAV , MP3 , or OGG format. A plan for where each sound or track will be used. Add sounds or music owned by your mod ¶ Open the mod in the in-game editor menu. Launch the Audio Editor. Choose Mod mode. Drop the mod folder into the editor if prompted. Add sound files for effects, voices, or short cues. Add music files for stages, menus, or cutscenes. Set loop points for music that should loop. Save. Reference the audio from character events, level music settings, cutscenes, or scripts. Replace Classic audio ¶ Open the Audio Editor. Choose Classic Reskin mode. Select the target voice, SFX, or music entry. Drop replacement audio on the entry or choose audio already in the mod. Set loop points for replacement music. Save and test in game. docs.text: Character Select Background ¶ Character select background work is part of a broader visual reskin workflow. Treat it like a small presentation scene: prepare the art, import it through the Level Editor workflow, and test it from the real character select screen. docs.text: Create a Container Object ¶ Containers are destructible item entities that can drop another item when broken. Goal ¶ Create a breakable object such as a crate, barrel, box, or scenery prop. Prerequisites ¶ A source mod under Editor . Sprites for the intact object and, optionally, breaking debris. A target item to drop, such as food, points, a weapon, or a custom item. Steps ¶ Open the mod in the in-game editor menu. Launch the Character Editor. Choose Mod mode and the Items filter. Create a new item entity for the container. Import the container sprites. Build the idle/intact animation and the break animation. Set body boxes so attacks can hit the container. Set item or reference behavior for a breakable container. Configure the contained item: target mod, item name, and any mode or spawn settings the behavior requires. Save the container. Open the Level Editor and place the container in a test level. Testing ¶ Hit the container from both directions. Confirm it breaks once, plays the expected animation and sound, and drops the expected item. Confirm the dropped item can be picked up or used. Test several containers on screen at once. Test with alternate palettes if the container uses palette effects. docs.text: Create a Custom Mod ¶ Create the editable source folder that all other modding work will use. Goal ¶ Make a new mod, give it basic identity, and confirm the game can load it. Prerequisites ¶ Streets of Rage 2 New Era is installed. You can open the in-game editor menu. Any thumbnail image you want to use is ready as a PNG . Steps ¶ Run the game and open the in-game editor menu. Choose the option to create a new mod. Enter a clear mod name. This name becomes the source folder name under Editor and the exported file name under Mods . Add a short description so players know what the mod changes. Add or replace the thumbnail if your mod has one. Review dependencies. If your mod uses content from another mod, add that dependency before export. Save the mod settings. After saving, the source folder should exist under Editor/<Your Mod Name> . Confirm the new mod appears with the expected name and thumbnail. Start the mod even if it has little content yet. If it does not appear, reopen the editor, check the mod name and settings, then restart the game. Links ¶ Mod Folder Anatomy Testing and Exporting Mod Settings Reference

docs.text: Create Cutscenes ¶ Cutscenes use level-style visual scenes without normal combat flow. They can introduce a level, present the mod, replace Classic presentation scenes, or end a story. docs.text: Package, Export, and Share ¶ Exporting turns your editable source mod from Editor into a playable .zip in Mods . Goal ¶ Prepare a mod for players, export it, and share the correct file. Prerequisites ¶ A source mod under Editor . The mod has been tested in game. Required dependencies are installed and listed in the mod settings. Pre-export checklist ¶ The mod name, description, and thumbnail are final enough for release. Unused test content has been removed or intentionally left in. Playable characters, enemies, levels, cutscenes, palettes, audio, and scripts have been tested. Dependencies are correct. Any dependency version used for export is the version players should use. Multiplayer users have a clear version number or release label to compare. Export ¶ Run the game. Open the in-game editor menu. Select the mod. Choose Export . Wait for the export to finish. Open the Mods folder. Find the exported file, usually Mods/<Mod Name>.zip . The exported .zip can be uploaded or shared. Players should place that file directly in their Mods folder. Share the mod ¶ When sharing, include: The exported .zip . A short description of what changed. Required dependencies and their versions. Whether the mod is intended for single-player, local multiplayer, online multiplayer, or all of them. Any known issues. Do not ask players to copy your source folder into Editor unless you are intentionally sharing an editable project for other modders. Multiplayer ¶ Both players need the same exported mod version. New Era checks checksum equality for the loaded mod and dependencies. If you update and re-export the mod, share the new .zip with every player. A small local edit creates a different checksum. Links ¶ Testing and Exporting Installing Community Mods Mod Folder Anatomy

docs.text: Playable Character From ROM Hack ¶ The Character Editor can import character data from a Streets of Rage 2 ROM file, including supported ROM hacks, and convert it into a New Era entity you can edit. ROM import only supports ROM hacks made from the US/western version of Streets of Rage 2. ROM hacks made from the Japanese version, Bare Knuckle 2 , or from more complex ROM hacks such as Streets of Rage 2 Syndicate Wars , are not supported. Goal ¶ Use a ROM hack as a starting point for a playable character, then finish the character with New Era tools. Prerequisites ¶ A source mod under Editor . A ROM file you are allowed to use. The ROM file is in a supported Genesis/Mega Drive format such as .bin , .gen , .md , or .smd . The ROM hack is based on the US/western Streets of Rage 2 ROM. Steps ¶ Open the mod in the in-game editor menu. Launch the Character Editor. Drop the mod folder into the Character Editor if prompted. Choose Mod mode. Drop the ROM file into the Character Editor. In the import dialog, choose Players . Select the character to import. Give the imported character a New Era name. Open the new character from the list. Review the imported animations, pivots, boxes, logic, and sprites. Save the character. Clean up after import ¶ Imported data is a starting point, not a finished release. Rename animations so you can find them later. Check pivots on every important movement and attack frame. Check hitboxes, body boxes, throw data, and attack sounds. Replace or add portraits, previews, palettes, and missing sprites. Remove unused frames or animations once the character is stable. Add New Era-specific events, scripts, or audio if the character needs them. Testing ¶ Test the imported character in a simple level. Compare basic moves against the ROM hack behavior you expect. Confirm attacks, throws, jumps, damage reactions, and death all work. Test with Classic enemies and with another custom character. Links ¶ Playable Character From Scratch Mod Character Palettes The Character Editor Workspace - panels, preview controls, and shortcuts The Inspector - every setting and what it means Character Editor Reference

docs.text: Playable Character From Scratch ¶ Build a playable character from your own sprites. Goal ¶ Create a new fighter, import sprites, build animations, tune combat boxes, and test the character in-game. Prerequisites ¶ A source mod under Editor . Character sprites as PNG files or an animated GIF . A plan for the character's core moves: idle, walk, jump, basic attacks, special attacks, grabs, being hit, knockdown, and death. Steps ¶ Open the mod in the in-game editor menu. Launch the Character Editor. Drop the mod folder into the Character Editor if prompted. Choose Mod mode and the Players filter. Choose Create New or drop your first sprite set into the editor. Name the character. Import all sprite frames into the character. Create the required animations and assign frames to each animation. Set pivots so the character's feet stay planted across idle, walk, attack, and hit reactions. Add body boxes for vulnerable frames. Add hitboxes for active attack frames. Add throw offsets, grab offsets, weapon points, projectile points, sound events, or scripts where the move needs them. Add a portrait and preview image if the editor does not generate the result you want. Save the character. Testing ¶ Test the character in a simple level before building the whole move set. Confirm the character appears on character select. Check idle, walk, jump, attack, hit, knockdown, and death animations. Verify that attacks connect only on the intended frames. Verify the character can be hit and grabbed. Test facing left and right. Test with two players if the character can be selected in multiplayer. Common problems ¶ Floating feet usually mean pivots are inconsistent between frames. Attacks hitting too early or too late usually mean the hitbox is on the wrong frame. A character that cannot be hit usually has missing or misplaced body boxes. Throw glitches usually need grab offsets and release offsets tuned on both facing directions. docs.text: Animation Names ¶ Animation names are editor labels stored with animation logic entries. The runtime primarily uses animation IDs, so names are for humans, tooling, and documentation. Where Names Appear ¶ Names commonly appear in logic.json : { "animationsLogic": [ { "name": "Standing", "duration": 266 }, { "name": "Walk", "duration": 40 } ] } The array index is the animation ID used by scripts, events, and animation behaviour. Renaming "Standing" does not change animation ID 0 . Suggested Naming Style ¶ Use short action labels: Standing Walk Run Jump Land from jump Attack 1 Attack 2 Blitz Defensive special Offensive special Grab front Grab back Throw Being hit Knocked down Lying down Stand up Death Keep capitalization consistent within one entity. The editor and runtime do not require a particular case, but consistent names make debugging much easier. IDs Are The Contract ¶ Scripts and events use IDs: character.set_animation(30) { "$type": "Sor2NewEra.Gameplay.JumpToAnimationEvent, Sor2NewEra", "frame": 8, "animationId": 30, "animationFrame": 0 } If you reorder animations, every ID reference can change. Avoid reordering established animations in Classic replacements unless you are ready to update scripts, events, hitboxes, and animation behaviour. Classic Replacement Guidance ¶ When replacing a Classic character, enemy, or item: keep original animation IDs when possible rename labels only to clarify, not to imply the ID changed keep common state animations near their original indexes update behaviour modes and events if you move an animation test every transition that jumps by ID Using Names In Documentation ¶ When documenting a move, include both: Animation 30: Close shuriken slash That lets another modder find the animation even if their local label differs.

docs.text: Audio ¶ Audio in editor packs is split into pack-owned sounds, pack-owned music, and optional replacement maps that redirect Classic audio keys to your pack. Folders ¶ Folder Purpose Sounds/ Short sound effects and voices. Musics/ Music tracks. Audio Replacements/<Target Pack>/ Replacement maps for another pack, usually Classic . The Audio Editor supports .wav , .mp3 , and .ogg in its normal drag-and-drop flow. Sound Names ¶ The runtime references sounds by base filename: Sounds/heavy-hit.wav is referenced as: heavy-hit Lua example: game.this_character.play_sound("My Pack", "heavy-hit", 1) Music Names ¶ Music uses the same base-filename rule: Musics/stage-theme.ogg is referenced as: stage-theme Scene example: { "musicPackName": "My Pack", "musicName": "stage-theme" } Loop Metadata ¶ Loop metadata sits next to the music file: Musics/stage-theme.ogg Musics/stage-theme.json { "loopStartTimeInSeconds": 18.75, "loopEndTimeInSeconds": 95.0 } The runtime converts seconds to samples using the loaded clip frequency. Classic Music Replacement ¶ Audio Replacements/Classic/music-replacements.json { "M00": { "packName": "My Pack", "musicName": "go-straight-remix" } } Missing keys fall back to Classic music. Classic Sound Replacement ¶ Audio Replacements/Classic/sound-replacements.json { "29": { "packName": "My Pack", "soundName": "axel-attack" } } Missing keys fall back to Classic sounds. Channels ¶ Sound events and Lua sound calls can specify channels. Common channel meanings are: Channel Typical use 0 SFX 1 SFX or BGM-adjacent effect 2 Voice 3 Priority sound Use the same channel as a similar original sound unless you have a reason to change mixing behavior.
