docs.text: Set afterimages: true on an animationsLogic entry to show recent player poses through the existing Ninpo shadow renderer. This is visual only: it does not enable clone attacks or add collision bodies. Defaults to false, is suppressed during cinematics, and rejects history from another entity or animation. Requires the generic authored-afterimage engine support.
docs.title: Visual afterimages

docs.text: logic.weaponHealth > 0 opts a weapon into a health budget instead of Classic's drop counter. weaponDropHealthCost is consumed on landing or swap. animationsLogic[].weaponHealthCost charges on completion if at least one hit connected (misses and interrupted moves do not pay), while hitboxes[].weaponHealthCost charges per connected hitbox; both are independent of damage multipliers. Exhaustion drops the held weapon and its next landing expires it. All counters are in ItemModel , not Lua upvalues, and are restored by rollback. Zero-valued configuration preserves Classic behaviour. Normal attacks without authored wear do not consume health. Lua item.weapon_health reads/writes the rollback health counter, allowing original spawn or container tables to override the default budget. This does not enable the feature on entities whose weaponHealth configuration is zero. weaponContactHealthCost optionally overrides a positive hitbox wear cost using the held weapon's own value. Zero preserves attack-authored costs. Zero-cost hitboxes remain free, and animation-completion fees are unaffected. Use this for weapons whose wear differs even when they share a character move.
docs.title: Weapon health budgets

docs.text: Enums and Identifiers ¶ Every numeric constant the JSON files use, in one place, plus the identifier tables you need to reference Classic content. Animation slots ¶ animations.json animations and logic.json animationsLogic are indexed by animation id . For entities built on Classic behaviour, animation id i corresponds to the original AnimationId value i * 2 . Everything that names an animation — JumpToAnimationEvent.animationId , OffsetData.opponentAnimation , SpawnItemEvent.animationId , ReferenceBehaviourData.animationId — uses the id in the first column. Id AnimationId Meaning 0 0x00 Standing 1 0x02 Walk 2 0x04 Jump 3 0x06 Grab jump 4 0x08 Grab front 5 0x0A Grab back 6 0x0C Being front grabbed 7 0x0E Being back grabbed 8 0x10 Being grab hit 9 0x12 Being hit 10 0x14 Knocked down 11 0x16 Lying down 12 0x18 Stand up 13 0x1A Electrocuted 14 0x1C Pick 15 0x1E Land from jump 16 0x20 Land from jump kick 17 0x22 Fall 18 0x24 Front slammed by Max 19 0x26 Back slammed by Axel 20 0x28 Back slammed by Max 21 0x2A Front slammed by Blaze 22 0x2C Thrown by Max 23 0x2E Being atomic dropped 24 0x30 Front grab throw 25 0x32 Back grab throw 26 0x34 Static jump attack 27 0x36 Jump forward attack 28 0x38 Jump down attack 29 0x3A Normal punch 30 0x3C Third punch 31 0x3E Combo end A 32 0x40 Combo end B 33 0x42 Grab attack 34 0x44 Grab combo end 35 0x46 Defensive special 36 0x48 Blitz 37 0x4A Offensive special 38 0x4C Back attack 39 0x4E Static grab attack 40 0x50 Throw 41 0x52 Atomic drop 42 0x54 Use knife 43 0x56 Use pipe 44 0x58 Weapon throw 45 0x5A Use sword 46 0x5C Use kunai 47 0x5E unused 48 0x60 unused 49 0x62 Hold-B attack 50 0x64 Use knife extra Ids 47 and 48 have no Classic meaning and are free for custom animations, as is anything from 51 upwards. Custom entities are not limited to this table: an entity that drives itself entirely with events and scripts can use any index it likes, as long as animations.json and animationsLogic agree. Entity types ¶ logic.json entityType : Value Name Meaning 0 Player Playable character. 1 BasicEnemy Common street enemy. The difficulty system may multiply these. 2 Enemy Boss-class enemy. 3 PickUpItem Weapon, food, or score pickup. 4 Container Breakable object holding something. 5 Scenery Non-interactive object. 6 Other Anything else, such as effects. The Character Editor only offers 0-3. Values 4-6 are authored by hand or produced by the ROM importer. Audio channels ¶ channel on SoundEvent , HitboxData , and projectileHitSoundChannel : Value Name 0 sfx 1 sfxBgm 2 voice 3 prioritary Sounds sharing a slot cut each other off. The runtime treats the value as a plain index and allocates as many slots as it encounters, so any non-negative number is a valid private channel — useful when a sound must not be interrupted by anything else. Existing mods use values well above 3 for exactly this. Input buttons ¶ JumpToAnimationOnInputButton.input is a flag value from InputButtons : Value Button Value Button 1 Up 256 Hold Up 2 Down 512 Hold Down 4 Left 1024 Hold Left 8 Right 2048 Hold Right 16 B 4096 Hold B 32 C 8192 Hold C 64 A 16384 Hold A 128 Start 32768 Hold Start 65536 X 262144 Hold X 131072 Y 524288 Hold Y 1048576 Z 4194304 Hold Z 0 is Empty. Input combos ¶ JumpToAnimationOnInputCombo.input is a string , one character per step, matched in order: Character Step ^ Up v Down < Left > Right a b c x y z Face buttons Parsed case-insensitively. Left and right mirror with facing, so a combo authored facing right also works facing left. Any other character is ignored as an Empty step, which will never match. Examples: "vv" is down, down. "v>a" is down, forward, A. Weapon angles ¶ AnimationFrameWeaponData.direction : Value Angle Value Angle 0 Up 4 Down 1 Up-left 5 Down-right 2 Left 6 Right 3 Down-left 7 Up-right Scene enums ¶ Enum Field Values Scene enter sceneEnterCodeId 0 JumpInFromTop, 1 Standing, 2 WalkFromLeft, 3 StartAhead Scene exit sceneExitCodeId 0 None, 1 SimpleFadeOut, 2 LeaveToTheRight, 3 BreakTruckDoor, 4 EnterBaseballElevator, 5 LeaveBaseballElevator, 6 Level8ElevatorHealth, 7 LevelEnding, 8 EndGame Screen shake screenShakeType 0 Default, 1 Truck, 2 Boat Start offset startOffsetType 0 Default, 1 ClosedRoom, 2 Stage1Poster, 3 Stage3SwingingBoat, 4 Stage5TopBoat, 5 Stage7Elevator, 6 Stage8Elevator Wall shape shapeType 0 Wall, 1 Treadmill, 2 Pit, 3 Custom1, 4 Custom2 Layer update updateType 0 Normal, 1 BackyardRain, 2 TruckBrokenDoor, 3 Stage4Elevator, 4 ArenaSpectators, 5 Stage7Elevator, 6 Stage7ElevatorExtra, 7 Stage8Elevator, 8 AntiCameraY, 9 WaveEffect, 10 SmallWaveEffect, 11 SwingingBoat Wall flag bits on wallFlags : 1 left wall, 2 right wall, 4 left wall is vertical. Session enums ¶ config.json settings.bufferGlitchFixMode : Value Name Meaning 0 NoFix Reproduce the original sprite buffer glitch. 1 AllButGroundUpper Fix everything except the upper ground layer. 2 All Fix the glitch everywhere. Classic entity names ¶ The Classic pack is extracted from the original ROM. Use these exact names in entityName , in Entity Replacements/Classic/<name>/ folders, and in Palettes/Classic/<name>/ folders. Players: Max, Axel, Blaze, Skate. Enemies: Galsia, Donovan, Jack, Barbon, Electra, Signal, Biker, Ninja, Bongo, Hakuyo, Kickboxer, Jet, Zamza, R.Bear, Abadede, Particle, Mr.X, Shiva, Ninja (Kunai), Ninja (Sword), Blast, Vehelits, Vehelits (2). Enemy variants: Galsia (2), Galsia (3), Barbon Jacket. Weapons and pickups: Knife, Pipe, Sword, Kunai, Grenade, Cash Bag, Gold Bars, 1UP, Apple, Chicken. Containers and scenery: Bin, Manhole, Lamp, Menu, Table, Table (2), Table (3), Table (4), Chair, Trash Can, Oil Barrel, Truck door debris, Truck door debris (2), Electric box, Electric box (2), Barrier, Light, Arcade, Ship Pole, Obj 2, Obj 3, Obj 4, Obj 5, Sandbag, Sandbag (2), Sandbag (3), Sandbag (4), Crate, Metal Crate, Vase, Alien Egg. Interface and effects: Arrow, 1P, 2P, Go, Sunset Alphabet, Shadow, BlueHit, SmallHit, BigHit, GroundDust. Names are matched exactly, including spaces, capitalisation, and punctuation. R.Bear has no space; Ninja (Kunai) has one before the bracket. The name hash ¶ Pack names and entity names are reduced internally to a 32-bit signed hash. You never need to compute this yourself except for allowedCharacters in config.json , which stores hashes rather than names. hash = 23 for each character c in the name: hash = (hash * 31 + codepoint(c)) wrapped to signed 32-bit An empty or null name hashes to 0 . A pack with an id is identified by the hash of its id instead of its name: the same function over the id in its canonical form, lowercase and hyphenated ( 3f6c2a9e-8b1d-4c57-9e2f-7a0d5b4c1e88 ). In Python: def name_hash(name: str) -> int: if not name: return 0 h = 23 for ch in name: h = (h * 31 + ord(ch)) & 0xFFFFFFFF return h - 0x100000000 if h >= 0x80000000 else h Related pages ¶ Behaviour Modes for the per-character move controller tables. docs.text: Level Files ¶ A level is stored as a pair of files that must stay aligned: Levels/level 1.json gameplay: scenes, walls, scroll, spawns Levels/level 1 - art.json visuals: layers, images, animations, music Levels/level 1 - cutscenes.json optional cutscenes for that level Both files contain a scenes array, and scene i in one is the same scene as scene i in the other . The gameplay file decides where you can walk and what spawns; the art file decides what you see and hear. Three more files use the art format on their own, with no gameplay counterpart: Levels/title.json title screen Levels/presentation.json opening presentation Levels/ending.json ending sequence And the same five art-format file names appear under Level Replacements/Classic/ when you are reskinning the Classic game rather than building your own levels. Every image named by any of these files is a file in Levels/Art/ . level <n>.json ¶ Root object: LevelData . Field Type Meaning entitiesScale float Uniform scale applied to characters and items in this level. 0 is treated as 1 . The view draws the world at this scale about world Y 220, which stays on the screen bottom: below 1 the playable width is 400 / entitiesScale world pixels ( screen_width , half extra width 40 / entitiesScale ), the view shows 224 / entitiesScale pixels above Y 220, and scroll limits and camera positions stay in world pixels. Background art is not scaled: draw it at entitiesScale times the world's size. Jump-in entrances and respawns start that much higher, so they still fall in from above the view. Scenes array of SceneData Ordered scenes. Written with a capital S by the Level Editor; scenes also loads, because Newtonsoft matches case-insensitively. SceneData ¶ Transitions Field Type Meaning sceneEnterCodeId int How players enter: 0 JumpInFromTop, 1 Standing, 2 WalkFromLeft, 3 StartAhead. sceneExitCodeId int How the scene ends. See the table below. startOffsetType int Camera start offset preset: 0 Default, 1 ClosedRoom, 2 Stage1Poster, 3 Stage3SwingingBoat, 4 Stage5TopBoat, 5 Stage7Elevator, 6 Stage8Elevator. screenShakeType int 0 Default, 1 Truck, 2 Boat. centerScreenForWidescreen bool Centre the scene horizontally on widescreen instead of anchoring left. sceneExitCodeId values: 0 None, 1 SimpleFadeOut, 2 LeaveToTheRight, 3 BreakTruckDoor, 4 EnterBaseballElevator, 5 LeaveBaseballElevator, 6 Level8ElevatorHealth, 7 LevelEnding, 8 EndGame. 6 is the odd one out: it is a health refill, not an exit, and the scene does not end on it. Palette Field Type Meaning alternativePalette string Name of an alternative palette applied to enemies in this scene. Empty means default. copyAltPalette bool Reuse the previous scene's alternative palette instead of loading this scene's own. Walls and walkable area Field Type Meaning wallLimitsData array of exactly 6 ints The walkable area, in pixels. See below. wallFlags int Bit flags over wallLimitsData . bottomWallLimit int Absolute world Y of the lowest walkable depth for players and enemies. 0 keeps the native limit, which follows the camera (camera Y + 216): set it when a scripted camera Y (a bobbing ship, a shaking elevator) must not push characters up. respawnPosition {x, y} int Where a respawning (or continuing) player drops in, in world pixels: x from the playable view's left edge (negative: from its right edge, and the player faces left), y the absolute world Y, like bottomWallLimit , so a scripted camera Y (a bobbing ship, a shaking elevator) does not move it. Leave it unset in a scene whose camera scrolls vertically. Each further player drops 16 pixels higher. The spot is kept above bottomWallLimit and, with customWallShapes , moved to the nearest point clear of walls and pits. Zero on both axes keeps the native spot, at the bottom left of the screen. customWallShapes array Extra collision shapes beyond the rectangular limits. wallLimitsData positions, in order: Index Level Editor label Meaning 0 Horizon Y (Base) The base depth line: the nearest edge of the walkable floor. 1 Max Depth Y The far edge of the walkable floor. 2 Left Gate X Where the left wall blocks movement. 3 L. Diag Anchor Anchor for a slanted left wall. 4 R. Diag Anchor Anchor for a slanted right wall. 5 Right Gate X Where the right wall blocks movement. wallFlags bits: 1 left wall enabled, 2 right wall enabled, 4 left wall is vertical rather than slanted. Remaining bits are unused. When the left wall flag is set, the engine requires index 1 to equal index 0, and the Level Editor enforces that. A deep floor with a far wall is only possible with the left wall off. customWallShapes entries ( WallCollisionShapeData ): Field Type Meaning shapeType int 0 Wall, 1 Treadmill, 2 Pit, 3 Custom1, 4 Custom2. points array of {x, y} int Corner points in pixels, joined in order. isClosed bool Join the last point back to the first. collideInsideOrAbove bool Which side of the shape blocks movement. treadmillVelocity {x, y} int Push applied to anyone standing on a Treadmill shape. pitDamage int Damage from a Pit shape. 0 makes it harmless. maxHeight int Wall shapes only. Above 0 , the wall only stops entities lower than this many pixels above the ground (a rail or low fence): higher jumps, throws and knockdowns pass over it. A thrown character (object modes 0x10 / 0x12 ) is measured at its real height like anything else: it clears the wall during the high part of its arc and hits it when low, at the start or the end of the flight. A character left inside such a wall (it came down on it from above) is pushed out on the floor side, or, when knocked down or in a throw's airborne flight, onto a pit beyond it, through which it falls. A character whose move animation ends while it is still airborne above a pit keeps falling into it. thrownMaxHeight int Wall shapes with a maxHeight only. Above 0 , a thrown character in the airborne part of its throw passes over the wall from this height instead of maxHeight (throws arc lower than jumps). 0 uses maxHeight . Scripts mark a scripted thrown body with the item's wallThrownFlight ( 3 while airborne). A player walking horizontally into a Wall edge that is close to horizontal (a shallow diagonal) stops at it; it slides along the edge in depth (up to 8 pixels) only while it is moving in depth itself. Pushing against a wall never moves a character in depth on its own. Scrolling Field Type Meaning scrollXLimit int Horizontal scroll extent, in pixels. Editor-authored scenes use a negative value for a scene that scrolls to the right. diagonalScrollLimit {x, y} int Diagonal scroll bound. Zero on both axes means horizontal scrolling only. cinematicCameraRoute object or null Optional known directional route for cinematic presentation: {start: {x, y}, end: {x, y}} , in absolute Lua camera viewport pixels, plus optional actorY : a fixed depth, in pixels below the route's camera Y, for cinematic actors that cross the view on one line (0 or omitted: the script chooses). This declares geometry; it does not drive gameplay scrolling. Native forward scroll geometry can be queried without a declaration. A cinematic cannot infer the route owned by an arbitrary camera script. For a scripted stage with a known straight or diagonal route, declare its endpoints for each wave; decreasing X identifies right-to-left travel. X endpoints must differ. Y is sampled linearly between them. Coordinates must match the stage script's actual bounds at the configured viewport width; no widescreen correction is inferred. Free-scrolling or changing custom routes should leave this field null, so events can fall back to an earlier scene with known directional geometry. "cinematicCameraRoute": { "start": {"x": 1800, "y": 0}, "end": {"x": 448, "y": 256} } Spawns loadcues is a SceneLoadcuesData : Field Contains enemies1 , enemies2 The two enemy wave tracks, which run in parallel. items Items, weapons, food, and containers. extraEnemies1 , extraEnemies2 , extraItems Additional content used by the higher Classic difficulties. Enemy loadcues ¶ CharacterLoadcueData . Every enemy in a level is one of these. Field Type Meaning packName string Pack owning the entity. Empty means Classic. entityName string Entity folder name within that pack. position_A_C {x, y} int Spawn position in pixels. x is along the scene, y is depth. collisionBox_3_4_5 BoundingBox Collision override. See the warning below. triggerType int What makes this wave spawn. See below. triggerArgument int Distance, enemy count, or delay, depending on triggerType . minimumDifficulty int Lowest difficulty this enemy appears on. Below it, it is left out entirely. useBossSlot bool Treat as the level boss: reserves the boss slot and shows the boss health bar. health int Starting health, nibble-encoded: (health & 0xF) + (health >> 4) * 12 hit points before the difficulty multiplier, every 12 of which is an extra life. 0 gives 8 hit points; there is no entity default. See Classic Game Mechanics . deathScore int Points for defeating it. enemyAgressiveness int AI aggression, cautious at low values to relentless at high ones. introductionType int Which introduction sequence plays on appearance, such as dropping in or climbing out of a sewer. palettePackName string Pack owning the palette. Empty means Classic. paletteIndex int Palette index for this entity within that pack. bikerWeaponFlag bool Give a spawned biker their pipe. bikerGrenadeFlag bool Spawn a foot biker holding a grenade instead of a pipe. Written by the ROM importer; the Level Editor shows it as Biker Grenade. ninjaHookHeight int Height a hooking ninja descends from, in pixels. displayName string Editor-only label. Does not affect the game. Trigger types, as the Level Editor presents them: triggerType triggerArgument Spawns when 0 unused Immediately, once the previous wave is cleared. 1 distance in pixels The player has travelled that far. 2 enemy count, below 7 Fewer than that many enemies remain on screen. 2 7 or more That enemy count is reached, or a timer expires. 3 delay After that delay. The split on triggerArgument 7 within type 2 is why the editor shows "Enemy Count" and "Time OR Enemy Count" as separate choices for the same underlying type. Item loadcues ¶ ItemLoadcueData . Weapons, food, score pickups, and breakable containers. Field Type Meaning packName , entityName string The object to place. position_A_C {x, y} int Position in pixels. collisionBox_3_4_5 BoundingBox Collision override. See the warning below. status_2 int Spawn flags: bit 0 vulnerable, bit 1 obstacle, bit 2 active; bit 7 spawns a decorative sub-item instead of an interactive item. Use 7 for a hittable scripted fixture. animation_6 int Animation the object starts in. mode_7 int Object mode. For items this is (controller index + 1) * 2 , so 2 is the first item controller. height_8 int Height above the ground, in pixels. containedItemPackName string Pack owning the item hidden inside. containedItemEntityName string Item revealed when this container is broken open. insideForTwoPlayersOnly_10_b7 bool Only place the contained item in a two player game. palettePackName , paletteIndex string, int Palette for the object. The _2 , _6 , _7 , _8 suffixes are byte offsets in the original ROM structure. They are part of the field names; do not drop them. collisionBox_3_4_5 ¶ The runtime reads this field as a BoundingBox . That is the canonical shape — the only one the game deserializes, and what both the ROM importer and the Level Editor write: "collisionBox_3_4_5": { "halfWidth": 14, "height": 72, "depth": 6 } All three values are raw ROM bytes, from offsets 0xD , 0xE , and 0xF . halfWidth is half the box width, so the box spans -halfWidth to +halfWidth around the spawn position. A height of 0 means "no override": the entity falls back to its animation body box, and then to its global body box. Two superseded shapes still exist in files written by older builds. The Level Editor reads all three and always writes the canonical one, so opening a level and saving it migrates that level. tools/migrate_collision_boxes.py converts files in bulk without opening them. Legacy shape Written by Converts to {depth, rect: {x, y, width, height}} The runtime, before mid-2024. halfWidth = rect.width , height = rect.height , depth = depth . {x, y, width, height} The Level Editor, before it was fixed. Nothing recoverable — an all-zero box. rect.width is a half width, not a full width The build that wrote the nested shape stored the raw ROM byte in rect.width , then derived rect.x = -rect.width / 2 . So rect.width already holds halfWidth . Halving it when converting shrinks every box to half its intended size. The flat shape carries no information at all: the editor parsed the field as a plain rectangle, which dropped halfWidth and depth on load and wrote them back as zeros. Levels saved in that state lost their per-spawn overrides for good, and need them re-authored. Until a file is migrated, the runtime reads any non-canonical shape as all zeros and ignores the override entirely. Art files ¶ Root object: LocalLevelBackgroundData . Used by - art.json , - cutscenes.json , title.json , presentation.json , and ending.json , in Levels/ and in Level Replacements/<Target Pack>/ alike. Field Type Meaning scenes array of LocalSceneBackgroundData One per scene. A null entry reuses the previous scene's background. animationsDefinition array of LocalLayerAnimation The file's animation library. Layers reference entries by array index , so reordering silently repoints every reference. Scene background ¶ Field Type Meaning layers array Visual layers, drawn by zOrder . musicPackName string Pack the music is loaded from. Empty means this pack. musicName string Music track, base file name without extension. screenShakeType int 0 Default, 1 Truck, 2 Boat. cutsceneEndTimeInSeconds float How long a cutscene scene lasts before advancing. -1 , the default, means it does not advance on its own — which is what gameplay scenes use. Scene music lives here, in the art file, not in the gameplay file. Some older files carry musicName and musicPackName inside level <n>.json scenes; the runtime ignores them there. Layers ¶ Field Type Meaning layerName string Editor label. zOrder float Draw order. Lower values draw in front. Built-in backgrounds use about 10 , and foregrounds use about -6 . parallax {x, y} float Scroll speed relative to the camera. 1 moves with the camera, below 1 is a slower background, above 1 a faster foreground. Defaults to {1, 1} . autoScroll {x, y} float Constant self-scrolling in pixels per second, independent of the camera. scrollLoopLimits {x, y} float Wrap distance per axis. A positive value tiles the layer endlessly over that span; 0 disables wrapping on that axis. positionOffset {x, y} float Shift applied to everything on the layer, in pixels. reactToQuakeEffect bool Shake with the screen during a quake. The shake is an offset on top of the layer's own position, so a layer that scrolls vertically or is moved by its visualScript keeps moving while it shakes. updateType int Special per-frame behaviour. See below. staticImages array Still images placed on the layer. titleScreenImages array Animated entrance images, for title and character select screens. animations array Placed instances of animationsDefinition entries. updateType values: 0 Normal, 1 BackyardRain, 2 TruckBrokenDoor, 3 Stage4Elevator, 4 ArenaSpectators, 5 Stage7Elevator, 6 Stage7ElevatorExtra, 7 Stage8Elevator, 8 AntiCameraY, 9 WaveEffect, 10 SmallWaveEffect, 11 SwingingBoat. These reproduce specific original-game effects and mostly assume the scene is laid out like the stage they came from. 0 is what a new layer wants. Local WaveEffect and SmallWaveEffect layers use the Classic wave shader, wave tables and effect-camera ordering. Static images and animated children on all matching layers receive that effect. Dry scenes reset their render layers and disable the effect camera. useClassicLayerMotion: true separately delegates the layer transform to the original controller, preserving elevator and other stage-specific movement. For stationary Classic layers, staticParallaxType also preserves widescreen registration: 0 Normal, 1 Skyline, 2 Stage7Elevator. It requires useClassicLayerMotion: true ; the controller then supplies the native -34px vertical offset, so do not add that offset a second time in positionOffset . Images and animations ¶ staticImages entries: Field Type Meaning imageName string File name inside Levels/Art/ , including its extension . position {x, y} float Position within the layer, in pixels. scale float Size multiplier. 0 is treated as 1 , and the absolute value is used. titleScreenImages entries add an entrance animation on top of those three fields: Field Type Meaning initialXPosition float Horizontal offset the image starts from. initialDelay float Seconds to wait before it starts moving. lerpSpeed float How quickly it eases towards position . Higher catches up faster. wiggleAmplitude float How far it wiggles off its path, in pixels. 0 disables. wiggleFrequency float How fast it wiggles. requireCharacterName bool Only use this entry when the character's name matches, rather than for everyone. isAICharacter bool Present this portrait as computer-controlled rather than as a player. animations entries are just a placement: Field Type Meaning animationId int Index into this file's animationsDefinition . position {x, y} float Placement within the layer, in pixels. animationsDefinition entries hold frames : Field Type Meaning imageName string File name inside Levels/Art/ , including extension. delayFrames int Game frames this image is held. pivotInPixels {x, y} float The point of the image that sits at the placement position, in pixels from its bottom-left corner. scale float Size multiplier. 0 is treated as 1 . The same animation can be placed many times on many layers; that is the point of the shared library. Example ¶ { "animationsDefinition": [ { "frames": [ { "imageName": "water-1.png", "delayFrames": 8, "pivotInPixels": { "x": 0, "y": 0 }, "scale": 1 }, { "imageName": "water-2.png", "delayFrames": 8, "pivotInPixels": { "x": 0, "y": 0 }, "scale": 1 } ] } ], "scenes": [ { "musicPackName": "My Pack", "musicName": "stage-1", "cutsceneEndTimeInSeconds": -1, "layers": [ { "layerName": "Sky", "zOrder": -30, "parallax": { "x": 0.25, "y": 0.25 }, "scrollLoopLimits": { "x": 512, "y": 0 }, "staticImages": [ { "imageName": "clouds.png", "position": { "x": 0, "y": 0 }, "scale": 1 } ] }, { "layerName": "Water", "zOrder": -10, "parallax": { "x": 1, "y": 1 }, "animations": [{ "animationId": 0, "position": { "x": 120, "y": 40 } }] } ] } ] } Related pages ¶ Levels, Scenes, and Cutscenes Background Layers Create Custom Levels Enums and Identifiers Scripted stage extensions ¶ Scenes support scriptedItems for explicit item spawning through game.spawn_scene_item(index) . Scenes support updateScript , and updateScriptDuringCinematics: true to keep running it, for presentation only, behind a gameplay cinematic. Art layers support tilemap and visualScript . See the scripted-stage Lua documentation for coordinates, data formats and rollback rules. Scene enterScript uses the same reference as updateScript . scriptedEntrance skips automatic entrance walking when the script owns placement. scriptedClock leaves the HUD timer under Lua control. scriptedEnemies disables automatic enemy cues so the stage script can spawn individual enemies1 cues with game.spawn_scene_enemy(index) and maintain persistent area encounters. See Scripted stages for lifecycle, units and rollback rules. Scripted waves inside a scene ¶ scriptedWaveCount (default 0, equivalent to one) exposes multiple authored waves in the custom-game wave selector. scriptedWaveCustomValue (0–16; zero disables seeding) selects the game custom variable receiving the one-based starting wave. These are camera-lock encounter groups within one background scene; scene fades still occur only at physical scene boundaries. Use game.complete_scene() from the gameplay script to execute the configured walk/fade or stage-clear exit before advancing to the next physical scene.

docs.text: Root object: LocalLevelBackgroundData . Used by - art.json , - cutscenes.json , title.json , presentation.json , and ending.json , in Levels/ and in Level Replacements/<Target Pack>/ alike. Field Type Meaning scenes array of LocalSceneBackgroundData One per scene. A null entry reuses the previous scene's background. animationsDefinition array of LocalLayerAnimation The file's animation library. Layers reference entries by array index , so reordering silently repoints every reference.
docs.title: Art files

docs.text: Field Type Meaning layers array Visual layers, drawn by zOrder . musicPackName string Pack the music is loaded from. Empty means this pack. musicName string Music track, base file name without extension. screenShakeType int 0 Default, 1 Truck, 2 Boat. cutsceneEndTimeInSeconds float How long a cutscene scene lasts before advancing. -1 , the default, means it does not advance on its own — which is what gameplay scenes use. Scene music lives here, in the art file, not in the gameplay file. Some older files carry musicName and musicPackName inside level <n>.json scenes; the runtime ignores them there.
docs.title: Scene background

docs.text: Field Type Meaning layerName string Editor label. zOrder float Draw order. Lower values draw in front. Built-in backgrounds use about 10 , and foregrounds use about -6 . parallax {x, y} float Scroll speed relative to the camera. 1 moves with the camera, below 1 is a slower background, above 1 a faster foreground. Defaults to {1, 1} . autoScroll {x, y} float Constant self-scrolling in pixels per second, independent of the camera. scrollLoopLimits {x, y} float Wrap distance per axis. A positive value tiles the layer endlessly over that span; 0 disables wrapping on that axis. positionOffset {x, y} float Shift applied to everything on the layer, in pixels. reactToQuakeEffect bool Shake with the screen during a quake. The shake is an offset on top of the layer's own position, so a layer that scrolls vertically or is moved by its visualScript keeps moving while it shakes. updateType int Special per-frame behaviour. See below. staticImages array Still images placed on the layer. titleScreenImages array Animated entrance images, for title and character select screens. animations array Placed instances of animationsDefinition entries. updateType values: 0 Normal, 1 BackyardRain, 2 TruckBrokenDoor, 3 Stage4Elevator, 4 ArenaSpectators, 5 Stage7Elevator, 6 Stage7ElevatorExtra, 7 Stage8Elevator, 8 AntiCameraY, 9 WaveEffect, 10 SmallWaveEffect, 11 SwingingBoat. These reproduce specific original-game effects and mostly assume the scene is laid out like the stage they came from. 0 is what a new layer wants. Local WaveEffect and SmallWaveEffect layers use the Classic wave shader, wave tables and effect-camera ordering. Static images and animated children on all matching layers receive that effect. Dry scenes reset their render layers and disable the effect camera. useClassicLayerMotion: true separately delegates the layer transform to the original controller, preserving elevator and other stage-specific movement. For stationary Classic layers, staticParallaxType also preserves widescreen registration: 0 Normal, 1 Skyline, 2 Stage7Elevator. It requires useClassicLayerMotion: true ; the controller then supplies the native -34px vertical offset, so do not add that offset a second time in positionOffset .
docs.title: Layers

docs.text: staticImages entries: Field Type Meaning imageName string File name inside Levels/Art/ , including its extension . position {x, y} float Position within the layer, in pixels. scale float Size multiplier. 0 is treated as 1 , and the absolute value is used. titleScreenImages entries add an entrance animation on top of those three fields: Field Type Meaning initialXPosition float Horizontal offset the image starts from. initialDelay float Seconds to wait before it starts moving. lerpSpeed float How quickly it eases towards position . Higher catches up faster. wiggleAmplitude float How far it wiggles off its path, in pixels. 0 disables. wiggleFrequency float How fast it wiggles. requireCharacterName bool Only use this entry when the character's name matches, rather than for everyone. isAICharacter bool Present this portrait as computer-controlled rather than as a player. animations entries are just a placement: Field Type Meaning animationId int Index into this file's animationsDefinition . position {x, y} float Placement within the layer, in pixels. animationsDefinition entries hold frames : Field Type Meaning imageName string File name inside Levels/Art/ , including extension. delayFrames int Game frames this image is held. pivotInPixels {x, y} float The point of the image that sits at the placement position, in pixels from its bottom-left corner. scale float Size multiplier. 0 is treated as 1 . The same animation can be placed many times on many layers; that is the point of the shared library.

docs.text: Scenes support scriptedItems for explicit item spawning through game.spawn_scene_item(index) . Scenes support updateScript , and updateScriptDuringCinematics: true to keep running it, for presentation only, behind a gameplay cinematic. Art layers support tilemap and visualScript . See the scripted-stage Lua documentation for coordinates, data formats and rollback rules. Scene enterScript uses the same reference as updateScript . scriptedEntrance skips automatic entrance walking when the script owns placement. scriptedClock leaves the HUD timer under Lua control. scriptedEnemies disables automatic enemy cues so the stage script can spawn individual enemies1 cues with game.spawn_scene_enemy(index) and maintain persistent area encounters. See Scripted stages for lifecycle, units and rollback rules.

docs.text: scriptedWaveCount (default 0, equivalent to one) exposes multiple authored waves in the custom-game wave selector. scriptedWaveCustomValue (0–16; zero disables seeding) selects the game custom variable receiving the one-based starting wave. These are camera-lock encounter groups within one background scene; scene fades still occur only at physical scene boundaries. Use game.complete_scene() from the gameplay script to execute the configured walk/fade or stage-clear exit before advancing to the next physical scene.

docs.text: Pack Layout and Conventions ¶ Every rule on this page applies to all file formats. Read it once before the per-format pages. Source folder structure ¶ Editor/<Mod Name>/ config.json thumbnail.png Entities/ <Entity Name>/ spriteSettings.json animations.json logic.json dependencies.json 0.png, 1.png, 2.png, ... portrait.png preview.png Palettes/ palette 0.png, palette 1.png, ... Entity Replacements/ Classic/ <Classic Entity Name>/ same files as an entity Levels/ level 1.json level 1 - art.json level 1 - cutscenes.json title.json presentation.json ending.json Art/ <any image files> Level Replacements/ Classic/ level 1 - art.json level 1 - cutscenes.json title.json presentation.json ending.json Palettes/ <Target Pack>/ <Entity Name>/ palette 0.png, palette 1.png, ... Sounds/ <any audio files> Musics/ <any audio files> <track name>.json loop points Audio Replacements/ <Target Pack>/ music-replacements.json sound-replacements.json Scripts/ <any .lua files> Only the folders your mod uses need to exist. Missing folders and missing files are not errors; the loader treats them as "this mod provides nothing here". The folder name under Editor/ is the pack name. Renaming the folder renames the pack, which changes its hash and breaks every packName reference pointing at the old name. The three kinds of content ¶ Understanding which of these you are authoring decides where the files go. Own content lives under Entities/ and Levels/ . It belongs to your pack and is addressed as (your pack name, entity or level name) . Replacements live under Entity Replacements/<Target Pack>/ and Level Replacements/<Target Pack>/ . They substitute content of another pack, in place, keeping that pack's identity. This is how a reskin works: your Entity Replacements/Classic/Axel/ becomes what the game shows when it draws Classic's Axel. The folder name under the replacements folder must match an entity or file name that exists in the target pack. Contributions live under Palettes/<Target Pack>/ and Audio Replacements/<Target Pack>/ . They add to or redirect part of another pack without replacing whole entities. <Target Pack> is almost always Classic , the built-in pack extracted from the original ROM. How names resolve ¶ Almost every cross-reference in these files is a (packName, name) pair of plain strings. An empty or omitted packName means the Classic pack in loadcues and dependencies, and the current pack in editor-written sound and script references. The per-format pages state which applies. Names are matched by folder or file name exactly as written, including spaces and capitalisation. Internally, both names are reduced to a 32-bit hash. You never need to compute this except for allowedCharacters in config.json ; see Enums and Identifiers . A reference to a pack that is not loaded is not a load-time error. It fails at the moment the game tries to use it, which usually looks like a missing sprite or a silent sound. List every pack you reference in config.json dependencies . File naming rules ¶ These are matched by prefix and suffix in code, so they are exact. Pattern Meaning Levels/level <n>.json A level's gameplay data. The prefix is level with a trailing space. Levels/level <n> - art.json That level's visuals. The suffix is - art.json . Levels/level <n> - cutscenes.json That level's cutscenes. The suffix is - cutscenes.json . Levels/title.json , presentation.json , ending.json Fixed names for the non-level screens. Entities/<name>/<i>.png Own sprite frame i , zero-based, no padding. Palettes/.../palette <n>.png Palette n . Sorted numerically by the trailing digits, not alphabetically. Musics/<track>.json Loop points for Musics/<track>.<audio extension> . Level discovery scans Levels/ for files starting with level and not ending in the art or cutscenes suffix, so a stray level notes.json would be picked up as a level. Keep the folder tidy. Palette sorting deserves a note: files are ordered by the digits at the end of the base name, so palette 2.png comes before palette 10.png . Plain alphabetical order would get this wrong, and everything downstream — exporting, deleting, the paletteIndex a loadcue refers to — assumes the numeric order. Assets ¶ Asset Format Notes Sprite frames PNG One image per frame. Transparency preserved. Frame count comes from spriteSettings.json pivots , not from how many PNGs exist. portrait.png , preview.png PNG Optional. Character select portrait and preview. thumbnail.png PNG Optional. Shown in mod listings. Level art PNG or JPG Anything the engine's texture loader accepts. Referenced by file name including extension. Palettes PNG See Palette Files . Sounds and music .wav , .mp3 , .ogg Referenced by base name without extension. Level art images are drawn with point filtering by default, which keeps pixel art sharp. An image used only at non-integer scales is switched to bilinear filtering automatically. If the same image is used at both an integer and a non-integer scale anywhere in the pack, point filtering wins for all of its uses. Editing safely ¶ Never reorder an indexed array. animations , animationsLogic , and animationsDefinition are addressed by position. Inserting an entry in the middle silently repoints every reference past it. Keep parallel arrays aligned. animations.json animations[i] and logic.json animationsLogic[i] describe the same animation. Either may be shorter, and either entry may be null . Prefer omitting a field to writing a zero , especially on an entity that sets referencePackName . On a referencing entity, 0 is indistinguishable from "not set" and falls through to the reference. See Entity Files . Close the editor before hand-editing. The Godot editors hold the loaded model in memory and rewrite the whole file on save, so a save after your edit will discard it. Related pages ¶ Mod Folder Anatomy Asset Requirements Validating a Mod

docs.text: Package Format ¶ An exported mod is a single file under Mods/ : Mods/My Mod.cne encrypted package, the normal export Mods/My Mod.zip plain package, the unencrypted variant Players drop this file into their Mods/ folder; the game detects what is there at startup. Do not author packages directly A package is a build output, not an editing format. Its sprites have been repacked into texture atlases and its per-frame PNGs no longer exist as separate files, so there is nothing sensible to hand-edit. Author the source folder under Editor/<Mod Name>/ and re-export. Structure ¶ Both extensions are ZIP archives. .cne writes the archive through an encryption stream; .zip writes it plainly. The archive contents are otherwise identical. Inside, the layout mirrors the source folder, with the same config.json , entity JSON, level JSON, audio, and scripts. Three things differ. Sprites become atlases. Individual 0.png , 1.png frames are gone. Their pixels are packed into shared texture pages under Sprite Atlases/ : Entry Contents Sprite Atlases/core <n>.png Entity sprite pages. Sprite Atlases/presentation.png Presentation and menu art. Sprite Atlases/palette.png The default palette, stored separately so its index stays coherent. Levels/Sprite Atlases/level <level>-<scene> <n>.png Level background pages. Levels/Sprite Atlases/animation <n>.png Level animation pages. Atlas pages are capped at 4096 pixels square and target about 80% occupancy, so a large pack produces several numbered pages. atlasesData.json is added at the archive root. It maps every original sprite to its page and rectangle. It is generated during export and has no meaning outside a package. Checksums are filled in. config.json dependenciesChecksums , empty in a source pack, is populated with the actual checksum of each dependency at export time. id is kept as is, and dependenciesIds records the id of each dependency that has one. Music may also be trimmed on export: a track with a loopEndTimeInSeconds can be cut at that point, since nothing after it is ever heard. Exporting ¶ Export is done from the in-game editor's export step, which is also where you choose encrypted or plain. It reads Editor/<Mod Name>/ and writes to Mods/ . The name of the output file comes from the pack's display name, which is the source folder name. A mod with an id is the same mod under any name: exporting it after a rename replaces the file exported under the previous name. Sharing ¶ The exported file is the whole mod. Players copy it into Mods/ and restart the game. Because dependency checksums are captured at export, a mod that depends on another pack expects that specific version. Re-export after a dependency changes. Related pages ¶ Export a Mod Package, Export, and Share Testing and Exporting Installing Community Mods
docs.title: Package Format

docs.text: Palette Files ¶ Palettes are PNG images. There is no JSON involved. What a palette PNG means depends entirely on where it sits. Two locations, two meanings ¶ Palette guides , for entities your pack owns: Entities/<Entity Name>/Palettes/palette 0.png Entities/<Entity Name>/Palettes/palette 1.png Final palettes , contributed to entities another pack owns: Palettes/<Target Pack>/<Entity Name>/palette 0.png Palettes/<Target Pack>/<Entity Name>/palette 1.png These are not interchangeable, and the difference is the single most important thing on this page. Guides, for your own entities ¶ Your entity's sprites are ordinary full-colour PNGs. The game cannot recolour them until it knows which colours are the palette. Guides tell it. On load, the pack builds a default palette from the guides, converts every one of the entity's own sprite frames into an indexed-colour form against that palette, and then treats each guide as one selectable colour set. Guide palette 0.png is the default: the colours as the sprites were drawn. Each further guide is the same colour slots in the same order, recoloured. At least two guides are required for indexing to happen at all. With fewer, the converter does nothing and the entity keeps its literal sprite colours with no palette switching. Final palettes, for other packs' entities ¶ An entity from another pack — a Classic character, say — is already indexed. Your pack does not need to teach the game anything about its colours; it just supplies extra colour sets. Files under Palettes/<Target Pack>/<Entity Name>/ are loaded directly as palette textures and appended to that entity's palette list. This is how you add new colour choices for Classic Axel without touching Classic's own files: Editor/My Reskin/Palettes/Classic/Axel/palette 0.png Editor/My Reskin/Palettes/Classic/Axel/palette 1.png A folder under Palettes/ whose name matches your own pack is skipped: own-pack palettes belong with the entity, under Entities/<name>/Palettes/ . File naming and order ¶ Files are named palette <n>.png and sorted numerically by the trailing digits , not alphabetically. palette 2.png comes before palette 10.png . This matters because the position in that sorted order is the palette index — the number a level loadcue's paletteIndex or a character select choice refers to. Plain alphabetical sorting would reorder every palette from 10 onwards. A file whose base name does not end in digits sorts last. Authoring rules ¶ Whichever kind you are making: Keep the same dimensions across every palette for one entity. Keep the colour order identical . Slot k in palette 3.png recolours whatever slot k in palette 0.png was. Preserve transparent or reserved colours in the slots where the reference palette has them. Palette 0 is the default and should be the entity's natural colours. The safest way to make a new palette is to copy palette 0.png and recolour it in place, never adding, removing, or reordering pixels. If a palette PNG fails to load as an image, the loader logs a warning and continues; the entity ends up with a placeholder in that slot rather than a hard failure. A silently wrong-looking character is usually a corrupt or wrongly-sized palette file. How palettes get used ¶ Character select cycles through the palettes available for the chosen character. In multiplayer, the select screen tries to skip palettes already taken so two players on the same character stay distinguishable. Level loadcues pick a palette per spawn with palettePackName and paletteIndex , which is how the same enemy appears in different colours through a stage. Scenes can apply an alternativePalette by name to the enemies in that scene. HUD icons use the selected palette, via spriteSettings.json iconIndex . An entity that borrows another entity's art through spriteSettings.json also borrows that entity's palette identity: palettes resolve against the reference entity, not the borrower. Related pages ¶ Add New Color Palettes for the Classic playable-character workflow. Create Palettes for Your Own Character Create Palettes for Classic or Other Mod Characters Color Palette Editor

docs.text: Validating a Mod ¶ The game is forgiving about malformed mod data. Unknown fields are ignored, missing files are treated as "this mod provides nothing here", and a broken reference fails at the moment it is used rather than at load. That is good for robustness and bad for finding mistakes: a typo usually shows up as an invisible sprite or a silent sound effect, several minutes into a playtest. Two tools close that gap. JSON Schemas ¶ Machine-readable schemas for every JSON format live in docs/schemas/ . Schema Validates config.schema.json config.json spriteSettings.schema.json Entities/*/spriteSettings.json animations.schema.json Entities/*/animations.json logic.schema.json Entities/*/logic.json , including every logic event dependencies.schema.json Entities/*/dependencies.json level.schema.json Levels/level <n>.json level-art.schema.json - art.json , - cutscenes.json , title.json , presentation.json , ending.json audio-replacements.schema.json music-replacements.json , sound-replacements.json music-loop.schema.json Musics/<track>.json common.schema.json Shared value types, referenced by the others They are JSON Schema draft 2020-12 and reference each other by file name, so keep them in one folder. Every field carries a description , which makes them useful as a lookup as well as a check. Fields marked deprecated are ones older builds wrote and the runtime ignores: they validate so existing mods do not drown in noise, but do not write new ones. The schemas are checked against every mod in the repository's Editor/ folder, so they accept what the tools actually produce, not an idealised version of it. Using them ¶ With Python: pip install jsonschema import json from jsonschema import Draft202012Validator from referencing import Registry, Resource from referencing.jsonschema import DRAFT202012 import glob, os resources = { os.path.basename(p): Resource.from_contents(json.load(open(p, encoding="utf-8")), default_specification=DRAFT202012) for p in glob.glob("docs/schemas/*.json") } registry = Registry().with_resources(resources.items()) validator = Draft202012Validator(resources["logic.schema.json"].contents, registry=registry) data = json.load(open("Editor/My Mod/Entities/My Fighter/logic.json", encoding="utf-8-sig")) for error in validator.iter_errors(data): print("/".join(str(p) for p in error.absolute_path), error.message) Most editors also accept a $schema pointer or a workspace mapping, which gives you completion and inline errors while hand-editing. The validator script ¶ tools/validate_mod.py runs the schemas plus the cross-file checks a schema cannot express. python tools/validate_mod.py "Editor/My Mod" Options: Option Effect --schemas <path> Where the schema folder is. Found automatically in the usual layouts. --strict Exit non-zero on warnings too, not just errors. --no-collapse List every finding instead of collapsing repeats of the same one. It needs jsonschema for the schema pass and optionally Pillow for palette size checks. Without either, the remaining checks still run. Findings come in three levels: ERROR — something is broken and will not work: a sprite that draws nothing, an animation id past the end of the list, a sound that does not exist. WARN — suspicious but possibly deliberate: an animation whose logic duration outruns its frames, an undeclared dependency, a level whose art has more scenes than its gameplay. NOTE — informational, including checks that were skipped because they needed a pack that is not part of this mod. Repeats of the same finding in the same file collapse to one line with a count, so one systemic problem reads as one problem. What it checks beyond the schemas ¶ Entities pivots length against the numbered PNGs, erroring only when an animation actually references a missing frame and noting the rest. imageId and iconIndex against the real sprite count, accounting for borrowed reference frames. animationsLogic length against animations . Every animationId in events and throw offsets against the animation count. Every sound name against Sounds/ , and every script name against Scripts/ . Event $type spelling, unknown event classes, and input combo strings containing characters that can never match. Frame numbers past the end of an animation, and negative frames left behind by editor frame shifts. Levels Every imageName against Levels/Art/ . Every layer animationId against the file's animationsDefinition . Scene counts between a level and its art file. wallLimitsData length, and the horizon/depth constraint when the left wall flag is set. Loadcues with no entityName , and collision boxes stored in the shape the game cannot read. Scene music against Musics/ . Palettes Duplicate or non-contiguous palette indices, and files that do not end in a number. Entity palette guides numbering fewer than two, which silently disables palette switching. Palette images of differing sizes within one set, with Pillow installed. Audio and config Replacement maps pointing at audio that does not exist, and empty maps that are silently skipped. Loop end before loop start, and loop files with no matching track. dependenciesChecksums and dependenciesIds lengths against dependencies . id and each dependenciesIds entry being a UUID. Difficulty entries with too few per-player-count settings. Any pack referenced anywhere in the mod but missing from dependencies . What it cannot check ¶ Anything that needs the other pack's contents. If your entity borrows Classic Axel's art, the validator cannot know how many frames Classic Axel has, so it skips the sprite index checks for that entity and says so in a note. The same applies to sounds and entities referenced from another mod. It also says nothing about whether your mod is any good: a hitbox in the wrong place, a jump that feels bad, or a palette with muddy colours all validate perfectly. Runtime regression checks ¶ Construct character fixtures through the normal spawn/initialization path and retain the flags it produces. Setting convenient flags by hand can hide a script that excludes every real enemy. For example, enemy initialization leaves the item/projectile is_active flag clear; it does not mean that the enemy is absent. Exercise the whole frame pipeline, including the victim controller, position resolution and animation update. Checking only the attacker's script state or pending animation does not establish the frame or position that is drawn. Record both characters' rendered sprite, pivot, position and height at each choreography transition and at throw release. Include different victim packs, both facings, wall-adjacent grabs, and enemies with extra health bars. Start grab moves after several different hold durations, and test a player victim both before and after the attacker in player-slot order. A victim that updates first can observe the previous attacker's clock even when a later-slot victim behaves correctly. For input regressions, use the normal player controller's input preprocessing. Smooth controls can replay a press through host spam timers; a Lua controller that keeps its own input latch must consume the host buffer when it captures the press. Test one press, a held button, a fresh second press and hit interruption. For cinematics, assert health and death transitions while the fire is landing, not merely a queued hit flag or a result after the event ends. Check the complete camera trip, including a return to zero, with actual frame timing when testing interpolation. Keep these scratch harnesses and extraction scripts outside the committed mod and production tools unless they are intended as maintained tooling. docs.text: Classic Reskinning ¶ Classic reskinning is the path for making a new look and sound for the original Streets of Rage 2 experience without rebuilding the full game rules from scratch. It is meant for packs that keep the Classic dependency and replace or extend presentation assets: title screen, character select presentation, level backgrounds, cutscenes, ending screens, characters, enemies, items, music, sounds, and playable-character palettes. Use these pages when your goal is "make Classic look and sound like my version." Use the scripting pages when your goal is "change what an entity does." What A Classic Reskin Can Replace ¶ Area Main editor Output location Title screen Level Editor, Classic Reskin mode Level Replacements/Classic/title.json and Levels/Art/* Presentation and extra cutscenes Level Editor, Classic Reskin mode Level Replacements/Classic/presentation.json , Level Replacements/Classic/level <n> - cutscenes.json Character select presentation Level Editor, Classic Reskin mode Level Replacements/Classic/title.json title-screen image entries Classic level backgrounds Level Editor, Classic Reskin mode Level Replacements/Classic/level <n> - art.json Ending screens Level Editor, Classic Reskin mode Level Replacements/Classic/ending.json Classic characters, enemies, and items Character Editor, Classic Reskin mode Entity Replacements/Classic/<Entity Name>/ Playable character palettes Palette workflow Palettes/Classic/<Playable Character>/palette <n>.png Music and sound replacements Audio Editor, Classic Reskin mode Audio Replacements/Classic/*.json , Musics/ , Sounds/ Pack Layout ¶ A typical Classic reskin pack looks like this: Editor/ My Reskin/ config.json thumbnail.png Levels/ Art/ city-back.png title-logo.png Level Replacements/ Classic/ title.json level 1 - art.json level 1 - cutscenes.json ending.json Entity Replacements/ Classic/ Axel/ Galsia/ Palettes/ Classic/ Axel/ palette 0.png palette 1.png Audio Replacements/ Classic/ music-replacements.json sound-replacements.json Musics/ stage1-theme.ogg stage1-theme.json Sounds/ punch-heavy.wav The Classic folder names are intentional. They tell the runtime which original pack your replacements target. Recommended Reading Order ¶ Workflow Title Screen Classic Levels Add Cutscenes Classic Characters Classic Enemies and Items Add New Color Palettes Replace Music Replace Sounds Keep the file format reference and troubleshooting page nearby when editing JSON by hand.

docs.text: Add Cutscenes ¶ Classic reskins can add or replace presentation screens, level cutscenes, and ending scenes without creating new level logic. Cutscene File Locations ¶ Cutscene File Opening or presentation Level Replacements/Classic/presentation.json Level-specific cutscene Level Replacements/Classic/level <n> - cutscenes.json Ending Level Replacements/Classic/ending.json Title screen Level Replacements/Classic/title.json All of these files use the same LocalLevelBackgroundData format. Images are shared through Levels/Art . Add A Level Cutscene ¶ Open the Level Editor. Choose Classic Reskin . In the cutscene list, press add. Choose the level number you want to attach the cutscene to. Add scenes, layers, images, and optional animations. Set cutsceneEndTimeInSeconds on each scene if the scene should advance automatically. Level numbers are human-facing and start at 1 . A file named level 3 - cutscenes.json targets Classic stage 3. Scene Timing ¶ cutsceneEndTimeInSeconds controls automatic advancement: -1 means no automatic end time. a positive value means the scene can advance after that many seconds. When a cutscene has multiple scenes, each scene can have its own timing and music fields. Music Per Scene ¶ Set musicPackName and musicName on a scene when you want a specific track to start with that scene. Use the base music filename without extension. { "musicPackName": "My Reskin", "musicName": "stage-clear-remix", "cutsceneEndTimeInSeconds": 8.0, "layers": [] } Reusing Art ¶ Put shared art in Levels/Art once and reference it from several cutscene JSON files. This is safer than duplicating images across folders because the packer and runtime expect level-art references to resolve from that shared art folder. Testing ¶ Test cutscenes in game, not only in the editor. Confirm: the correct cutscene starts at the expected point music starts and loops cleanly images are not missing scene timing is long enough for fade-ins or moving title images widescreen framing looks correct

docs.text: Add New Color Palettes ¶ Add new color palettes is a playable-character workflow. It adds extra palette choices for Classic playable characters on character select. It is not the workflow for enemy palettes, item palettes, level palettes, or full sprite replacements. Supported Target ¶ Use this workflow for playable characters only, such as: Axel Blaze Skate Max Shiva other playable Classic entities exposed by the current build Do not use this page for Galsia, Donovan, weapons, food, containers, or background objects. File Location ¶ Place palette PNGs under: Editor/<Pack Name>/Palettes/Classic/<Playable Character>/palette <n>.png Example: Editor/My Reskin/ Palettes/ Classic/ Axel/ palette 0.png palette 1.png palette 2.png The folder name Classic targets the Classic pack. The character folder name targets the playable entity. Palette Image Expectations ¶ Palette files are PNG images used as palette providers. Keep them consistent with the character's indexed-color expectations: use the same palette dimensions as the generated or reference palette files keep color order stable keep transparent or reserved colors where the reference palette uses them name files consistently as palette 0.png , palette 1.png , and so on If you generated palettes through the editor, keep the generated output instead of rebuilding by hand unless you know the palette format. How The Game Uses Them ¶ The runtime collects palette providers for the target playable entity. On character select, players can cycle through available palettes. In multiplayer, the select screen skips already-used palettes when possible so two players choosing the same character can remain visually distinct. Testing ¶ Test palette additions on the character select screen and in gameplay: every added palette appears in the selector HUD icons use the selected palette sprites do not show unexpected color bands multiplayer selection still gives distinct colors when possible special effects or alternate sprites still look acceptable Common Mistakes ¶ Symptom Check Palette does not appear Folder path must be Palettes/Classic/<Playable Character>/ . Palette appears on wrong character Check the character folder name. Sprite colors look scrambled Palette color order or dimensions do not match the expected guide. Enemy palette did not change This workflow is only for playable characters. Use entity art, scene palette data, or entity replacement work for enemies.

docs.text: Character Select ¶ The Classic character select presentation uses a mix of normal UI, playable character data, palettes, and reskin screen art. A Classic reskin can affect it in three main ways: replace playable character art through Entity Replacements/Classic/<Character>/ add selectable palettes for playable characters through Palettes/Classic/<Character>/ replace presentation art through title screen or replacement screen data in Level Replacements/Classic Character Art ¶ Use the Character Editor in Classic Reskin mode to replace Classic playable characters. The editor writes each replacement to: Editor/<Pack Name>/Entity Replacements/Classic/<Character Name>/ The select screen uses entity metadata such as preview, portrait, icon index, and palettes. When replacing a playable character, check the character in the select screen after editing: icon is visible and not cropped portrait or preview uses the intended sprite palette choices are readable name and character display still line up Character Select Screen Art ¶ The Level Editor's Classic Reskin mode includes title-screen-oriented image data. Title screen image entries can animate into position and can optionally be tied to character-related conditions. Use titleScreenImages when a piece of art should slide, wiggle, or appear conditionally. Use staticImages for fixed decoration. Relevant fields: Field Meaning requireCharacterName The image is intended to appear only for a matching character selection. isAICharacter The image represents an AI or companion character layer. initialXPosition Start position for a slide-in. lerpSpeed Slide speed. initialDelay Delay before movement starts. Palettes On Character Select ¶ Palette selection is only documented here for playable characters. Use Add New Color Palettes to add extra color choices for Axel, Blaze, Skate, Max, Shiva, or any playable character exposed by the Classic pack. Do not use the playable-character palette workflow for enemies or items. Enemy and item colors are part of entity art, scene palette data, or explicit entity replacement work. Recommended Checks ¶ Before considering character select complete: start a one-player run and a multi-player run choose every replaced playable character cycle every added playable palette check both normal and widescreen modes if your pack supports widescreen confirm your character select art does not hide UI text or selected portraits

docs.text: Classic Characters ¶ Classic character reskinning replaces playable Classic entities while keeping their original identity and select-screen slot. Use this for Axel, Blaze, Skate, Max, Shiva, and any other playable Classic entity exposed by the editor reference data. File Location ¶ The Character Editor writes Classic replacements to: Editor/<Pack Name>/Entity Replacements/Classic/<Character Name>/ A replacement folder can contain: File Purpose spriteSettings.json Sprite pivots, scale, icon index, and optional sprite reference settings. animations.json Animation frame lists. logic.json Entity type, movement, combat data, animation logic, events, scripts, and reference logic. dependencies.json Extra sounds, entities, or music referenced by the entity. 0.png , 1.png , etc. Sprite frames. preview.png Select or editor preview image. portrait.png Portrait image where supported. Start From A Classic Reference ¶ In the Character Editor: Open your pack folder. Choose Classic Reskin . Select the original character you want to replace. Edit sprites, pivots, frames, animation timing, and optional logic. Save and test in character select and gameplay. The editor uses the original Classic entity as a logic and timing reference. By default, the replacement uses your custom art only. The Classic sprites may appear as ghost/base sprites in the preview so you can line up frames, but they are not saved as reused replacement art unless you explicitly set Use Sprites from . Import Player Skins From A ROM ¶ In Classic Reskin mode, you can drop a supported modded SOR2 ROM onto the Character Editor and import Max, Axel, Blaze, Skate, or All Players . The editor creates or updates each skin in the matching classic character folder under Entity Replacements/Classic . Imported skins use the extracted ROM sprites as custom art and leave Use Sprites from empty. ROM import only supports ROM hacks made from the US/western version of Streets of Rage 2. ROM hacks made from the Japanese version, Bare Knuckle 2 , or from more complex ROM hacks such as Streets of Rage 2 Syndicate Wars , are not supported. Reusing Existing Art ¶ Use Use Sprites from only when the replacement should build on another existing entity's art. Typical examples are making an enemy playable or making a playable character into an enemy. This is different from choosing the Classic entity as the logic reference. When a replacement reuses existing art, it must respect the referenced art entity's color palette layout and should work with palettes made for that art entity. Most new skins, sprite imports, and ROM imports should leave Use Sprites from empty. If Use Sprites from is set, an animation can be filled from one of the referenced entity's animations. For Classic Reskins this action copies only the frame/art data. It does not copy hitboxes, body boxes, events, scripts, throw data, or other animation logic, because the reskin keeps Classic reference logic. Keep The Entity Playable ¶ Playable character replacements should keep entityType as Player in logic.json . If a playable character accidentally becomes an enemy or item entity type, the select screen or game start flow may fail. See Entity Types and Behaviour Modes for entity categories and objectMode values. Animation And Hit Timing ¶ When replacing sprites without changing mechanics, keep the original: animation IDs frame count where possible hitbox timing bodybox timing throw offsets reference behaviour If your sprite proportions change, update: pivots in spriteSettings.json body boxes hit boxes throw offsets icon and portrait framing Scripts And Events ¶ A character animation can use logic events and Lua scripts. Events are useful for deterministic frame actions such as sound, velocity, spawns, or animation jumps. Lua scripts are useful when logic needs conditionals, input checks, targeting, or state changes. If an animation defines events, those events override default referenced Classic behaviour for that animation. This prevents unwanted original side effects from running alongside custom event logic. See Lua Scripting and Logic Events . Final Checks ¶ Test every replaced playable character for: select screen icon and portrait standing, walking, jumping, attacking, grabbing, throwing, being hit, death weapon pickup and weapon throw if supported palette choices multiplayer palette uniqueness any custom scripts or spawned items

docs.text: Classic Enemies And Items ¶ Classic enemy and item reskinning uses the same Character Editor workflow as playable characters, but the target folders live under Entity Replacements/Classic for the original enemy or item name. File Location ¶ Editor/<Pack Name>/Entity Replacements/Classic/<Enemy Or Item Name>/ Examples: Entity Replacements/ Classic/ Galsia/ Donovan/ Knife/ Bin/ Enemy Replacements ¶ Enemy replacements should preserve the entity type expected by their original slot: BasicEnemy for simple common enemies where applicable Enemy for full AI enemies and bosses When changing enemy art, test: walking and pathing attack startup and active frames being hit knockdown and recovery death animation spawn introductions boss-specific behavior Enemy AI often relies on behaviour modes, timers, and enemy-specific counters. If you change animation IDs or behaviour modes, use the Behaviour Modes reference. Item Replacements ¶ Items include weapons, containers, scenery, pickups, projectiles, and special objects. Item mode values differ from player and enemy mode values: item mode 0x02 selects the first item controller, so item mode values are offset from the controller index. Test item replacements by spawning or reaching the original object in game: pickup and throw behavior for weapons break behavior for containers collision behavior for obstacles animation and lifetime for projectiles reward behavior for food, money, or 1UP items Shared Sounds And Dependencies ¶ If an enemy or item uses custom sounds, add them to Sounds/ and make sure the entity references the correct pack and sound names. For spawned entities or projectiles, add entity dependencies when required so the packer and runtime can resolve the reference. When To Use Lua ¶ Use Lua when an enemy or item needs behavior beyond frame events: choosing a target switching attacks based on distance spawning projectiles conditionally reacting to the current player changing health, damage, or movement state dynamically See Scripting Examples .

docs.text: Classic Levels ¶ Classic level reskinning replaces the visual art of the original SOR2 levels while keeping their original stage flow, walls, load cues, and gameplay structure. File Locations ¶ Classic reskin level art is saved under: Editor/<Pack Name>/Level Replacements/Classic/ The main files are: File Purpose level <n> - art.json Replacement background art for Classic level <n> . level <n> - cutscenes.json Optional cutscene data for Classic level <n> . presentation.json Optional opening or presentation sequence. title.json Optional title screen replacement. ending.json Optional ending replacement. Image files are placed in: Editor/<Pack Name>/Levels/Art/ What Stays From Classic ¶ In Classic Reskin mode, the original level reference data remains the source for: scene order scroll limits wall boundaries enemy and item spawn data exits and transitions original gameplay timing Your level <n> - art.json replaces the visual background data for matching scenes. If a replacement scene has no replacement art, the runtime can keep using the last valid background or the original reference, depending on context. Scenes And Layers ¶ Each level art file contains a scenes array. Scene indexes correspond to the original Classic reference scenes. Each scene can contain multiple layers. Use layers to separate: far background midground architecture floor or interactable-looking foreground overlays and foreground elements animated effects Common layer fields: Field Use layerName Human-readable label in the editor. parallax How quickly the layer moves relative to the camera. autoScroll Continuous movement for the layer. scrollLoopLimits Looping limits for repeating layers. positionOffset Offset applied to the layer. reactToQuakeEffect Whether the layer reacts to screen shake. zOrder Render ordering. useClassicLayerMotion Opt into Classic motion for the layer's updateType , including original elevator movement. Requires the updated engine. The updated runtime also applies the Classic water shader to updateType: 9 (WaveEffect) and 10 (SmallWaveEffect) in local backgrounds. It keeps the native wave tables and camera ordering, affects static and animated children on each matching layer, and restores normal rendering when entering a dry scene. Images ¶ Each image entry uses: Field Use imageName Filename in Levels/Art . position.x / position.y Placement in scene space. scale Scale multiplier. Negative scale can be used by editor tooling for flips in some contexts. Use pixel-art scales like 1 , 2 , or 0.5 when you want crisp nearest-neighbor rendering. Non-integer scaling can be smoothed by the runtime's art filtering resolver. Animations ¶ Layer animations are stored in animationsDefinition and placed with animations references on layers. Use animations for water, lights, smoke, signs, or other repeated effects. Keep large full-screen videos out of animation frames unless you have tested memory and load times. Palette cycles and Classic motion ¶ Indexed tilemap layers support paletteCycles . In the Level Editor, select the layer to edit the base palette, cycle start slot, colour count, ticks per frame, and each frame's colours. The preview runs the cycles at 60 ticks per second and pauses them with layer animation preview. Colours snap to Genesis channel levels. Enable Classic Motion to reuse the original movement controller selected by Update Type , including the original vertical art offset. Existing custom layers default to their previous movement when this flag is absent. Elevator decorations should be additional images on the elevator layer; duplicating a moving layer can advance the Classic elevator's shared motion state twice. Visual scripts still require an in-game test to preview their game state. Music across scenes ¶ Scenes that resolve to the same music player keep the current playback position when their background art changes. This also applies when different scene music references resolve to one replacement track. Background cleanup preserves the music controller's current player, including paused or pending playback, and keeps a shared preload needed by the next local background. Changing tracks still lets the music controller stop and release the previous player. Testing Levels ¶ For each replaced level: walk from the start to the end verify parallax does not drift away from the playable area check every screen transition check boss arenas and elevator-like scenes test widescreen if hasWideScreen is enabled verify music fields if you changed scene music

docs.text: Ending Cutscenes ¶ Classic reskins can replace the ending presentation with Level Replacements/Classic/ending.json . Create Or Replace The Ending ¶ Open the Level Editor. Choose Classic Reskin . In the cutscene list, add Ending if it does not already exist. Add scenes, layers, images, and animations. Set scene timing with cutsceneEndTimeInSeconds . Test by finishing a run or using the fastest available local route to the ending. File Layout ¶ Editor/<Pack Name>/ Levels/ Art/ ending-bg.png ending-card-1.png Level Replacements/ Classic/ ending.json ending.json uses the same LocalLevelBackgroundData format as title screens, presentation screens, and level cutscenes. Scene Design ¶ An ending can be a single scene or a sequence: single scene: one screen with a long cutsceneEndTimeInSeconds sequence: multiple scenes, each with its own timing and layer composition music-driven ending: set musicPackName and musicName on the first scene If your ending relies on music timing, use music loop metadata carefully. A bad loop point can be more noticeable in a quiet ending than during combat. Practical Limits ¶ Keep ending art easy to load: prefer a few larger background images over dozens of tiny decorative pieces reuse images from Levels/Art when possible avoid very large transparent PNGs when a cropped image would work test with the same display mode you expect players to use Troubleshooting ¶ If the original ending appears instead: confirm the file is Level Replacements/Classic/ending.json confirm the pack is loaded as a Classic reskin or has Classic as a dependency confirm ending.json has a non-empty scenes array confirm each visible scene has at least one layer with art

docs.text: Replace Music ¶ Music replacement for Classic reskins is handled by the Audio Editor in Classic Reskin mode. The replacement map targets Classic music keys and points each key to a track in your pack. Files ¶ Place music files in: Editor/<Pack Name>/Musics/ Place the Classic replacement map at: Editor/<Pack Name>/Audio Replacements/Classic/music-replacements.json Supported editor-facing audio extensions include .wav , .mp3 , and .ogg . Replacement JSON ¶ The music replacement file maps Classic music slots to music references: { "M00": { "packName": "My Reskin", "musicName": "go-straight-remix" }, "M03": { "packName": "My Reskin", "musicName": "bar-theme" } } Use the music base filename without extension. For example, go-straight-remix.ogg is referenced as go-straight-remix . Classic Music Keys ¶ Classic music keys use the M00 , M01 , M02 pattern. The Audio Editor labels these slots with friendly names where known. The JSON key is the stable identifier the runtime reads. If a key is missing from music-replacements.json , Classic uses its original music for that slot. Loop Points ¶ Loop metadata lives next to the music file with the same base name and a .json extension: Musics/go-straight-remix.ogg Musics/go-straight-remix.json The metadata stores loopStartTimeInSeconds and loopEndTimeInSeconds : { "loopStartTimeInSeconds": 12.35, "loopEndTimeInSeconds": 90.0 } Use the Audio Editor's loop-point tools to avoid hand-editing sample-accurate values. If you do edit by hand, use seconds. Testing ¶ Check: title and menu transitions stage start scene transitions where two scenes use the same or different music pause and resume loops after at least one full cycle If music is silent, confirm the replacement packName , base filename, and extension. See Audio Reference .
