docs.text: Replace Sounds ¶ Sound replacement for Classic reskins maps Classic sound keys to sound files in your pack. Use this for hits, voices, jumps, deaths, impacts, and UI-like effects exposed by the Classic sound lists. Files ¶ Place sound files in: Editor/<Pack Name>/Sounds/ Place the Classic replacement map at: Editor/<Pack Name>/Audio Replacements/Classic/sound-replacements.json Replacement JSON ¶ The sound replacement file maps a Classic sound key to a sound reference: { "0": { "packName": "My Reskin", "soundName": "heavy-hit-1" }, "29": { "packName": "My Reskin", "soundName": "axel-attack-3" } } Use the sound base filename without extension. For example, heavy-hit-1.wav is referenced as heavy-hit-1 . Voice And SFX Categories ¶ The Audio Editor separates Classic sound replacement work into voice and SFX views for usability. Both categories write to the same sound-replacements.json file. The category only affects how the editor lists original sounds. Volume And Format ¶ Prepare sounds before importing: trim silence at the start normalize related hit sounds to similar loudness avoid long tails on short combat effects prefer .wav for short SFX when file size is acceptable test voice lines during busy combat, not only in isolation Missing Replacements ¶ If a key is absent from sound-replacements.json , Classic keeps the original sound. This is useful for incremental work: replace a small set, test, then continue. Testing ¶ Test replacements in the context where they play: player attacks enemy deaths throws and knockdowns landing, jumping, and weapon sounds boss attacks pause or menu sounds if replaced If the wrong sound plays, check for duplicate base filenames and confirm you mapped the correct Classic key.

docs.text: Title Screen ¶ Classic title screen replacements are edited in the Level Editor's Classic Reskin mode. The runtime loads the reskin title from: Editor/<Pack Name>/Level Replacements/Classic/title.json Image files referenced by the title JSON live in: Editor/<Pack Name>/Levels/Art/ Create A Title Screen ¶ Open the Level Editor. Drop or select your pack folder. Choose Classic Reskin . In the cutscene list, add Title Screen if it does not exist. Add one or more scenes, layers, and images. Save by changing any property or using the editor save flow. The editor stores title screen images in the same LocalLevelBackgroundData format used by other cutscenes and level art, with one title-specific image type: titleScreenImages . Static Images Vs Title Screen Images ¶ Use staticImages for background pieces that simply render at a position. Use titleScreenImages for animated title elements. These support: Field Purpose initialXPosition Starting X position before the image moves to position.x . lerpSpeed How quickly the image moves from the initial position to the final position. initialDelay Delay before the movement starts. wiggleAmplitude Amount of idle wiggle after the image appears. wiggleFrequency Speed of the idle wiggle. requireCharacterName Only show this image when a matching character is selected. isAICharacter Treat the image as an AI or companion character image. The editor can convert a selected static image to a title screen image when you are editing the title screen. Layering Tips ¶ Use separate layers for: full-screen background art logo and foreground objects moving title elements selectable or character-dependent overlays Set zOrder so foreground artwork renders above background artwork. Keep parallax at 1, 1 for normal screen-space title art unless you intentionally want background movement. Music ¶ Each title scene can set musicPackName and musicName . Use your pack name if the music file lives in your pack's Musics folder. Leave both blank if you want the default title music behavior. If you add custom music, add loop metadata next to the audio file when needed: Musics/title-theme.ogg Musics/title-theme.json See Replace Music and Audio Reference . Common Problems ¶ If the title screen does not appear, confirm: the file is Level Replacements/Classic/title.json referenced image names exist in Levels/Art the pack depends on Classic the scene has at least one layer the layer has at least one staticImages , titleScreenImages , or animation reference

docs.text: Open the Level Editor. Drop or select your pack folder. Choose Classic Reskin . In the cutscene list, add Title Screen if it does not exist. Add one or more scenes, layers, and images. Save by changing any property or using the editor save flow. The editor stores title screen images in the same LocalLevelBackgroundData format used by other cutscenes and level art, with one title-specific image type: titleScreenImages .
docs.title: Create A Title Screen

docs.text: Use staticImages for background pieces that simply render at a position. Use titleScreenImages for animated title elements. These support: Field Purpose initialXPosition Starting X position before the image moves to position.x . lerpSpeed How quickly the image moves from the initial position to the final position. initialDelay Delay before the movement starts. wiggleAmplitude Amount of idle wiggle after the image appears. wiggleFrequency Speed of the idle wiggle. requireCharacterName Only show this image when a matching character is selected. isAICharacter Treat the image as an AI or companion character image. The editor can convert a selected static image to a title screen image when you are editing the title screen.
docs.title: Static Images Vs Title Screen Images

docs.text: Use separate layers for: full-screen background art logo and foreground objects moving title elements selectable or character-dependent overlays Set zOrder so foreground artwork renders above background artwork. Keep parallax at 1, 1 for normal screen-space title art unless you intentionally want background movement.
docs.title: Layering Tips

docs.text: Each title scene can set musicPackName and musicName . Use your pack name if the music file lives in your pack's Musics folder. Leave both blank if you want the default title music behavior. If you add custom music, add loop metadata next to the audio file when needed: Musics/title-theme.ogg Musics/title-theme.json See Replace Music and Audio Reference .
docs.title: Music

docs.text: If the title screen does not appear, confirm: the file is Level Replacements/Classic/title.json referenced image names exist in Levels/Art the pack depends on Classic the scene has at least one layer the layer has at least one staticImages , titleScreenImages , or animation reference
docs.title: Common Problems

docs.text: Classic Reskin Workflow ¶ This workflow assumes you are creating an editor pack under Editor/<Pack Name> and using the three standalone editors: Level Editor, Character Editor, and Audio Editor. 1. Create Or Open A Pack ¶ Create a pack from the mod selector, or copy the Editor/Mod Name template and rename the folder. The folder name becomes the pack name used by scripts, audio replacement JSON, palette paths, and dependencies. A pack created from the mod selector also gets an id , its permanent identity; if you copy a folder, give the copy a new id or remove it (see Mod identity ). For a Classic reskin, config.json should keep Classic as a dependency: { "isChronicle": true, "description": "A Classic visual and audio reskin.", "dependencies": ["Classic"], "dependenciesChecksums": [""], "settings": {} } Most editor-created packs already include a complete settings block. Keep it unless you intentionally want to change lives, difficulty, player count, or game-mode behavior. 2. Decide Which Editor Owns Each Change ¶ Use the Level Editor for screens and level visuals: Level Replacements/Classic/title.json Level Replacements/Classic/presentation.json Level Replacements/Classic/ending.json Level Replacements/Classic/level <n> - art.json Level Replacements/Classic/level <n> - cutscenes.json images in Levels/Art/ Use the Character Editor for entity art and animation data: Entity Replacements/Classic/<Classic Entity>/ replacement sprites, spriteSettings.json , animations.json , logic.json , and dependencies.json Use the Audio Editor for sounds, music, loop points, and Classic replacement maps: Sounds/* Musics/* Musics/<music>.json Audio Replacements/Classic/music-replacements.json Audio Replacements/Classic/sound-replacements.json Use the palette workflow for extra playable-character color choices: Palettes/Classic/<Playable Character>/palette <n>.png 3. Work In Small Passes ¶ The safest rhythm is: Replace one area. Launch the pack in game. Check the log or visible result. Commit or back up the pack folder. Move to the next area. This matters because Classic reskins often reuse original data. A broken filename, missing dependency, or mismatched scene count can make a whole screen fall back to the original or fail to load. 4. Keep Names Stable ¶ The runtime resolves most mod content by folder and base filename: A sound file named kick.wav is referenced as kick . A music file named stage1.ogg is referenced as stage1 . A replacement folder named Axel targets Classic Axel. A palette folder named Axel targets Classic Axel palettes. Avoid renaming pack folders, entity folders, or audio base filenames late in a project. If you do rename them, update JSON references at the same time. 5. Keep Reskin Data In Level Replacements/Classic ¶ Classic reskin level art belongs under Level Replacements/Classic , not next to the normal level files. The normal level files describe custom levels. The replacement files describe visual replacements for the original Classic levels. When the Level Editor opens a pack in Classic Reskin mode, it loads the original SOR2 reference data and saves your replacement art to Level Replacements/Classic . This lets you line up new art against the original while keeping original walls, spawns, and scene flow intact. 6. Test The Actual Target ¶ Preview panels are useful, but the game is the final test. Open the pack in the in-game editor menu and choose Test : the reskin is applied on top of the original content for that session, so you can play it without exporting and without changing your own skin options. Check: title screen transitions character select visibility stage start music scene boundaries and parallax cutscene timing boss or enemy palettes player palette selection audio volume and loop points If something looks correct in an editor but not in game, check the file format reference and troubleshooting .
docs.title: Reskin Workflow

docs.text: Lua Scripting ¶ For scene hooks, rollback-safe game variables, camera overrides, indexed tilemaps and isolated background effects, see Scripted stages . For temporary Lua ownership of simulation and selective actor updates, see Script-owned cinematics . Lua scripting is the modding layer for behaviour that cannot be expressed cleanly with art, palettes, audio replacements, logic events, or animation behaviour alone. Use it for custom movement, conditional attacks, AI decisions, projectiles, parries, recovery states, hit reactions, and global runtime rules. The scripting bridge is intentionally close to the game engine. A script can read and write the same model fields used by the original movement controllers, then either let the original controller continue or stop it and fully own the frame. Where Scripts Live ¶ Put Lua files in your pack's Scripts folder: Editor/<Pack Name>/Scripts/<script name>.lua Scripts are referenced from entity logic.json data. A script for one particular move normally lives inside that animation's script field: { "script": { "packName": "My Pack", "scriptName": "Aerial Control" } } An enemy-wide decision script instead uses the entity-level aiScript field: { "aiScript": { "packName": "My Pack", "scriptName": "Enemy AI" } } The engine uses this AI automatically whenever that entity is spawned as an enemy, including from a level in a custom mod. Nothing needs to be added to the level spawn itself. See Enemy AI for the execution order and examples. Runtime Model ¶ Every script runs as a MoonSharp module and receives a global game object. From there you can reach the current context: game.this_character game.this_player game.this_enemy game.this_item You can also resolve entities by object ID: game.get_player(id) game.get_enemy(id) game.get_character(id) game.get_item(id) game.get_sub_item(id) Objects are layered: Player or Enemy -> Character -> Item -> SubItem The Lua bridge flattens the layers. A player exposes player input fields, character combat fields, item physics fields, and sub-item animation fields on the same object. This means game.this_player.position_x , game.this_player.health , and game.this_player.current_animation_frame all work. Script Structure ¶ A script file is a Lua chunk that returns its update function . The engine runs the chunk once, the first time the script is used, and then calls the returned function on every update: local SPEEDS = {2, 3, 4} -- built once local function chase(enemy, target) -- ... end return function() local enemy = game.this_enemy if enemy == nil then return true end chase(enemy, game.get_player(0)) return false end Everything outside the function ( require calls, constant tables, helper functions) runs once. Everything inside it runs on every call. Every example in these docs uses this shape; a fragment shown on its own is an excerpt from inside an update function. Fetch The Context On Every Call ¶ The same function runs for every entity that uses the script, and game.this_character , game.this_player , game.this_enemy , and game.this_item change from one call to the next. Fetch the context entity inside the function, at the start of every call: return function() local character = game.this_character if character == nil then return true end -- ... return true end Helper functions that need the entity take it as a parameter, like chase above. Alternatively, declare an upvalue before the helpers and assign it first thing in the function: local e -- assigned at the start of every call local function face(target) e.is_facing_right = target.position_x > e.position_x end return function() e = game.this_enemy if e == nil then return true end face(game.get_player(0)) return true end Never read the context at the top level of the chunk: that code runs only once, for whichever entity happened to use the script first. Keep State In Entity And Game Fields ¶ Locals outside the function are shared by every entity that uses the script, and they are not rolled back with the game state. Keep them for constants, lookup tables that are never modified, helper functions, and require d modules. Never store gameplay state there: no counters, timers, flags, or remembered targets. A value that must survive from one call to the next belongs in an entity or game field, such as custom_value_1 on the entity or game.custom_value_1 , which are saved and restored with the game state. Initialise Every Local ¶ In this Lua runtime a bare declaration such as local a, b inside a loop or a function body can keep the value it had on a previous pass instead of starting as nil . Code that then tests only one of the two values can compare a stale number against nil and stop the script with an error. Always give locals an explicit value: local target, distance = nil, nil and check every value a branch uses before using it. The Return Value ¶ The update function's return value matters: return true Continue the normal update path after the script. For an animation script, this lets animation behaviour or the fallback/original controller run after your Lua code. return false Stop the normal update path for this entity on this frame. Use this when the script has already performed movement, collision checks, hit checks, landing logic, or state transitions. Many complex projectile, custom jump, and aerial special scripts return false because they replace the built-in movement controller. If the function exits without returning a boolean, MoonSharp returns nil . In this engine that behaves like false when the C# side reads result.Boolean , so always return true or false deliberately. For an entity-level enemy aiScript , the same values have a narrower meaning: false skips the enemy's native controller for that frame, while true lets it continue. The AI script runs before any script belonging to the current animation. Some hooks read the value differently: a pickup or special-move script accepts with true , a HUD script returns sprite commands, and a visual script returns a table of offsets. Hooks whose return value is ignored say so where they are described. Performance ¶ Scripts can run once per entity per frame, so their cost adds up: Re-running a chunk rebuilds every table and closure it defines. The update-function form builds them once; keep constant tables and helper functions outside the function. Prefer plain arithmetic to bit32 calls when the values are non-negative: each bit32 call is a host call. For example, value / 16 instead of bit32.rshift(value, 4) , and value % 16 instead of bit32.band(value, 15) . Prefer native features to Lua loops over entities. For example, read game.number_of_alive_enemies instead of looping over enemy slots to count them. Every property read, property write and method call on an entity or on game is a host call, and so is every call to a small Lua helper: read a property once into a local when a branch tests it several times, and inline one-line helpers on paths that run for every enemy. game.get_player(id) , game.get_enemy(id) , game.get_item(id) and game.get_entity(id) return the same object for the same slot for as long as game is the same object, whether or not the slot is in use. A script may keep those objects in a table, as long as it starts over when game changes ( if game ~= cached_game then ... end ). Keep only the objects there, never values read from them: those belong to the frame being simulated. Deprecated Form ¶ Older scripts return their result directly from the chunk, so the engine runs the whole chunk, helpers and tables included, on every call. That form still works, but the engine logs a one-time warning for each such script: "Lua script ... returns a result instead of an update function". To convert one, move its constants and helper functions to the top of the file, wrap the rest in return function() ... end , and pass the context entity to any helper that read it as an upvalue. Custom HUD and pickups ¶ Playable entities can also declare playerUpdateScript , run once before their controller in every animation, and specialMoveScript , which owns special admission and entry cost. Both use game.this_player . The update hook's return value is ignored. The special hook must explicitly return true to accept; false or an error rejects the input. It runs after direction/height and move availability checks, replaces the native 8-HP admission rule, and suppresses the later native special health charge. Check eligibility before modifying state. Scripted cancels can call player.try_special_move() to use this same path. Custom move scripts must remove their own fixed health deductions. invincibleOffensiveSpecial: true initializes offensive specials as invulnerable and suppresses native Blaze's later vulnerability window. Custom scripts and events must retain invulnerability through their own timeline and restore it when the move ends. These entity hooks are independent of campaign mechanics selection; their state belongs in rollback-owned fields, never Lua globals. A playable entity can add hudScript at the root of its logic.json : "hudScript": { "packName": "My Pack", "scriptName": "My HUD" } The view calls the script's update function for that player while its health bar is visible. It runs in a separate Lua VM with a copied hud table; there is no mutable game object. Available fields are frame , player_number (1–4), health , lives , score , custom_dec_buffer_14 , custom_bullet_lifetime_dec_buffer_18 , base_x , base_y (the bar's relocated pixel origin), screen_width (320 or 400), and entity_name . weapon_health and weapon_max_health report the held weapon's remaining durability and configured health capacity. Both are zero when no health-based weapon is held. These are read-only snapshot values; displaying them does not initialize or consume durability. The function returns up to 16 sprite commands. Each command names an entity frame from a loaded pack and uses x / y in pixels relative to the bar origin . pack defaults to the player's pack; scale_percent defaults to 100 (normal size). Use an integer percentage such as 50 for half size; gameplay Lua accepts integer literals. return function() if hud.health <= 0 then return {} end return { {entity = 'HUD Art', image = 0, x = 112, y = 8}, {entity = 'HUD Art', image = 1, x = 120, y = 8, scale_percent = 50} } end The art entity uses ordinary Entities/<Name>/ numbered PNGs, pivots, spriteSettings.json , animations.json , and logic.json , so it works in raw and exported packs. The HUD script only draws; keep gameplay counters in the rollback-owned player or game model. Missing art or an invalid command is skipped. The view hides commands when the player bar is hidden, during continue selection, and when the player is gone. An item can add pickupScript at the root of its logic.json : "pickupScript": { "packName": "My Pack", "scriptName": "Collect Token" } When a player attempts to collect it, the gameplay script's update function runs with game.this_player and game.pickup_item set. Check eligibility before changing state . Return true to apply the effect and consume the item. Return false to leave it in the world, including for characters that do not recognize it. Failure also leaves it unconsumed. For example: return function() local player = game.this_player if player == nil or player.packName ~= 'My Pack' then return false end player.customValue1 = player.customValue1 + 1 return true end The pickup must still be a vulnerable, active item with a suitable body box and placement. A custom item with no pickup script and no Classic weapon or goodie identity is ignored. A pickup script on a Classic-derived item replaces that item's usual collection effect. Use the script base name without .lua . Subfolders are supported by the loader, but simple flat script names are easier to maintain. Naming Rules ¶ The C# runtime uses camelCase and PascalCase internally. Lua scripts can usually use: documented snake_case : current_animation_frame exact bridge names: currentAnimationFrame mixed names that camelify cleanly: positionOffset_y MoonSharp resolves a Lua member by trying the exact name, an uppercase-first variant, a camelified variant, and an uppercase-first camelified variant. The docs use snake_case for normal fields because it is the clearest style for Lua. When a script reads or writes object_mode , use the Entity Types and Behaviour Modes reference for the Classic behaviour values. The Character Editor hides the technical numbers in its pickers, but scripts and hand-edited JSON still use the numeric objectMode values. Some low-level fields expose original memory suffixes, such as enemySpecific_C0 or customVelocity_DecBuffer_0_4_X . Those suffixes are part of the C# member name and do not camelify cleanly from plain snake_case. The API reference marks them with their exact bridge spelling; copy those names exactly. Units And Scaling ¶ The engine stores world coordinates, velocities, impulses, and accelerations in raw 16.16 fixed point ( 65536 raw units per pixel). The Lua bridge divides these by 1000 when reading and multiplies by 1000 when writing, so one pixel is approximately 65.536 script units. Camera coordinates are pixels; custom_z_order is raw engine depth. Check each property's units before transferring values between them. For script authors, this means: position_x , position_y , velocity_x , velocity_y , impulse_x , impulse_y , impulse_z , acceleration_x , acceleration_y , and acceleration_z are already in script units. position_offset_y < 0 means the item is above the ground. position_offset_y == 0 means grounded. Animation IDs in Lua are editor-facing IDs. Internally the engine stores them doubled; the bridge handles that conversion. Animation frames are integer frame counters inside the current animation logic entry. Sound pitch is a percentage, so 100 is normal pitch and 80 is lower. Gameplay Lua uses signed 32-bit integer arithmetic. Division truncates toward zero, and multiplication can overflow before a later division reduces the result. For fixed-point scaling, split the quotient and remainder when the intermediate product would exceed the integer range: local function rescale(value, numerator, denominator) local quotient = value / denominator local remainder = value - quotient * denominator return quotient * numerator + remainder * numerator / denominator end Both smaller products must still fit in 32 bits. Derive the remainder as shown; % uses a different convention for negative operands. Avoid dividing away the fraction before multiplying, which loses precision. Available Lua Standard Library ¶ Scripts run in a limited sandbox. The registered modules are basic Lua functions, strings, tables, table iterators, bit32, and load/require support. The math , os , io , coroutine, debug, and JSON modules are not available to gameplay scripts. There is no math table in any script : gameplay, AI, pickup, HUD and level visual scripts alike. math is nil , so math.floor(x) raises "attempt to index a nil value". The error only reaches the game log; in game the script just stops doing its work for that update, which looks like a frozen palette cycle, an idle enemy or a missing HUD element rather than a crash. Numbers are 32-bit integers and / already truncates toward zero, so floor is rarely needed; write the small helpers you need yourself, as below. Write tiny helpers when needed, outside the update function so they are defined once: local function abs(value) if value < 0 then return -value end return value end API Reference ¶ Game Character Player Enemy Item SubItem Start Here ¶ Getting Started Events And Script Timing Object Model Examples Health-based weapons may set weaponHudFallbackDelay in logic.json to a positive number of seconds. This enables held-weapon fallback in the interacted-entity HUD row after that delay; enemy interactions take priority. Zero keeps usage-triggered display. The view reads snapshot state without adding simulation state.

To convert one, move its constants and helper functions to the top of the file, wrap the rest in return function() ... end , and pass the context entity to any helper that read it as an upvalue.

docs.text: Playable entities can also declare playerUpdateScript , run once before their controller in every animation, and specialMoveScript , which owns special admission and entry cost. Both use game.this_player . The update hook's return value is ignored. The special hook must explicitly return true to accept; false or an error rejects the input. It runs after direction/height and move availability checks, replaces the native 8-HP admission rule, and suppresses the later native special health charge. Check eligibility before modifying state. Scripted cancels can call player.try_special_move() to use this same path. Custom move scripts must remove their own fixed health deductions. invincibleOffensiveSpecial: true initializes offensive specials as invulnerable and suppresses native Blaze's later vulnerability window. Custom scripts and events must retain invulnerability through their own timeline and restore it when the move ends. These entity hooks are independent of campaign mechanics selection; their state belongs in rollback-owned fields, never Lua globals. A playable entity can add hudScript at the root of its logic.json : "hudScript": { "packName": "My Pack", "scriptName": "My HUD" } The view calls the script's update function for that player while its health bar is visible. It runs in a separate Lua VM with a copied hud table; there is no mutable game object. Available fields are frame , player_number (1–4), health , lives , score , custom_dec_buffer_14 , custom_bullet_lifetime_dec_buffer_18 , base_x , base_y (the bar's relocated pixel origin), screen_width (320 or 400), and entity_name . weapon_health and weapon_max_health report the held weapon's remaining durability and configured health capacity. Both are zero when no health-based weapon is held. These are read-only snapshot values; displaying them does not initialize or consume durability. The function returns up to 16 sprite commands. Each command names an entity frame from a loaded pack and uses x / y in pixels relative to the bar origin . pack defaults to the player's pack; scale_percent defaults to 100 (normal size). Use an integer percentage such as 50 for half size; gameplay Lua accepts integer literals. return function() if hud.health <= 0 then return {} end return { {entity = 'HUD Art', image = 0, x = 112, y = 8}, {entity = 'HUD Art', image = 1, x = 120, y = 8, scale_percent = 50} } end The art entity uses ordinary Entities/<Name>/ numbered PNGs, pivots, spriteSettings.json , animations.json , and logic.json , so it works in raw and exported packs. The HUD script only draws; keep gameplay counters in the rollback-owned player or game model. Missing art or an invalid command is skipped. The view hides commands when the player bar is hidden, during continue selection, and when the player is gone. An item can add pickupScript at the root of its logic.json : "pickupScript": { "packName": "My Pack", "scriptName": "Collect Token" } When a player attempts to collect it, the gameplay script's update function runs with game.this_player and game.pickup_item set. Check eligibility before changing state . Return true to apply the effect and consume the item. Return false to leave it in the world, including for characters that do not recognize it. Failure also leaves it unconsumed. For example: return function() local player = game.this_player if player == nil or player.packName ~= 'My Pack' then return false end player.customValue1 = player.customValue1 + 1 return true end The pickup must still be a vulnerable, active item with a suitable body box and placement. A custom item with no pickup script and no Classic weapon or goodie identity is ignored. A pickup script on a Classic-derived item replaces that item's usual collection effect. Use the script base name without .lua . Subfolders are supported by the loader, but simple flat script names are easier to maintain.
docs.title: Custom HUD and pickups

docs.text: The C# runtime uses camelCase and PascalCase internally. Lua scripts can usually use: documented snake_case : current_animation_frame exact bridge names: currentAnimationFrame mixed names that camelify cleanly: positionOffset_y MoonSharp resolves a Lua member by trying the exact name, an uppercase-first variant, a camelified variant, and an uppercase-first camelified variant. The docs use snake_case for normal fields because it is the clearest style for Lua. When a script reads or writes object_mode , use the Entity Types and Behaviour Modes reference for the Classic behaviour values. The Character Editor hides the technical numbers in its pickers, but scripts and hand-edited JSON still use the numeric objectMode values. Some low-level fields expose original memory suffixes, such as enemySpecific_C0 or customVelocity_DecBuffer_0_4_X . Those suffixes are part of the C# member name and do not camelify cleanly from plain snake_case. The API reference marks them with their exact bridge spelling; copy those names exactly.
docs.title: Naming Rules

docs.text: The engine stores world coordinates, velocities, impulses, and accelerations in raw 16.16 fixed point ( 65536 raw units per pixel). The Lua bridge divides these by 1000 when reading and multiplies by 1000 when writing, so one pixel is approximately 65.536 script units. Camera coordinates are pixels; custom_z_order is raw engine depth. Check each property's units before transferring values between them. For script authors, this means: position_x , position_y , velocity_x , velocity_y , impulse_x , impulse_y , impulse_z , acceleration_x , acceleration_y , and acceleration_z are already in script units. position_offset_y < 0 means the item is above the ground. position_offset_y == 0 means grounded. Animation IDs in Lua are editor-facing IDs. Internally the engine stores them doubled; the bridge handles that conversion. Animation frames are integer frame counters inside the current animation logic entry. Sound pitch is a percentage, so 100 is normal pitch and 80 is lower. Gameplay Lua uses signed 32-bit integer arithmetic. Division truncates toward zero, and multiplication can overflow before a later division reduces the result. For fixed-point scaling, split the quotient and remainder when the intermediate product would exceed the integer range: local function rescale(value, numerator, denominator) local quotient = value / denominator local remainder = value - quotient * denominator return quotient * numerator + remainder * numerator / denominator end Both smaller products must still fit in 32 bits. Derive the remainder as shown; % uses a different convention for negative operands. Avoid dividing away the fraction before multiplying, which loses precision.
docs.title: Units And Scaling

docs.text: Scripts run in a limited sandbox. The registered modules are basic Lua functions, strings, tables, table iterators, bit32, and load/require support. The math , os , io , coroutine, debug, and JSON modules are not available to gameplay scripts. There is no math table in any script : gameplay, AI, pickup, HUD and level visual scripts alike. math is nil , so math.floor(x) raises "attempt to index a nil value". The error only reaches the game log; in game the script just stops doing its work for that update, which looks like a frozen palette cycle, an idle enemy or a missing HUD element rather than a crash. Numbers are 32-bit integers and / already truncates toward zero, so floor is rarely needed; write the small helpers you need yourself, as below. Write tiny helpers when needed, outside the update function so they are defined once: local function abs(value) if value < 0 then return -value end return value end

This enables held-weapon fallback in the interacted-entity HUD row after that delay; enemy interactions take priority. Zero keeps usage-triggered display. docs.text: Script-owned cinematics ¶ An entity or scene script can temporarily take control of simulation from its update function: local player = game.this_player if game.begin_cinematic(player.pack_name, "Police cinematic REV00", player.object_index, 1800) then return false end The script name has no .lua extension. Use the runtime pack_name of an entity from the target pack; this also works with Editor [draft] pack identities. Acquisition requires an existing player, enemy, or item owner, the InGame scene state, a loadable script, a positive deadline, and no active cinematic. Starting the event stops the remaining normal actor/world update pipeline. Its script begins on the next host frame. While active, the normal scene hook, input processing, Twitch spawns, slow motion, actors, camera, animations, stage effects, and game clock remain suspended. There is no update whitelist or blacklist. The cinematic script's update function runs once per host frame and chooses every update. Select existing enemies using is_enabled / is_alive and the intended entity classification, not is_active . The latter is an item/projectile flag; ordinary enemy spawning leaves it clear. Damage and death handling belong to the selected enemy controller: after queuing a hit, advance that controller and its animation while the event owns simulation. Clearing is_blocking alone does not change which native move controller runs. For an impact that must interrupt the current move, queue its hit fields and use check_being_hit() to consume the shared reaction before selectively advancing the resulting controller. Test blocking, airborne and boss reactions as well as standing enemies. Include enemies with extra health bars in the verification; current health alone does not represent their remaining life. API Behavior game.is_cinematic Whether an event owns simulation. game.cinematic_tick Zero-based host tick, saved in rollback snapshots. game.cinematic_owner_id Owner's object ID; -1 outside a cinematic. game.get_cinematic_value(index) / game.set_cinematic_value(index, value) 32 event-local integers, indexed 0..31 . The optional presentation API reserves 29..31 when used. Values reset per event and do not overwrite scene custom values. game.update_entity_controller(id) Advance one player, enemy, or item through its full controller, including its usual physics/position resolution and pack scripts. Does not advance animation. game.update_entity_animation(id) Advance only that object's normal animation/hit-pause logic. Also supports render-only subitems. game.is_cinematic_actor(id) Whether the event owns this helper slot. Select event helpers by ownership rather than matching their type to the owner. game.schedule_cinematic_quake(amplitude_pixels, duration_frames) Schedule an exact alternating background-plane quake for this event. Amplitude is 1..8 pixels and duration is 1..600 display frames; invalid values and calls outside a cinematic are ignored. The event passes through the rollback-aware visual effect queue. game.get_entity(id) Resolve a player, enemy, item, or subitem with its actual Lua wrapper; invalid IDs return nil . game.first_item_id , game.item_capacity Item slot range. game.first_sub_item_id , game.sub_item_capacity Render-only subitem slot range. helper.initialize(pack_name, entity_name, animation_id, mode) Initialize a free item/subitem returned by a free-slot lookup; default mode is 2 . Retains the slot's object ID and resets previous data. game.end_cinematic(keep_camera) Release control, restore the camera state from acquisition (unless keep_camera is true: the camera stays where the script moved it, for a walk into the next room), and remove helpers initialized during this event. For gravity without AI, adjust the actor's height/impulse fields directly, then resolve any required world collision through update_position_and_check_world_collisions . Do not also call the full controller unless a second physics step is intended. Render-only subitems have no built-in controller; a cinematic can execute its own Lua actor routine and selectively call the animation update. Nested actor scripts temporarily change game.this_player , game.this_enemy , or game.this_item . The selective controller API restores the cinematic's context afterward. Cinematic scripts themselves have no implicit current entity; resolve the owner by ID. Re-entering an actor's controller recursively returns false . The deadline, script failure, owner removal/identity change, and scene/level change also release control. No normal simulation update runs on that release frame. The cleanup list records created helper ownership only ; it never determines which actors update. Existing actors and scene custom values remain pack-owned. Keep all mutable state in cinematic values or actor model fields. Lua VM globals, module caches, and retained mutable upvalues are not rollback state. The update function's return value does not end the event; call end_cinematic explicitly. Cinematic state is included in GameModel copying, raw session serialization, and the session checksum. During a cinematic the checksum also includes helper and actor custom state used by selective simulation. Stage presentation without gameplay transitions ¶ A cinematic can temporarily display other stage art without changing the live fight's level, wave, loadcues, music or actor state. Do not use change_scene for this: a gameplay scene change ends the cinematic and reinitializes the scene. API Behavior game.get_scene_camera_path(level_id, scene_id) Read-only stage-wave geometry, or nil for invalid IDs. Coordinates are viewport pixels, positive right/down. game.get_previous_presentation(level_id, scene_id) Previous wave's geometry; at level start, previous playable level's final valid wave; nil if absent. game.get_previous_known_presentation(level_id, scene_id) Most recent earlier wave with known directional scroll geometry, scanning earlier scenes/levels and skipping unknown routes; nil if none. game.set_cinematic_presentation(level_id, scene_id) Select resolved replacement/inherited art for valid loaded stage IDs. Returns false outside a cinematic or for invalid IDs. It does not change gameplay scene IDs. game.set_cinematic_dark_presentation() Hide stage art and use a black backdrop. Clear the global cinematic fade to show owned helpers against that backdrop. Existing entities are masked separately. game.restore_cinematic_presentation() Select the presentation captured at acquisition. game.cinematic_fade Read/write integer 0..1000, clear to black. Snapshot-driven; the script owns fade timing. game.cinematic_hide_existing_entities Read/write view mask for existing actors, bodies, shadows and effects. Cinematic-owned helpers remain visible. Original actor rendering flags are preserved. Camera-path records expose level_id , scene_id , start_x , start_y , end_x , end_y , min_x , max_x , min_y , max_y , has_diagonal , diagonal_x , diagonal_y , previous_level_id , previous_scene_id , contiguous_previous , scripted , scroll_direction (+1 right, -1 left, 0 unknown), is_known_directional , has_authored_route , route_actor_y (the route's actorY , 0 when unset), playable_width , floor_far_y and floor_near_y . The floor values describe the entry viewport; its near edge at another camera Y is camera_y + 216 . path.floor_far_at(world_x) also accounts for the native sloped wall segment and post-segment horizon at that world X. Vertical blockers, custom polygons and pits are separate collision geometry: path.is_ground_obstructed(x, y, margin) is true when world point (x, y), in pixels, is inside or within margin pixels of one of the wave's Wall , Pit or Custom2 custom wall shapes (the same test that keeps native jump-in respawns off holes). Use it to stage helpers on solid ground, for example by sampling a car's path across the view and moving its depth until clear. When the shown scene's route sets actorY , use camera_y + path.route_actor_y instead: the Streets of Rage 1 police car keeps the original's fixed line there (round 7), whatever the caller's depth. diagonal_x retains the native signed threshold, not a positive viewport coordinate. path.sample_y(x) returns unobstructed one-pixel native forward geometry. Player positioning can delay actual camera Y, and scripted stages can follow arbitrary paths; anchor a retreat to the actual acquired camera and do not infer a scripted route from the native fields. Optional scene cinematicCameraRoute declares absolute start/end viewport pixels for a known scripted direction; sample_y then samples its bounded linear Y instead of the native diagonal gate. Use playable_width for placement in the displayed level, whose rendering scale can differ from that of the live fight. A fixed-camera wave (an elevator) can declare a cinematicCameraRoute too, over art drawn beside its room, so a retreat has somewhere to go; a round-clear scene that keeps its last wave's art should repeat that wave's route. When a cinematic has no room in the current wave and must borrow other art, walk back with get_previous_presentation while each previous wave shares the current art ( contiguous_previous ) and has no known route, and take the first wave with other art (the previous background or level, even a fixed-camera one, whose end_x is where its camera stopped). The Streets of Rage 1 police call does this. Because an authored route gives absolute camera positions, a camera that is off it (an elevator high above the street it starts from: its route lies at the street's camera Y) should first move onto it vertically and come back the same way: the Streets of Rage 1 police call scrolls down, then along the route, and back along it, then up. A route's actorY also places lanes that depend on the depth below the caller's camera (the police fire). Staging actors on walls: when no line across the shown view is clear of walls, rails and pits (a wave walled in, like an elevator), place the actor already inside, on ground clear under its whole length (and a band in front of it), instead of driving it in; and let effects that land on the ground (the police fire and rain) land only on walkable ground, falling on through a pit otherwise. An unhooked stationary final combat wave can retain the direction of its contiguous native scene while keeping its actual zero-span bounds. Exit barriers, script hooks and fixed-room/elevator cameras stop that inheritance. The presentation API reuses cinematic values 29..31 rather than adding game or character state fields. Once used, keep script-owned values in 0..28 . Helpers still use ordinary actor custom fields. IDs, fade and visibility therefore copy, serialize and hash through the existing cinematic state. Cleanup also restores presentation when the owner disappears, the deadline expires or Lua fails. Encoded zero IDs in values 29 and 30 select the dark backdrop; use the named API rather than writing this encoding yourself. It remains distinct from a full-screen fade, which also covers cinematic helpers. Switch distant scenes while fully dark. Their render camera snaps under black, then follows the ordinary scripted-camera interpolation. Resource preparation does not unload music or change the currently displayed palette. Readiness stays local to the view: it holds black until requested art is loaded and never becomes a Lua simulation branch. Preserved native fade callbacks resume after cinematic control is released.

docs.text: Events And Script Timing ¶ Scripts run as part of entity movement logic. They are most commonly attached to an animation in logic.json , next to duration, hitboxes, body boxes, throw logic, logic events, and animation behaviour. Animation Update Order ¶ For local player, enemy, and item controllers, the important order is: Pack-level pre-entity scripts run. Logic events on the current animation run. If the animation has events, default physics may run before Lua. For a local custom enemy, its entity-level aiScript runs. If the AI script returns false , the entity update stops for this frame. The current animation's script runs. If the animation script returns false , the entity update stops for this frame. If it returns true , animation behaviour can run. If no animation behaviour handles the move, fallback/original behaviour can run. Pack-level post-entity scripts run. Later in the frame, animation frame counters advance. This order is why frame checks work: current_animation_frame == 0 is visible to the script before the animation system increments it. Events Vs Scripts Vs Animation Behaviour ¶ Use logic events for deterministic frame-bound actions: play a sound at frame 4 set velocity at frame 7 spawn an item at frame 12 jump to another animation on landing enable or disable invincibility Use Lua when the action needs state: choose an animation based on distance or input detect a parry window by predicting incoming hits alter damage only while blocking run custom projectile physics use custom values as per-entity timers stop the reference controller for only some frames Use animation behaviour when you want the original Classic controller to keep driving the move after your custom events or script. If a script needs to inspect or assign object_mode , look up the technical values in Entity Types and Behaviour Modes . Use an entity-level enemy aiScript when a decision must apply across several animations or states—for example choosing targets while standing, continuing a retreat while walking, and selecting an attack after lining up. This avoids copying the same decision script into every animation. Keep move-specific effects in animation scripts. Entity-Level Enemy AI ¶ Add aiScript beside animationsLogic in the enemy's logic.json : "aiScript": { "packName": "My Pack", "scriptName": "Enemy AI" } It receives the normal game bridge, and game.this_enemy identifies the enemy whose update is running. The hook belongs to the entity, not to a level: every instance spawned from that custom entity uses the script automatically. return true augments the existing AI by allowing the native controller to continue. return false replaces it for the current frame. A replacement script must perform any required hit, movement, collision, landing, and state-transition work that the skipped native controller would otherwise have done. Return Values In Animation Scripts ¶ return true from the update function says "I changed some state, now continue the normal update path." Typical uses, inside the update function: -- Set a parameter used by a shared air-control script, -- then let the original jump controller continue. game.this_character.custom_value_1 = 2 return true return false says "Lua owns this frame." Typical uses, inside the update function: -- Run custom projectile movement and stop the fallback item controller. item.check_projectile_hits() item.velocity_x = item.velocity_x + item.impulse_x item.update_position_and_check_world_collisions() return false Returning false is powerful, but it also means you are responsible for whatever the skipped controller would have done: hit checks, hit pause, movement, acceleration, landing, world collision, animation changes, and cleanup. Script Frequency ¶ An animation script's update function is called on every update while the animation is active. Write it so it is safe to run more than once. Use frame checks for one-time actions: return function() local character = game.this_character if character ~= nil and character.current_animation_frame == 12 then -- Offsets and velocity are relative to facing direction inside TrySpawnItem. character.try_spawn_item("My Pack", "Fireball", 0, -1, 12, 0, 520, 0) end return true end Use custom values for persistent per-object state: return function() local item = game.this_item if item == nil then return true end if item.custom_value_1 == 0 then item.custom_value_1 = 1 item.play_sound("My Pack", "spawn", 0) end return true end Pack-Level Scripts ¶ config.json can define preEntityUpdateScripts and postEntityUpdateScripts . These run for each active player, enemy, and item around the entity's normal update. Pre-entity scripts can cancel the entity update by returning false . In that case the movement controller and the post-entity scripts for that entity are skipped. Post-entity scripts run after the entity update, but their return value is accumulated only for the script array and does not re-run the skipped controller. Pack-level hooks are useful for broad mechanics such as global input rules, challenge mutators, or passive status effects. Keep them cheap: they can execute once per active entity per frame (see Performance ). Animation Advancement ¶ Animation frames are advanced by AllEntitiesAnimationsController after movement logic. When an animation changes, set_animation(id, start_frame) sets next_animation_id and next_animation_frame ; the animation controller later copies those into current_animation_id and current_animation_frame . This means a script can call set_animation(10, 4) and still see the old current_animation_id until the animation step applies the queued change. Use return false after a decisive state change when you need to prevent the old controller from acting on the old animation for the rest of the frame. Hit Pause ¶ Characters and items have hit_pause_timer and custom_hit_pause_delay_frames . Default physics decrements hit pause and returns early. If Lua replaces physics with return false , you must decrement or honor hit pause yourself, early in the update function: if character.hit_pause_timer > 0 then character.hit_pause_timer = character.hit_pause_timer - 1 return false end Event Override Detail ¶ If an animation defines logic events, those events can change how much of the original behaviour runs. The local controllers treat event-driven moves as custom logic and may run default physics before Lua. This prevents original behaviour-mode side effects from blindly running after custom events. Scripts can still run on animations that also have events. Be deliberate: events set fixed state at exact frames Lua branches on live state animation behaviour provides inherited controller logic
docs.title: Script Events and Entry Points

docs.text: Scripts run as part of entity movement logic. They are most commonly attached to an animation in logic.json , next to duration, hitboxes, body boxes, throw logic, logic events, and animation behaviour.
docs.title: Events And Script Timing

docs.text: For local player, enemy, and item controllers, the important order is: Pack-level pre-entity scripts run. Logic events on the current animation run. If the animation has events, default physics may run before Lua. For a local custom enemy, its entity-level aiScript runs. If the AI script returns false , the entity update stops for this frame. The current animation's script runs. If the animation script returns false , the entity update stops for this frame. If it returns true , animation behaviour can run. If no animation behaviour handles the move, fallback/original behaviour can run. Pack-level post-entity scripts run. Later in the frame, animation frame counters advance. This order is why frame checks work: current_animation_frame == 0 is visible to the script before the animation system increments it.
docs.title: Animation Update Order

docs.text: Use logic events for deterministic frame-bound actions: play a sound at frame 4 set velocity at frame 7 spawn an item at frame 12 jump to another animation on landing enable or disable invincibility Use Lua when the action needs state: choose an animation based on distance or input detect a parry window by predicting incoming hits alter damage only while blocking run custom projectile physics use custom values as per-entity timers stop the reference controller for only some frames Use animation behaviour when you want the original Classic controller to keep driving the move after your custom events or script. If a script needs to inspect or assign object_mode , look up the technical values in Entity Types and Behaviour Modes . Use an entity-level enemy aiScript when a decision must apply across several animations or states—for example choosing targets while standing, continuing a retreat while walking, and selecting an attack after lining up. This avoids copying the same decision script into every animation. Keep move-specific effects in animation scripts.
docs.title: Events Vs Scripts Vs Animation Behaviour

docs.text: Add aiScript beside animationsLogic in the enemy's logic.json : "aiScript": { "packName": "My Pack", "scriptName": "Enemy AI" } It receives the normal game bridge, and game.this_enemy identifies the enemy whose update is running. The hook belongs to the entity, not to a level: every instance spawned from that custom entity uses the script automatically. return true augments the existing AI by allowing the native controller to continue. return false replaces it for the current frame. A replacement script must perform any required hit, movement, collision, landing, and state-transition work that the skipped native controller would otherwise have done.

docs.text: Scripting Examples ¶ This section is a cookbook, not a minimal tutorial. The examples are adapted from the Test chronicle sandbox and rewritten with neutral names, safer guards, and comments that explain why each engine field is touched. Use these pages by intent: Goal Page Air control, run/walk speed tiers, wall jumps, rolling movement, charge movement Movement And Input Spawn projectiles, move projectiles, persistent hitboxes, stationary effects, projectile bursts Projectiles And Items Blocks, parries, break specials, weapon-specific move overrides, hit-pause reactions Combat And Defense Front grabs, grab walking, air grabs, piledriver-style throws, victim positioning Grabs And Throws Pack-level pre/post update scripts, wall bounce, juggle/multi-hit rules, recovery escape Global Update Hooks Entity-level enemy behaviour, targeting, distance gates, hook/fall setup, scripted attack selection Enemy AI How To Read These Examples ¶ Every example has three jobs: show a complete script, returning its update function, that can be attached to an animation, an enemy entity, or a global hook explain the internal engine state that makes the script work show when to return true and when to return false The numbers are intentionally visible. Animation IDs, frame numbers, offsets, velocities, and object_mode values are part of scripting. Change them to match your own character's animations and sprite alignment. For Classic behaviour values, use Entity Types and Behaviour Modes . Common Adaptation Rules ¶ Replace pack names, entity names, sound names, and animation IDs with your own data. Keep the nil guards unless the script is absolutely guaranteed to run in one context. If the script calls check_hitting_entities , moves position_offset_y , or calls update_position_and_check_world_collisions , it probably owns that frame and should return false . If the script only sets a parameter, spawns once on a frame, or nudges input state before animation behaviour, it can usually return true . Use custom_value_1 through custom_value_10 for per-object script state, not Lua locals, when the value must survive across frames. Locals outside the update function are shared by every object using the script and are not rolled back. Avoid math.* ; the gameplay sandbox does not register the Lua math module. Example Style ¶ The examples prefer documented snake_case names: character.current_animation_frame character.position_offset_y character.hit_pause_timer The runtime also accepts exact bridge names such as currentAnimationFrame , but mixing styles makes scripts harder to review.
docs.title: Cookbook Overview

docs.text: Getting Started With Lua ¶ A Lua script is a text file with the .lua extension. The game loads it from a mod pack when an animation, entity, or pack-level update hook references it. Minimal Script ¶ A script returns its update function . The game runs the file once, then calls that function on every update; the function's return value tells the engine what to do next. See Script Structure . return function() local character = game.this_character -- The same script can be accidentally attached to an item or global hook. -- Guarding the context keeps the script safe. if character == nil then return true end -- This field is set by the combat controller after hitbox collision checks. -- If the original controller has not run yet this frame, it may still reflect -- the previous frame, so use it for reactions, not for guaranteed startup. if character.is_hitting_someone then character.play_sound("My Pack", "impact-heavy", 1) end -- true means "continue with animation behaviour or original controller". return true end Add The Script To A Pack ¶ Create the script: Editor/<Pack Name>/Scripts/Impact Sound.lua Open the entity in the Character Editor. Select the animation that should run the script. Assign the script in the animation logic. Test the animation in game. The saved logic.json entry looks like: { "script": { "packName": "My Pack", "scriptName": "Impact Sound" } } The game Global ¶ The game object is the entry point for the current update. Read the context objects from it inside the update function, on every call: local character = game.this_character local player = game.this_player local enemy = game.this_enemy local item = game.this_item Only some of these are valid in a given context: Context Valid objects Player animation script this_player , this_character Enemy animation script this_enemy , this_character Item animation script this_item Pack-level player hook this_player , this_character Pack-level enemy hook this_enemy , this_character Pack-level item hook this_item Always check context-specific objects for nil before using them. First Safe Reads ¶ Start with scripts that read state and call one helper: return function() local player = game.this_player if player == nil then return true end -- pressed_button_b is true only on the frame the attack button was pressed. if player.pressed_button_b then player.play_sound("My Pack", "debug-click", 0) end return true end First Safe Writes ¶ Then move to state changes. Frame 0 is useful for one-time setup because the animation frame is advanced later by the animation controller. return function() local character = game.this_character if character == nil then return true end if character.current_animation_frame == 0 then -- Stop inherited horizontal motion at the start of this animation. character.velocity_x = 0 character.impulse_x = 0 end return true end Replacing The Controller ¶ If your script performs its own physics, collisions, and hit checks, return false . return function() local item = game.this_item if item == nil then return true end -- Item projectiles normally need manual movement when Lua owns the frame. local should_destroy = item.check_projectile_hits() item.velocity_x = item.velocity_x + item.impulse_x item.velocity_y = item.velocity_y + item.impulse_z item.inner_timer = item.inner_timer - 1 if item.inner_timer <= 0 then should_destroy = true end if item.update_position_and_check_world_collisions() then item.play_sound("Classic", "SE10", 0) should_destroy = true end if should_destroy then item.set_animation(48) item.is_active = false end -- false stops fallback item physics so the projectile is not moved twice. return false end Debugging ¶ Use print() for temporary logs: the text goes to the game log ( Player.log , or the Unity console in the editor) with a [Lua] prefix, and while debug is enabled (as when testing a pack from the editor) it is also shown on screen, at most one message per second, so a print every frame does not flood the screen. Script errors are reported through the game's error display and log, with the script name and line; this includes runtime errors in background visual scripts and HUD scripts, which stop running after their first error. If a script appears to do nothing: check the filename and scriptName check that scriptName omits .lua check the pack name exactly confirm the animation actually reaches the scripted frame confirm the entity is the expected type guard against nil context objects return the update function from the script, and an explicit boolean from that function avoid math.* , os.* , and io.* , which are not registered in the gameplay sandbox look for a "script exceeded instruction budget" error: the script ran a loop that does not end (see below) Lua Pitfalls ¶ No math module ¶ The game's Lua uses 32-bit integers and ships no math module in any script VM: gameplay, background visual ( visualScript ) and HUD scripts alike. math is nil , so math.floor(x) fails with "attempt to index a nil value". Division already truncates toward zero, so a / b is the integer result; write small helpers for the rest: local function abs(x) if x < 0 then return -x end return x end local function min(a, b) if a < b then return a end return b end local function max(a, b) if a > b then return a end return b end For random numbers in gameplay scripts use game.random(range) , which is replay and netplay safe. Every call has an instruction budget ¶ Each call into a script (its update function, a hook, a HUD or background visual script) may run at most 10 million Lua instructions, counting everything it calls. That is far more than a normal update needs (shipped scripts use tens of thousands), so only a loop that never ends reaches it: while true do end , a repeat whose condition never becomes true, or a for loop whose bounds come from a broken value. The call then stops with a "script exceeded instruction budget" error, shown on screen with the script line. The game stays responsive, but whatever the script changed before it was stopped stays changed. A gameplay script that exceeds the budget is disabled for the rest of the run, so its entity or stage carries on without it; a HUD or background visual script stops, as after any other error. Fix the loop and start a new run. Waiting for something across frames belongs in entity or game fields checked once per update, never in a loop inside one update. Initialise every local ¶ A local declared without a value, especially several at once ( local a, b ), has been seen to keep a value from an earlier pass of the same loop or update in this Lua build, instead of starting as nil . Code that then tests only one of them reads a stale value. Always give locals an explicit value, and check every value a branch uses: -- risky: j and p may not start as nil local j, p -- safe local j, p = nil, nil if k ~= nil then j, p = find_slot(k) end if j ~= nil and p ~= nil then -- use j and p end Loading other files ¶ require("Pack/module") loads Scripts/module.lua from that pack (a name without a pack prefix uses the script's own pack). dofile and loadfile take a "Pack/path/file.lua" path. Paths must stay inside the pack: .. , absolute paths, drive letters and \ separators are refused, and only .lua files can be loaded. See Troubleshooting .
docs.title: Getting Started

docs.text: Object Model ¶ The Lua API mirrors the runtime model used by Streets of Rage 2 New Era. Understanding the layers is the fastest way to write scripts that work with the original engine instead of fighting it. Containment ¶ Player contains Character contains Item contains SubItem Enemy contains Character contains Item contains SubItem Standalone Item contains SubItem Standalone SubItem What Each Layer Owns ¶ Layer Owns Examples SubItem Visual identity, animation, palette, facing, object mode, script custom values current_animation_id , current_animation_frame , object_mode , is_facing_right , custom_value_1 Item Physical state, world position, velocity, impulses, collision, active flags, projectile fields position_x , position_offset_y , impulse_x , is_active , is_vulnerable , hit_pause_timer Character Combat state, health, score, victims, attackers, grabs, combo state, sounds health , damage_taken , victim , attacker , check_being_hit() Player Human input, pressed/held buttons, combo checks, player timers pressed_forward , is_holding_button_b , has_input_combo() Enemy AI mode, target selection fields, aggressiveness, enemy-specific counters mode , mode_timer , homing_target_id , enemy_agressiveness For Classic object_mode values, see Entity Types and Behaviour Modes . Those tables list the descriptive behaviour names together with their hex and decimal values. Flattening ¶ The bridge exposes lower-layer properties directly on higher-layer objects. Inside an update function: local player = game.this_player player.position_x = 5000 player.health = player.health - 10 player.current_animation_frame = 0 That is equivalent to walking down the internal chain from player to character to item to sub-item, but it is shorter and less error-prone. The same is true for enemies. Standalone items expose item and sub-item fields, but not character or player fields. IDs And Objects ¶ The engine tracks active entities by global object IDs. Some fields expose IDs; other properties resolve the ID into an object for you. local character = game.this_character local attacker = character.attacker if attacker ~= nil then attacker.health = attacker.health - 5 end Manual resolution is also available: local attacker_id = character.attacker_character_id if attacker_id >= 0 then local attacker = game.get_character(attacker_id) if attacker ~= nil then attacker.health = attacker.health - 5 end end Use object shortcuts for readability. Store IDs in custom_value_* fields when you need a reference to survive across frames, then resolve the ID again when you need the object. Object ID Ranges ¶ The global order is: players enemies items sub-items Do not hard-code exact ranges. The game has 4 player slots, 20 enemy slots, 20 item slots, and 40 sub-item slots in the current bridge, but scripts should use game.get_* , game.get_free_* , and object properties instead of numeric range checks. Facing Direction ¶ is_facing_right is the visual and gameplay facing flag. direction_signal is derived from it: 1 when facing right -1 when facing left Most custom horizontal movement should multiply by direction_signal when the move is meant to go forward: character.velocity_x = character.velocity_x + character.impulse_x * character.direction_signal For absolute left/right air control, write impulse_x directly as positive or negative and let facing change separately. Ground And Air State ¶ is_in_the_air is derived from position_offset_y < 0 . The engine uses negative vertical offsets for airborne objects and 0 for grounded objects. Typical manual air movement: if character.position_offset_y < 0 or character.impulse_y < 0 then character.position_offset_y = character.position_offset_y + character.impulse_y character.impulse_y = character.impulse_y + 32 if character.position_offset_y >= 0 then character.position_offset_y = 0 end end impulse_y controls vertical height. impulse_z contributes to velocity_y , which is depth movement on the belt-scroller plane. Animation IDs And Frames ¶ Lua uses editor-facing animation IDs. The engine internally stores currentAnimationId and nextAnimationId doubled. The bridge converts automatically: character.set_animation(4) -- editor animation 4 Setting current_animation_id directly changes the current internal animation ID while preserving the low internal bit. Prefer set_animation(id, start_frame) for normal state transitions because it also queues the starting frame. current_animation_frame is the current animation logic frame. It is not the sprite frame index. The animation controller increments it after movement scripts run. Custom Values ¶ custom_value_1 through custom_value_10 live on the sub-item layer, so they are available on players, enemies, characters, items, and sub-items. They are ideal for per-entity script state: one-shot flags cooldowns mode selectors stored object IDs temporary speed tiers They persist while the object slot is alive. Clear them when reusing an object slot or when changing to a state that should not inherit old script state. Nil Safety ¶ Always check objects that might not exist, starting with the context object at the top of the update function: local enemy = game.this_enemy if enemy == nil then return true end local target = enemy.get_nearest_opponent(true, true, true) if target == nil then return true end game.get_player(-1) , game.get_enemy(-1) , game.get_item(-1) , and game.get_sub_item(-1) return nil . Passing a positive ID to the wrong lookup can throw an error, so use game.get_character(id) for attacker/victim IDs unless you know the target type.

docs.text: The bridge exposes lower-layer properties directly on higher-layer objects. Inside an update function: local player = game.this_player player.position_x = 5000 player.health = player.health - 10 player.current_animation_frame = 0 That is equivalent to walking down the internal chain from player to character to item to sub-item, but it is shorter and less error-prone. The same is true for enemies. Standalone items expose item and sub-item fields, but not character or player fields.
docs.title: Flattening

docs.text: The engine tracks active entities by global object IDs. Some fields expose IDs; other properties resolve the ID into an object for you. local character = game.this_character local attacker = character.attacker if attacker ~= nil then attacker.health = attacker.health - 5 end Manual resolution is also available: local attacker_id = character.attacker_character_id if attacker_id >= 0 then local attacker = game.get_character(attacker_id) if attacker ~= nil then attacker.health = attacker.health - 5 end end Use object shortcuts for readability. Store IDs in custom_value_* fields when you need a reference to survive across frames, then resolve the ID again when you need the object.
docs.title: IDs And Objects

docs.text: The global order is: players enemies items sub-items Do not hard-code exact ranges. The game has 4 player slots, 20 enemy slots, 20 item slots, and 40 sub-item slots in the current bridge, but scripts should use game.get_* , game.get_free_* , and object properties instead of numeric range checks.
